CHAPTER 3

MedChemInformatics: An Introduction to Machine Learning for Drug Discovery

MATTHEW G. ROBERTS AND RAE LAWRENCE[\*](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#affa)

Cancer Research UK – Manchester Institute, Drug Discovery Unit, Alderley Park, Macclesfield SK10 4TG, UK

\*Email: [Rae.Lawrence@cruk.manchester.ac.uk](mailto:Rae.Lawrence@cruk.manchester.ac.uk)

## 3.1 Introduction

Before delving into the mysteries of Machine Learning, it is appropriate to categorically state that every discussion of computational results should be prefaced with statements like “the model *suggests…*” and “the models are lies, but they can be useful.” In generating models, we generate ideas – lots and lots of ideas. We fully recognise that most of those ideas are less than stellar; but in the muck of weak ideas, there are flecks of gold that can be panned out. And the harsh reality is that in order to establish whether an idea is gold or silt, we need to nicely ask our wet chemistry colleagues to go into a laboratory and do real work. With those newly minted real-life results, our models can be iteratively improved and evolve so that they can start approaching the truth.

### 3.1.1 Artificial Intelligence *vs.* Machine Learning

In recent years, a prevailing theme across multiple areas of research (from marketing, to economics, to drug discovery) has been Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning. There is not a clear delineation of what these terms mean, and how they are related to, and differ from each other.

***Artificial Intelligence***

In the most basic of terms, Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to a machine/computer that has been programmed to do things that humans can presently do but better; further, AI algorithms can also be taught to do things that humans can not do using only their brains – for example, separating signals from noise. Systems incorporating AI use massive amounts of data with the goal being that knowledge of data and previous decisions will allow an algorithm to successfully solve new problems using complex problem-solving skills, as a human would. A good example of this approach is using AI algorithms to have computers beat chess masters – or more recently, the application of AI technology by Google's DeepMind to solve problems like protein folding,^([1](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit1)) to analyse diagnostic imaging results^([2](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit2)) or to play Alpha Go.^([3](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit3))

For an example relevant to medicinal chemistry, let's consider having a system incorporate and learn every reported chemical reaction, and ask the algorithm to devise efficient synthetic routes (with high yields) for new chemical entities. Can this be done today? It turns out that it can be done to some degree.^([4](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit4))

Can AI be used to condense all of the available protein, ligand, activity, selectivity, physicochemical properties, literature information, *etc.*, and suggest a clinical candidate? This is the million pound question. There are a number of dedicated companies working in this space, including BenevolentAI, GTN Ltd., and Exscientia, all of which have had initial technical successes and have secured investor capital^([5](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit5)) and pharmaceutical industry collaboration^([6](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit6)) to continue their efforts to perfect their AI approaches to accelerate development cycles, reduce spending, and produce effective drugs.

As of this writing, AI approaches have not been made routine, reduced to practice, or deployed as box-ware. However, we believe that it is only a matter of time before currently highly customised solutions are made generic and become widely available. Given the amount of time and money being invested, it is anticipated that success will come sooner rather than later.

***Machine Learning***

By contrast, Machine Learning (ML) is a sub-discipline of AI, but the approach focuses on modelling data and being able to extract knowledge. AI works in much the same way; however, many people now interpret AI as a synonym for Deep Learning methods, where the data are modelled in increasing layers of complexity.

In ML, the extracted knowledge is tested (in real life), results are fed back into the machine, and the model(s) are refined. For example, data can be mined to uncover the knowledge that active compounds have a particular combination of structural features. When a new compound that has a similar combination of features is encountered, it may be flagged as potentially active, followed by submission to the design-make-test-refine modelling cycle (see [Figure 3.1](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig1)), which incorporates real-life data into the model during iterative refinement.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f1.jpg)

Figure 3.1 The Design-Make-Test-Refine modelling cycle illustrates how modelling *via* Machine Learning relates to medicinal chemistry discovery.

This iterative, cyclic process is how the learning in ML takes place. Machines are slower than humans to learn – they need more examples, but they are faster at predicting results once they have learned.

Computational chemists have been using ML to successfully model data for a very long time: Hansch called it QSAR (Quantitative Structure–Activity Relationship) in his seminal paper in 1962,^([7](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit7)) where plant growth regulators were linked to Hammett parameters and hydrophobicity using multivariate regression. Hansch described the serendipitous birth of QSAR in his republished^([7](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit7)) piece in the issue of the Journal of Chemical Information and Modelling that celebrated his life and contributions to science. Shortly after came the publication of the Free-Wilson analysis,^([8](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit8)) which is still used today (with improvements, of course).

You may have just realised that you are already familiar with some ML approaches in medicinal chemistry!

### 3.1.2 Supervised *vs.* Unsupervised Learning

Machine Learning methods that employ “supervised learning” work with data that includes an observable (*e.g.*, potency or activity) and relate a set of features (descriptors, fingerprints) to the observable. Supervised learning methods use collections of features to generate predictions that can then be measured and fed back into the machine to further train the model.

Unsupervised learning methods do not make predictions, but these rather explore the relationships between features of a set of data. For example, we can cluster a collection of molecules based on their 3D fingerprint; however, this gives no prediction about their potency against any target. What this approach tells us is, simply, how similar molecules are to members of the same cluster or how different they are from other clusters.

## 3.2 Forewarned Is Forearmed

When embarking on data mining and the adventure of building ML models, there are a few common pitfalls and limitations to consider, which will be discussed briefly in this section.

### 3.2.1 Dataset Assembly and Curation

With the accessibility of big data, assembling large collections of information has become easier than ever. PubChem^([9](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit9)) alone has close to 96 *million* compounds spanning over 1 million BioAssays and boasting over 250 million bioactivities against over 70 000 targets. ChEMBL^([10](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit10)) features close to 2 million small molecule entries. Despite efforts by both groups to curate and ensure that the archived data are correct, errors are inevitable.^([11](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit11))

Assuming the odd error in structure or activity slips through, it may be absorbable in the noise of the dataset. What is likely of greater importance in assembling a dataset of structures with potency information is ensuring that the data comes from consistent experiments (assays) so that the comparison is of value.

The key thing to remember is that with any model, whether AI, ML, or anything else, if garbage goes in, garbage comes out (GIGO: Garbage In, Garbage Out).

### 3.2.2 Model Building

The first step to linking a chemical structure with an activity is coming up with an optimal set of “features” to describe the structure – descriptors or fingerprints. We have the capacity to generate thousands of descriptors, ranging from simple topological atom counts and combinations, bond counts, physicochemical properties (measured or calculated), molecular volumes, to more complex descriptors based on molecular graph theory and 3D conformation. While these “numerical features” will not be covered in detail here, there is an excellent review of descriptors and fingerprints in a previous study.^([12](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit12))

If we were to attempt to generate a regression model for a dataset using *all* of the available descriptors, there is a high likelihood that model predictions for the training set would be great and abysmally bad for the test set. In this case, the over-fitted model would have memorised the training set information and be unable to generalise it to new problems; the model captures random error instead of the true relationships.

To avoid over-fitting, we should aim to use as few descriptors as possible to capture the relationship between the structural and property features of the molecules and their activity and avoid modelling noise in the training set data. These descriptors should also be useful across a broad chemical space, and should show minimal degeneracy, meaning that descriptor calculations should generate different values for structurally different molecules, even if the differences are minute. Additionally, it is good practice to ensure that descriptors used in a model are as orthogonal as possible, in that, individually, they define characteristics that other descriptors do not cover.

To select an appropriate set of descriptors, a dimensionality reduction technique like Principal Component Analysis^([13](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit13)) can be used.

### 3.2.3 Principal Component Analysis

The most common dimensionality reduction method encountered in MedChemInformatics is Principal Component Analysis. PCA is about reducing the number of “descriptors” that describe the data. “Descriptors” was put in quotes because, when it comes to PCA, chemically meaningful descriptors no longer exist, as PCA combines correlated descriptors into components (hence the name) and each component is orthogonal (uncorrelated) to all others. The components are then used to explain the variance in the dataset and are ordered such that the first principal component explains the most variance, the second principal component the second most variance, and so on. Figures that show the amount of variance (as a percentage) that each component explains are known as scree plots; a typical example is shown in [Figure 3.2](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig2).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f2.jpg)

Figure 3.2 In this scree plot for fictitious data, the first principal component explains 50% of the variance, the second 30%, and the third 10%.

So how many components would you use for your model based on the scree plot in [Figure 3.2](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig2)? The curve plateaus from the 4th component onwards. This plateauing is referred to as the PCA “elbow” and can be the cut-off for the number of components that would be used. A general rule of thumb is to pick the number of components that explains around 80% of the variance.

### 3.2.4 When Machines Learn in 3D, Alignment IS EVERYTHING

2D descriptors have been used to successfully model activity. However, chemistry and life happen in 3D; how features map to a bioactive conformation of a molecule is usually more interesting in 3D.

In translating to a 3D model, we need to understand how molecules relate to each other in their 3D conformations. There are multiple ways of aligning molecules in three dimensions, ranging from “shape only” (*e.g.*, ROCS^([14](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit14))), to “shape+pharmacophore” (*e.g.*, coloured ROCS^([14](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit14))), to “shape+electrostatics” (*e.g.*, field-based alignment^([15](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit15))), and all of which can be biased with substructure matching to various degrees of stringency. There is equal merit in all of these approaches, but the key task at the end of any alignment *prior* to generating any model is to inspect the alignment and adjust as necessary to ensure that it is sensible and consistent.

The temptation will always be to generate the model, then look at the outliers and tweak alignments as necessary to generate models with improved statistics.

DO NOT DO THIS!

This introduces bias into the model, and while the revised model may give a brilliant improvement in the model statistics, the model is reliably nonsense. The best practice is to spend some time looking at your dataset and mining out compounds that do not belong (*e.g.*, wrong chemical series, big differences in molecular weight or other topologies, or the ones where you simply do not trust the data or the alignment), and THEN calculate the model.

### 3.2.5 Activity Range and Distribution of Activities for QSAR Modelling

As a rule of thumb, it is preferable to have an activity range of at least 2–3 log units, with an even distribution of data points through the activity range. Too many or too few data points in one slice of the activity range can be detrimental to the model.

*All of these warnings can be summed up with GIGO.*

Sadly, and in actuality, more often than we care to admit, you can have a super clean set of data, the perfect activity range, descriptors, and alignment, and you just can not squeeze out a predictive model that relates activity to structure features. Fortunately, most software companies working in this space have addressed this by providing tools for exploring the data qualitatively.

### 3.2.6 Outliers

Upon model inspection *via* plotting predicted *vs.* actual activities, there are occasionally data points that are quite far away from the regression line or far away from the rest of the data. How we deal with them depends on the nature of the outlier.

Sometimes, in assembling our data – especially from publicly available sources – we must consider whether the reported activity (or even the structure!) is accurate, or whether the compound may have an alternate mode of action. There are often discrepancies in reported activities when different assays are used. If we do not have confidence that the data are accurate, the mode of action is consistent with other members of the dataset, or whether the normalisation across different assay types is adequate, it is perfectly acceptable to remove the data point, with the considerations described below.

If the outlier does not affect the model or any assumptions derived from the model (see [Figure 3.3](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig3)), it can be removed with a footnote explaining what was done. For example, you may have a dataset that predominantly spans an activity range, but with a couple of points whose activities are quite far from the rest of the data, though model linearity is retained. If the regression equation does not change substantially when the point is removed, it is acceptable to do so, with a footnote.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f3.jpg)

Figure 3.3 A collection of data points (o's) and a single outlier (the *x*). The regression line without the outlier is the solid line and that with the outlier is a dashed line. The inclusion (or exclusion) of the outlier does not change the regression line substantially, and thus, it is acceptable that the outlier can be excluded with an explanatory footnote.

More often than not, removing outliers results in the regression changing (see [Figure 3.4](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig4)), along with the assumptions. You can run the analysis with and without the data point – if you choose to drop the outlier, you should make a note about which points were dropped, the reasons why, and how the model adjusted.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f4.jpg)

Figure 3.4 A collection of data points (o's) and a single outlier (the x) in the far upper right hand corner. The regression line without the outlier is a solid line, and that with the outlier is a dashed line. In this case, the inclusion (or exclusion) of the outlier changes the slope and intercept of the regression line, and thus, the outlier may be excluded with a footnote detailing how the model changed and why the outlier was excluded.

Other times, the data set can suggest that the outlier defines the relationship and without that outlier point, the data are completely random! In this case, the outlier should be dropped, and the model should not be reported with any significance or confidence.

If you are not comfortable dropping an outlier, sometimes a transformation like square root or log applied to your variables might yield a more reasonable model. Alternatively, you might consider that the relationship you are trying to model is nonlinear – and that is where Machine Learning can really help. *But in any case, it is critical that you understand your data, its origin, and the plausible relationships that can exist between the observable and the descriptors.*

## 3.3 Deep Learning and Neural Networks

In recent years, mentions of “Deep Learning” and “Neural Nets” in the drug discovery literature have resurged after some years of dormancy. Deep Learning is a sub-discipline of ML which incorporates Artificial Neural Networks. Simply put, the data are modelled in layers, with each layer increasing in complexity. Traditional applications of this approach were in speech recognition and natural language processing, but it has since been applied to many other areas.

These approaches are beyond the scope of this chapter, but we do recommend reading about Merck's Molecular Activity Challenge competition^([16](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit16)) in which invited participants were asked to identify the best approaches to predicting biological activity (on- and off-target) using numerical descriptors for structures. A computer science group from the University of Toronto won the challenge by invoking multi-task Deep Neural Networks.^([17](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit17))

## 3.4 Underlying Mathematics

### 3.4.1 “Observables” and “Features”

Before exploring the common ML methods used in medicinal chemistry informatics (which we are calling “MedChemInformatics”), we must first consider what features (variables) are to be correlated with the observable.

For example, if we consider a simple relationship between boiling point and the number of carbons in an alkyl chain, we know from our organic chemistry wisdom that smaller alkanes have lower boiling points, but the relationship becomes more complicated when functional groups are introduced, as additional molecular features (*e.g.*, polarity) are involved in making molecules stick together instead of escaping to the vapour phase.

An old article^([18](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit18)) details how boiling point is related to molecular features (derived empirically) *via* a linear relationship:

![image](images/eqn3-1.jpg)(3.1)

Here, *y* is a constant for each alkyl group and is related to molecular surface area; *p* and *q* are constants for functional groups that capture non-electrostatic and electrostatic forces. This linear relationship, when applied to a defined compound class (*e.g.*, acetates) reportedly predicts more than 80% of the boiling points to within 2 °C. In this case, the equation relates an observable (boiling point) with a set of variables that can be considered descriptors for each compound class.

#### 3.4.1.1 Molecular Descriptors and Fingerprints

In MedChemInformatics, we are often interested in ways that we can classify molecules as being highly similar or highly different in terms of their structural features and properties. There are many reasons we do this, including, but not limited to, virtual screening, identifying backup series, and establishing intellectual property position.

To assess similarity, we need to decide what underlying features are important. For example, we can group molecules together based on common scaffolds (*e.g.*, substructure matching, Murko scaffolds), or alternatively, we can use collections of properties (*e.g.*, DrugLike, BBB penetratability).

Descriptors have been covered at length in numerous reviews,^([19](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit19)) so these will only be briefly discussed here. Descriptors come in two flavours: those that are based on experimentally measured physicochemical properties (*e.g.*, logP, dipole moment) and those that are calculated in some fashion from the molecular structure (“theoretical descriptors”).

Theoretical descriptors that are regularly used in modelling can be further categorised:

*   0-Dimensional: these are “counts” that capture the constitution of a molecule (*e.g.*, # carbons).
*   1-Dimensional: these capture fragments and substructural features (*e.g.*, fingerprints).
*   2-Dimensional: these are chemical graph invariant descriptors derived from the 2D structure and are topological indices that capture the connectivity of atoms (*e.g.*, Wiener index).
*   3-Dimensional: these relate to molecular size, sterics, surface, and volume descriptors. For example, VSA (van der Waals surface area) mapped with partial charges of the atoms contributing to the volume. There are 3D fingerprints that capture pharmacophoric features.
*   4-Dimensional: these are derived from 3DQSAR methods such as Comparative Molecular Field Analysis^([20](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit20)) (CoMFA). Field or volume sampling points are established for a group of molecules that have been aligned using their preferred (binding mode) 3D conformations, and a field or steric value is calculated at the sampling point in space.

To conceptualise what a Fingerprint is, let's simplistically consider it as a series of checkboxes that are either ON (1) or OFF (0) and use it to compare a horse and an alligator using the chart shown in [Figure 3.5](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig5).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f5.jpg)

Figure 3.5 On/off checkboxes for each fingerprint feature convert to a bit string that captures the predefined characteristics.

The horse's fingerprint is (1,1,0,1,1,0,1); the alligator's fingerprint is (1,0,0,0,1,1,0). The fingerprint string is highly dependent on what features are used to describe the molecule. Similarity metrics are used to compare the bit strings ((1101101) and (1000110)) to score how similar they are, and the calculated similarity value depends on the fingerprint chosen for the comparison.

Fingerprints for molecules are long bit strings that query the molecule for features (atom types, substructure, *etc.*), in an effort to capture the molecular graph (2D connectivity of atoms), and in the case of 3D fingerprints, the arrangement of functional groups with respect to each other. Descriptors and Fingerprints have been described in the literature for many years and are widely implemented in commercial and open-source software packages, and these will not be discussed in detail here, but we suggest suitable papers to read for more information.^([21*a*](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit21a)–[*c*](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit21c))

Once descriptors are calculated for a set of molecules, we try to relate the combination of descriptors to the observable (*e.g.*, potency) to create groupings or clusters of molecules that have similar features and similar potencies, or to find a mathematical relationship between the features and the observable. The approaches to elucidating the mathematical relationship are discussed later.

### 3.4.2 Comparing Molecules Based on Their Descriptors

To determine whether two molecules are related to each other in some way based on their descriptors, we must be able to determine their similarity to each other (or conversely, distance from each other) in the descriptor space. The most common methods encountered in medicinal chemistry are Tanimoto Similarity, Tversky Index, and Dice Similarity. These values are usually normalised to be a number between 0 and 1, such that 1 is perfect similarity (100% match).

#### 3.4.2.1 Tanimoto Similarity

Tanimoto Similarity^([22](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit22)) first appeared in the literature in the late 1950's in efforts to classify plants and has since become widely adopted across other disciplines. This is the similarity metric you will see most often.

In descriptor space, the Tanimoto Similarity (Index) is given by:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t1.jpg)(3.2)

where *S*[*A,B*]\=Tanimoto Similarity coefficient; *n*\=number of features; *j*\=index/count variable; *x*[*jA*]\=*j*th feature of molecule *A; x*[*jB*]\=*j*th feature of molecule *B.*

In fingerprint space, this expression simplifies to:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t2.jpg)(3.3)

where *a*\=number of “on” bits in molecule *A*; *b*\=number of “on” bits in molecule *B*; *c*\=number of “on” bits in *both A* & *B.*

If we return to the comparison of horses (A) and alligators (B):

| Horse || 1 || 1 || 0 || 1 || 1 || 0 || 1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alligator || 1 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 1 || 1 || 0 |

*a* = 5;   *b* = 3;   *c* = 2

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t3.jpg)(3.4)

The Tanimoto Index (or score) is one of the most commonly encountered similarity metrics in MedChemInformatics. A general rule of thumb is that we use 0.85 as a cut-off for similar molecules;^([5](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit5)*d*) however, multiple studies have demonstrated that the cut-off is not reliable when different molecular representations are used.^([21*c*](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit21c),[23](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit23))

Tanimoto, while commonly used, has limitations and weaknesses – for example, a Tanimoto score of 0.3 is frequently returned for structurally distant molecules.^([24](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit24)) If we return to our horse-alligator comparison, with a Tanimoto score of 0.3, some awareness that this could be an artifact of the method is in order.

#### 3.4.2.2 Tversky Similarity

Another commonly encountered similarity metric used in MedChemInformatics is the Tversky coefficient,^([25](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit25)) which is given by:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t4.jpg)(3.5)

*   *Tv*[*α,β*]*(A, B)*\=Tversky coefficient;
*   *α,β*\=non-negative weighting factors;
*   *a*\=number of “on” bits in molecule *A*;
*   *b*\=number of “on” bits in molecule *B*;
*   *c*\=number of “on” bits in *both A* & *B.*

The larger the value of *α* compared to *β*, the more weight is placed on the unique features of molecule A and *vice versa*. This allows the introduction of asymmetry into the calculation of a similarity index or similarity score and exploration of the importance of common and unique features in the comparison to the reference compound *A*.

When *α* and *β* are set to one, the Tversky coefficient reduces to the Tanimoto similarity. When both coefficients are equal to 0.5, the Tversky coefficient reduces to the Dice Similarity.

If we again return to our horse-alligator comparison, and decide that the horse's features are twice as important as the alligator's (*α*\=2; *β*\=1):

| Horse || 1 || 1 || 0 || 1 || 1 || 0 || 1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alligator || 1 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 1 || 1 || 0 |

![image](images/eqn3-6.jpg)(3.6)

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t5.jpg)(3.7)

Conversely, if the alligator features are twice as important, the Tversky coefficient becomes 0.28 – thankfully, still not similar.

#### 3.4.2.3 Dice Similarity

A third approach to calculating similarity that is commonly encountered in chemistry is Dice Similarity.^([26](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit26)) Dice Similarity first appeared in 1940's ecology research but now is commonly used to compare molecules.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t6.jpg)(3.8)

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t7.jpg)(3.9)

*   *Dc*[*A,B*]\=Dice Similarity coefficient;
*   *n*\=number of features;
*   *j*\=index/count variable;
*   *x*[*jA*]\=*j*th feature of molecule *A;*
*   *x*[*jB*]\=*j*th feature of molecule *B*.

Returning one last time to our horse-alligator comparison:

| Horse || 1 || 1 || 0 || 1 || 1 || 0 || 1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alligator || 1 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 1 || 1 || 0 |

![image](images/eqn3-10.jpg)(3.10)

![image](images/eqn3-11.jpg)(3.11)

At this point, you should feel some intellectual indigestion about similarity coefficients. Using the same simplistic fingerprint, we arrived at three different similarity scores. This is often the case for the more complicated molecular fingerprints.

#### 3.4.2.4 Which Similarity Metric Works Best?

There are a few observations to make – for example, Dice and Tversky Similarities values tend to be slightly higher and are less symmetric than Tanimoto; further, Tversky and Dice give similar results, regardless of the reference feature weighting used in Tversky. But ultimately, a calculated similarity score has no absolute meaning – it is the ranking of compounds that is of more interest,^([22*d*](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit22d)) so one is as good as the next for general purposes.

### 3.4.3 Model Quality and Statistics

Let's return to predictive models. When generating models, we use whatever data that are available, and rarely is anyone upset about having too much data!

If we use all of the data available to build a model, we are limiting the model to a training set that can only be cross-validated against itself. The predicted value is then compared to the measured value. This is acceptable if only a small amount of data is available, but it is not a reliable approach. This could be an early model that could be used to feed the design-make-test-refine machine ([Figure 3.1](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig1)), to achieve improved (and statistically relevant) models as the amount of data available increases.

It is preferable to partition the dataset into a training set and a test set, either randomly or by selecting a subset that is evenly dispersed across the observable range. The general rule of thumb is that 20% of the data goes to the test set. The training set is used to build the model and cross-validate against itself, while the test set is used to apply the model to real compounds and assess whether the predicted and actual values match up for data points that are not included in the model training.

When a model is calculated, several statistical parameters are reported that relate to the quality of the model in terms of its statistical relevance and how predictive the model will be on new data.

It is worth noting that 95%/5% split is commonly used in Deep Learning because the models are built using vast quantities of data. A 5% test set still contains a LOT of data points in absolute terms!

#### 3.4.3.1 Coefficients of Determination

For linear models (assuming continuous data), the first value that comes to mind is the coefficient of determination (*r*² or *R*²), which captures how well the data are fitted to the regression line. *R*² is always between 0 and 1; the higher the value of *R*², the better the model fits the data.

*R*² can be expressed as:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t8.jpg)(3.12)

*   *i*\=number of samples;
*   *y*[expt(*i*)]\=experimental/measured value of the *i*th sample;
*   *y*[calc(*i*)]\=calculated value for the *i*th sample;
*   〈*y*[expt]〉=average experimental/measured value.

As the difference between the experimental value and the calculated value approaches zero, *R*² approaches 1, which suggests a perfect correlation between calculated and observed values in the training set (100% of the variance is captured by the model).

The second value to consider is the cross-validated coefficient of determination, *Q*² or *q*². This is similar to *R*²; however, it incorporates what the model would predict if it was built with one (Leave-One-Out – LOO) or many (Leave-Many-Out – LMO) of the data points omitted. The simplest cross-validation approach, Leave-One-Out, excludes each sample once and constructs a model with the training set less one sample, then calculating the variable. The residuals (differences between experiment and calculated values) are then used to calculate the correlation coefficient of determination according to:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t9.jpg)(3.13)

*   *i*\=number of samples;
*   *y*[expt(*i*)]\=experimental/measured value of the *i*th sample;
*   *y*[*v*(*i*)]\=calculated value for the *i*th sample from the internal validation (LOO model);
*   〈*y*[expt]〉=average experimental/measured value.

Cross-validation is intended to give an assessment of the robustness and predictiveness of the model. The higher the *Q*², the better the model should perform. Anecdotally, a *Q*²\>0.5 and *R*²\>0.6 is considered proof that a model is predictive, but that is not always the case. Additionally, a difference of 0.2–0.3 between *R*² and *Q*² suggests that the overfitting might be in play.

*R*² and *Q*², while a good place to start, are not the only considerations when assessing the quality of a model. The best approach is to use an external test set to assess whether a model is predictive or not.^([27](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit27))

#### 3.4.3.2 Kendall's Tau

Another statistical parameter that is worth considering is Kendall's Tau,^([28](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit28)) which is a measure of rank correlation. When calculated, it is a number bound by 0 and 1 and gives an estimation of how well a model can get the rank order correct, regardless of its success in calculating values with absolute accuracy.

### 3.4.4 Overtraining and Characteristics of Good Descriptors

Earlier, the term overfitting (“overtraining”) was used when there was a large discrepancy between *R*² and *Q*². This often happens when too many descriptors are used to build the model from the training set, and those descriptors are not universally related to the observable for other data. In other words, with enough descriptors, you have captured all of the variance in the noise – the model has basically memorised the training data.

Models that are over-trained violate Occam's Razor: to avoid over-training, find the simplest relationship with the fewest variables. You can do this using a dimension reduction technique like Principal Component Analysis.^([13](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit13))

## 3.5 Machine Learning Methods

In this section, we will discuss the more commonly encountered ML methods with drug discovery modelling as a context. Features will be called “descriptors” and the observable will be called “activity” (in most cases). Thus, we have a collection of molecules (training/test/validation sets), calculate a set of descriptors that capture their features, then relate the features to their activity in some mathematical fashion.

### 3.5.1 *k*\-Nearest Neighbours

The simplest Machine Learning algorithm used in medicinal chemistry is *k*\-Nearest Neighbours (*k*NN); this approach can be used for both classification and regression analyses. The essence of the *k*NN approach is captured in the proverb: “When the character of a person is not clear to you, look to their friends.”

*k*NN is a “lazy learning” method: in making predictions or classifications, the model is applied locally as opposed to globally. The *k*NN approach is non-parametric in the sense that it does not make any assumptions about the functional form of the relationship between the descriptor(s) and the activity – it could be linear, parabolic, quadratic, whatever. In the course of preparing a *k*NN model, the training set is “memorised”, and a test query is compared to every single data point in the training set in order to classify or make a prediction. This means that the model “trains” very quickly (no fancy math happening in the background). However, large amounts of data need to be kept in active memory and it takes time to compare a query to every single data point in the training set in order to make a prediction or classification for the query.

*k*NN can be used for both classification and regression models using 2D or 3D chemical descriptors, and it is less sensitive to noise in 3D structural alignments than partial least squares (PLS). Classification models are used when the data are not continuous, for example, ranges of % inhibition and classes such as “high”, “medium”, “low.” In a sense, *k*NN is about pattern recognition: molecules with similar features should exhibit similar biological activities.

A simplified *k*NN workflow is shown in [Figure 3.6](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig6).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f6.jpg)

Figure 3.6 The kNN workflow for predicting the activity of a query based on the training set. In calculating the distance, any similarity metric will suffice (*e.g.*, Euclidean distance, Tanimoto, Tverskey, Dice, *etc.*). The weighing factors are inverse distance or similarity – *i.e.*, training set molecules that are more similar to the query will contribute more to the activity prediction.

The most important parameter to adjust when using *k*NN modelling is the number of nearest neighbours (*k*). A high value of *k* results in a model that has more training set contribution to the prediction and is more resilient to outliers. This means that there is lower variance, but increased bias. On the other hand, a low or more restrictive *k* gives the most flexible fit in those cases where the functional form of the relationship between the descriptors and the activity may vary. Lower *k* values give high variance but low bias.

So, how do we pick the optimal value of *k*? The best *k* is the one that corresponds to the lowest error rate. Generally, the optimal value of *k* is found heuristically based on RMSE (and *Q*²) during cross-validation. Unfortunately, using a test set to tune *k* can result in over-fitting, so we need to consider using an independent validation set.

***Final Thoughts***

To summarise, *k*NN is the simplest of the ML methods that MedChemInformaticians are likely to encounter. Although it is a sound way to classify and predict (especially when the relationship is local as opposed to global), its application suffers from data storage and computational expense. *k*NN models have been employed successfully in drug discovery. A few examples include understanding QSAR and assisting with designing new potent inhibitors,^([29](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit29)) organ toxicity prediction,^([30](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit30)) hERG activity,^([31](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit31)) and protein function prediction.^([32](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit32)) For a more detailed description of kNN, see ref. [33](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit33).

### 3.5.2 Linear Regression

Probably, the most common of the ML methods encountered is based on different flavours of linear regression. Linear regression is the mathematical attempt to fit a straight line to a collection of data points to relate a descriptor (or set of descriptors) with an activity. We see this method regularly reported in articles detailing 2D and 3D QSAR models.

Regression modelling works on the assumption that there exists some relationship between a set of descriptors and the measured activity. One approach is to assume a linear relationship: meaning that each descriptor independently contributes with a *constant proportionality* to the activity. The predicted activity is, therefore, “explained” by the weighted sum of each descriptor; the magnitude of the weight indicates the significance of a descriptor towards the magnitude of the activity:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t10.jpg)(3.14)

*   *P*[*i*]\=predicted response of the *i*th observation;
*   *n*\=*n*th descriptor;
*   *N*\=maximum number of descriptors;
*   *F*[*i,n*]\=value of the *i*th observation for the *n*th descriptor.

The goal of linear regression analysis/algorithms is to find values for the weights, *w*[*n*], that will minimise the error between the predicted activity (*P*[*i*]) and the experimentally observed activity (*R*[*i*]):min ∑*ε*[*i*],

![image](images/eqn3-15.jpg)(3.15)

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and Partial Least Squares (PLS) are methods used to find weights under different conditions. What can be used, or definitely cannot be used, will depend on the number of observations (*i*) and the number of uncorrelated descriptors (*n*). The number of descriptors used for predicting the activity can be reduced, if required, by methods referred to as feature selection and feature extraction.

Feature selection refers to methods that select and use a subset of the original descriptors *without* modification to predict an activity. The regularisation regression algorithm Lasso^([34](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit34)) (Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) is an example of a feature selection method. Lasso uses the OLS method to find weights for the descriptors that minimise the error. However, Lasso not only looks to minimise the error, but also attempts to minimise the number of non-zero weights used in the regression analysis. This is achieved by adding a penalty term for each non-zero weight:^([35](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit35))

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t11.jpg)(3.16)

*   *c*\=cost function;
*   *i*\=*i*th observation;
*   *M*\=number of observations;
*   *R*[*i*]\=Response value for *i*th observation;
*   *j*\=*i*th descriptor;
*   *N*\=number of descriptors;
*   *w*[*j*]\=weight for feature *j*;
*   *F*[*i, j*]\=Value of *i*th observation for *j*th descriptor;
*   *γ*\=penalty coefficient.

Feature extraction, as done in PCA, involves creating new components from the original set of descriptors.

#### 3.5.2.1 Ordinary or Partial Least Squares?

Consider these equations:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t12.jpg)(3.17)

If we only had equation (a), there would be infinite many solutions to this equation: (*x*, *y*)=…; (5, −1); (4, 0); (3, 1); … (0,4); (−1, 5); … If we had (a) and (b), one solution exists: (*x*, *y*)=(2, 2).

However, with (a), (b), and (c), there is no solution that satisfies all three equations, but there is a solution that gives the best average result: (*x*, *y*)=(1.5,1.5) gives errors of −1, 0, and 1 for a, b, and c, respectively.

With only (a), there were 2 descriptors (*x* and *y*) and one observation so that the number of descriptors was greater than the number of observations. With (a) and (b), the number of descriptors equalled the number of observations. With (a), (b), and (c), the number of observations was greater than the number of descriptors.

**When # Observations> # Descriptors**

*If and only if* the number of observations is greater than the number of independent descriptors, it *may* be possible to use OLS to find the weights.

OLS is relatively simple. The dataset of observations and descriptors can be expressed as a matrix, **X**. The size of a matrix is expressed as number of rows first followed by the number of columns. So a matrix with *m* observations and *n* descriptors will have size \[m, n\]. If **Y** represents the response and we have a response for each observation, **Y** has size \[*m*, 1\]. As we want weights for each descriptor, weight matrix, **B**, will have size \[*n*, 1\]. The ordering of matrices is very important because, generally, **A**×**B**≠**B**×**A**. For matrix multiplication, we need the inner dimensions to agree. Therefore:

![image](images/eqn3-18.jpg)(3.18)

Taking a look at the dimensions: \[*m*, 1\]=\[*m*, *n*\]\[*n*, 1\], this is possible as the number of columns in **X** is equal to the number of rows in **B** – the inner dimensions agree. It is, therefore, important to understand the significance of multiplying on the left side or right side of matrices.

The next step involves multiplying by the transpose of **X**, or ***X***^(**T**). The transpose of a matrix means to convert the rows to columns and the columns to rows:

![image](images/eqn3-19.jpg)(3.19)

Next step involves left multiplying by the inverse of ***X***^(**T**)***X***, or (***X***^(**T**)***X***)^(**−1**):

![image](images/eqn3-20.jpg)(3.20)

(***X***^(**T**)***X***)^(**−1**)***X***^(**T**)***X*** will result in the identity matrix, **I**, such that:

![image](images/eqn3-21.jpg)(3.21)

The Achilles heel of OLS is that the inverse may not always exist. This occurs when the descriptors are not independent (or not independent enough), resulting in a determinant (a quantity necessary for calculating the inverse) that is zero and as the determinant is used in division, and the resulting matrix is referred to as being singular.

**When # Observations <# Descriptors**

When there are more descriptors than observations, OLS fails because the inverse, (***X***^(**T**)***X***)^(−1), definitely does NOT exist. Principal Component Regression and PLS are two methods that may overcome this hurdle.

Although Principal Component Regression uses OLS, it first undergoes feature extraction. Principal Component Analysis uses components that can represent a combination of correlated descriptors. PCA finds components that maximise the variance in the descriptor space without considering the response data. Components refer to eigenvectors that are ranked according to their corresponding eigenvalue from largest to smallest. Each component is orthogonal, meaning that there is no correlation between components. A number of components are picked – the first component explains the most variance, the second component the second most variance, and so on. Then after selecting how many components to use for predicting outcome, OLS can be used to find weights for each component (assuming that the number of observations is now greater than the number of components). The downside to this approach is that components that explain the most variance in the descriptor data are not necessarily the best predictors for the response.

Partial Least Squares addresses this issue by maximising the *covariance* between descriptors and the response. It does this by creating a covariance matrix, **X**^(**T**)**Y**, where **X** is a matrix consisting of the descriptor data and **Y** is the response data. PLS actually covers a class of algorithms. It was introduced in 1966,^([36](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit36)) and it has been improved and enhanced over the past 50 years. A commonly used implementation is NIPALS (Nonlinear Iterative Partial Least Squares):^([37](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit37))***X***[**0**]\=***X***, ***Y***[**0**]\=***Y***

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t13.jpg)(3.22)

Initial weights (w) are calculated from eigenvectors of **S**:

![image](images/eqn3-23.jpg)(3.23)

where *Eig*[max] refers to the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue.

Variables required to update matrices **X** and **Y** are calculated next:

![image](images/eqn3-24.jpg)(3.24)

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t14.jpg)(3.25)

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t15.jpg)(3.26)

Next, matrices **X** and **Y** are updated and deflated so that new matrices are the residuals:

![image](images/eqn3-27.jpg)(3.27)

This process is carried out *r* times with *r* being the *rank* of matrix **X**. *Rank* refers to linearly independent rows. If all the values of *w*, *t* and *p* are stored in **W**, **T** and **P** respectively, the weights, **B**, can be found by:

![image](images/eqn3-28.jpg)(3.28)

where:

![image](images/eqn3-29.jpg)(3.29)

and **Z**^(**+**) denotes the pseudoinverse such that:

![image](images/eqn3-30.jpg)(3.30)

It is important to note that PLS can suffer from scaling of descriptors.^([38](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit38)) The magnitude of the change in a descriptor will affect the covariance matrix and therefore will change the dominating eigenvector, thereby changing the weights in a nonlinear way; as Cramer stated, this is contrary to ordinary least squares as changing a linearly independent descriptor will change the weight by a factor that is the inverse of the change.

Comparing Principal Component Regression (PCR) and PLS, PCR looks to maximise variance in the descriptor space without consideration of the response, and the maximum varied descriptors may not necessarily account for variation in response. PLS, on the other hand, maximises covariance between descriptors and response.

***Final Thoughts***

Overfitting is not usually an issue with linear regression when the number of observations is greater than the number of descriptors. If there are more observations than descriptors, OLS should generally work. If there are more descriptors, PLS may be implemented.

### 3.5.3 Decision Trees and Random Forests

**Far** more complex and far more powerful is the use of Decision Tree approaches to model the relationship between descriptors and biological activity.

Decision Trees encompass algorithms that partition observations through careful ordering of descriptors for mainly classification analysis. Decision Trees take their name based on how their results are visualised. A Decision Tree starts off with a single node (or *root node*). Nodes represent descriptors. Branches, representing a partitioning criterion (decision), then stem off from this node that is either sufficient to categorise all observations that satisfy that decision, or lead to another node and, thus, another decision. Partitions are created until all observations are correctly categorised, or until a certain depth to the tree is reached. Two early and popular decision tree algorithms are ID3 and C4.5. ID3^([39](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit39)) is an algorithm that handles only categorical data whereas C4.5^([40](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit40)) can handle categorical and continuous data – we will discuss ID3 here, but refer you to Quinlan's article for further information on C4.5. To understand how these algorithms work, it is necessary to know what is meant by *information*.

#### 3.5.3.1 Information

Information theory states that information, or (Shannon) entropy, is a measure of uncertainty. Revealing the outcome of an event with lower probability will generally have more information than an event with higher probability. The equation for entropy is:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t16.jpg)(3.31)

*   *H*\=Entropy, (*N.B.:* Information Theorists use “H” instead of “S” for entropy);
*   *P*[*i*]\=Probability of event *i* occurring.

Tossing a biased coin with 100% chance of landing on heads will have zero entropy (this can alternatively be viewed as a 0% chance of landing on tails), in which case:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t17.jpg)(3.32)

A coin that has a 90% chance of landing on heads has slightly more entropy (∼0.14) and a fair coin has the most entropy (0.5). The value itself is not so important as log[2] is just used for convention (log[10] or the natural log can just as easily be used). What *is* important is the ranking of entropy values for different events.

Another way to view entropy is to consider how many *efficient* questions would need to be asked to reveal the outcome of events. Let's use another coin toss example, this time, 8 tosses of a *heavily biased* coin with tails favoured. Each coin toss could be queried; however, this would not be efficient given the knowledge that the coin is heavily biased. The more efficient approach is to group the coin tosses into fours, then ask: “does this group contain any heads?” As the coin is heavily biased against heads, the probability of a rare event (coin landing on heads) occurring in each group is low. Thus, we would expect to reveal 50% of the remaining toss outcomes after each question, and to reveal all coin toss outcomes after 3 questions. This illustrates why a fair coin has more entropy than a biased coin – each toss of a fair coin would need to be queried.

#### 3.5.3.2 Algorithms

The ID3 algorithm uses entropy to decide which descriptor to use at a node. Firstly, the entropy of the response is calculated as follows:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t18.jpg)(3.33)

*   *H*\=Entropy;
*   *R*\=Response;
*   *N*\=Number of unique responses;
*   *P*(*R*[*i*])=Probability of Response *i*, or the ratio of response *i* to total number of observations, such that ![inline](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t19.jpg).

Next, the information that is gained by partitioning the dataset using a descriptor is calculated for each descriptor:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t20.jpg)(3.34)

*   *I*(*F*, *H*)=Information gained by partitioning on descriptor *F* given the entropy *H*;
*   *P*(*F*[*j*])=Probability of descriptor *F* with value *j*;
*   *N*\=Maximum number of unique classes in a descriptor;
*   *H*(*R*, *F*[*j*])=Entropy of response for descriptor *F* with value *j*.

The C4.5 algorithm is very similar to ID3 with some small differences. The algorithm still uses information/entropy, but the decision function is based on *information gain ratio* instead of *information gain*. If the ID3 equations could be viewed generally as:

![image](images/eqn3-36.jpg)(3.36)

C4.5 algorithm uses:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t49.jpg)(3.37)

For more information about C4.5 and Gain ratios, see \[40\].

Decision Tree algorithms are considered “greedy.” Their calculations result in the ‘best’ decision made for the next immediate node. This does not necessarily result in the optimal classification for the entire dataset. Additionally, a Decision Tree does not incorporate any randomness, so the result will always be the same. To improve classification, ensemble Decision Tree approaches may be used.

#### 3.5.3.3 Decision Tree Ensembles

What is better than one decision tree? Thousands of decision trees, of course! However, it was just mentioned that Decision Trees follow a very strict procedure that would result in the same classification each time, so how would performing thousands of Decision Trees be helpful? By creating Decision Trees with different subsets of the original dataset, the ensemble allows generalisation across large datasets. Ensemble methods can be used to create multiple Decision Trees using random selection of the data. As the data are different, different decision trees will be created. Two different types of ensemble methods are bagging^([41](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit41)) and boosting.^([42](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit42))

Bagging stands for “*b*ootstrap *ag*gregation.” Bootstrapping means to sample with replacement. Therefore, bagging algorithms create new datasets from the original dataset where observations may be duplicated. Decision Trees are then created from these new datasets. Observations then get put through all the Decision Trees and a voting schema between the results from all the Decision Trees will decide how the observation gets classified. This method promotes generality and significantly reduces overfitting. Random Forest (RF) is a bagging algorithm that, in addition to using bootstrapping, creates decision trees using a random subset of the descriptors.

Boosting is another ensemble Decision Tree method. The goal of boosting algorithms is to strengthen *weak* classifiers; this is achieved by assigning weights to all the observations. Observations that are incorrectly classified have their weight increased while those that are correctly classified experience a decrease in their weighting. It is important to note that decision trees are generated sequentially. The second decision tree is a modified version of the first, the third is modified from the second, and so on.

***Final Thoughts***

Decision Trees and ensemble methods are an efficient way to classify large amounts of high-dimensional data, with the added benefit that the data can be used as it is, without scaling, transforming, or converting to other forms. On the downside, a large volume of data is required before these methods become truly useful. Further, the approach is simply a sorting algorithm – the model makes no attempt to interpret or understand the relationship between the data and the descriptors. Decision Trees (and Ensembles) have been used in drug discovery for tasks such as choosing the most informative set(s) of descriptors for large collections of compounds, and predicting and classifying on ADMET properties; a few sample articles are cited in ref. [43](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit43). More recently, these methods (along with PLS) were used to create Profile-QSAR at Novartis.^([44](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit44))

### 3.5.4 Support Vector Machines

Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithms were initially purposed to classify data into one of two groups with the assumption that the data were linearly separable.^([45](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit45)) Data are separated by finding a hyperplane that separates the data – any data on one side of the hyperplane are classified into one group while data on the other side are classified into a second group. A hyperplane is math jargon for a sheet or plane that cuts through an array of multidimensional data and separates (classifies) it; this separator would be a line if the data are 2-Dimensional.

This means that SVM algorithms are used when the descriptors are numerical and the response data are binary (*i.e.*, yes/no, 1/0, on/off, active/inactive). SVMs can be broken down into hyperplanes, kernels, and support vectors.

#### 3.5.4.1 Hyperplanes

SVMs find hyperplanes that separate data into their respective categories. But it is not just any hyperplane that successfully separates the data: it is a hyperplane that maximises the distance between the closest point(s) in both classes (see [Figure 3.9](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig9)).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f9.jpg)

Figure 3.9 Five hyperplanes (black lines) have been generated for three data points (two o's and one x) that represent two classes.

In [Figure 3.9](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig9), two of the hyperplanes (the two with steepest slopes) do not successfully classify the data points as there is one “o” data point on either side. The two remaining dashed hyperplanes separate the data points successfully; however, the distances from the hyperplane and the points are not maximised. The solid black hyperplane is the optimal hyperplane, as the data points are successfully classed and the distance from the data points to the hyperplane is maximised. The logic behind maximising the margin (described later) is that if any new data points are added, new points will possibly be close to existing data points of the same class. If a hyperplane was too close to a data point, it could dramatically change in order to accommodate the new data point. Maximising the margin promotes the most stable model.

#### 3.5.4.2 Kernels

Kernels are functions that transform the data or project the data into higher dimensions – the so-called “kernel trick.” In [Figure 3.10](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig10), we illustrate the idea of linearly separable and nonlinearly separable data and discuss kernels that are used for classifying/separating the data.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f10.jpg)

Figure 3.10 (a) Linearly separable data, and (b) nonlinearly separable data.

A SVM model may only be successful if the appropriate kernel is used. A linear kernel would not be appropriate if the data were distributed as [Figure 3.10](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig10)(b). When data are not linearly separable, different kernels need to be used. For example, in [Figure 3.10](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig10)(b), we have data plotted in 2D. If we project the data into a third dimension, *Z*, where *Z=x*²*\+ y*², we can see that the data separates (see [Figure 3.11](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig11)).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f11.jpg)

Figure 3.11 (a) Data from [Figure 3.10](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig10)(b) projected into the third dimension; (b) The projected data are then plotted on the *X*–*Z* axis to highlight how the nonlinearly separable data are now linearly separable after transformation.

Post-transformation, we can find a value of *Z* that classifies the data. With this example, we see that using the right kernel is fundamental to the success of the SVM model.

#### 3.5.4.3 Support Vectors

As previously described, the optimal hyperplane depends on the closest point(s) from either class. The distance between the hyperplane and the closest points is called the margin, and the closest points to the margin are called support vectors.

In [Figure 3.12](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#fig12), a hyperplane is generated (dark black line). The normal to the hyperplane is a unit vector that is perpendicular to the hyperplane. The arrow indicates the direction of the unit vector towards a data point. It does not matter where on the hyperplane the normal is found.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-f12.jpg)

Figure 3.12 The projected vector used to calculate the distance from the hyperplane to the data point; the arrow indicates the direction of the unit vector to the data point in question. The hyperplane is displayed as a dark line and the normal is rendered as a dotted line.

The calculation proceeds by the following steps:

1.  Select a point on the hyperplane.
2.  Find the normal, **w**, at that point.
3.  Ensure that the normal is converted to a unit vector, **u**.
4.  Generate vector **p**, which is the projection of the data point vector **a** onto the direction of the unit vector, **u**.
    
    ![image](images/eqn3-38.jpg)(3.38)
    
5.  We want the magnitude of **p** for the closest data point in one class to be the same for the magnitude of **p** for the closest point in the second class.

In calculating the vector **p**, we calculated the distance of a point from the hyperplane, (***u*** · ***a***). The dot product produces a dimensionless number (scalar), which gives us the magnitude of the distance to the hyperplane.

Now, if we define a normal vector (**w**) and a vector **x**, where **x**\=(x1, x2,…) and *b* is the intersection:

![image](images/eqn3-39.jpg)(3.39)

This equation defines the hyperplane. But, for points that are NOT on the hyperplane, the expression will not equal zero:

![image](images/eqn3-40.jpg)(3.40)

The dot product, representing distance, can be positive or negative, depending on which side of the hyperplane a point lies. Now, if we define *y* as:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t50.jpg)(3.41)

All points are correctly classified if:

![image](images/eqn3-42.jpg)(3.42)

For each hyperplane, the equation to be optimised (*Margin*) is given by:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t51.jpg)(3.43)

The normal, **w**, has been scaled by its magnitude, ‖***w***‖, to make the equation scale invariant.

If the equation is not scaled, the magnitude of the normal vector would greatly affect the results; the only factor should be the direction of the normal vector. This is achieved by converting the normal vector to a unit normal vector. With an equation that is scale invariant, multiple hyperplanes with different normal vectors can be compared.

*Margin* finds the distance of the closest point for each hyperplane, and this is the value that we want to maximise across all the hyperplanes.

max Margin,

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00037-t52.jpg)(3.44)

As real data are noisy, data won't always be entirely separable. Therefore, SVM algorithms can include hard and soft margins. Hard margins mean all data need to be correctly classified, whereas soft margins allow for some data points to be misclassified in order to improve generability.

Solutions to SVM algorithms are unique, as a result of it being a convex optimisation problem. Additional information regarding Support Vector Machines can be found in ref. [46](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit46).

***Final Thoughts***

One of the key advantages of SVM is that one very quickly arrives at a classification model. But there are considerations about applying it to large amounts of data (more than 10 000 data points) as the approach – like other canonical ML methods – does not always scale with the amount of data. This is why Deep Learning is used when the amount of data is vast. SVMs have been used in drug discovery for property prediction, assessing synthetic accessibility, and for exploring activity cliffs – a few examples can be found in ref. [47*a*](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit47a)–[*d*](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit47d).

## 3.6 Summary

Phew. That was a lot of maths. Congratulations if you have continued to read – you have cemented your reputation as a medcheminformatician who knows their stuff!

Now that you have been introduced to some popular ML algorithms/methods/tools, you may be thinking, “what is the best method?” Well, cross-validation does not only apply to datasets (remember to leave some out!) but also to ML approaches – in a nutshell, try them all and see what the models look like. The success of a ML approach depends on the inherent structure and values of the dataset. Some approaches will not be applicable at all, depending on your modelling needs (classifying or regression) or whether your data are numerical or not.

Reportedly, SVM and ensemble Decision Tree approaches have been found to be more accurate for classifications in general;^([48](#BK9781788017893-00037.xhtml#cit48)) however, there is no one method that works best for all problems.

The good (and incredibly relieving) news is that most commercial software packages have implementations of these algorithms with sensible starting parameters, so you can simply run ML models on your data with a few button clicks without worrying about the underlying science or the nuts and bolts of the approaches. However, it is our view (and the view of most computational scientists) that mindless button clicking is not a good approach to modelling. Awareness of the underlying algorithms and their strengths and limitations will allow you to select the most appropriate method for the data you are attempting to model and ultimately help avoid the trials, tribulations, and endless aggravation when the method you selected produces incomprehensible results.
