## 7.1 Introduction

Synthetic chemistry is at the heart of medicinal and materials chemistry. Anticipating how molecules will react (forward synthetic planning) and how a molecule can be synthesised (retrosynthesis) rely on the expert knowledge and experience of a synthetic chemist. Repositories such as Reaxys and SciFinder contain millions of compounds, reactions, references, and bioactivities. These repositories allow chemists to search through vast regions of chemical space to fill in any gaps in their knowledge. Reaction precedents on analogous structures and/or reaction types to molecules with no reported synthesis routes can be retrieved. Although integrated tools enable the search results to be filtered, analysing the information to make informed decisions is a manual process that requires the intellect and time of an expert synthetic chemist.

Automating retrosynthetic analysis, the recursive breakdown of a target molecule until reactant precursors are reached that are commercially available, would significantly reduce the time taken to plan chemical syntheses. The concept of using a computer to plan synthetic routes was first proposed around 50 years ago.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit1)) The history of CASD tools has been reviewed in detail,^([2](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit2)–[5](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit5)) from the pioneering work of E. J. Corey in the development of Logic and Heuristics Applied to Synthetic Analysis (LHASA)^([6](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit6)) to contemporary commercially available programs. Thus far, chemists are yet to implement these tools when planning synthetic routes to new molecules. A survey was completed in 2017 (13 chemists in two companies)^([3](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit3)) to determine what chemists expect from CASD tools. The following were identified as the most important aspects to include: (i) user-friendly, (ii) provide supportive literature examples, (iii) define possible bonds to be broken, (iv) lead to commercially available reactant precursors, (v) recognise conflicting reactivity and suggest protecting groups, and (vi) prioritise results. While aspects (i) to (v) can be implemented regardless of the chemist's area of expertise, prioritising results is a challenge. Chemists working in different parts of the chemical industry have different priorities when designing reactions. Their criteria for a suitable reaction could be based on cost, greenness, reaction conditions (such as temperature or catalysts), and so on. Therefore, CASD tools need to be flexible and rank pathways based on the criteria provided by the chemist.

Forward synthetic planning is the prediction of products given the reactants, reagents, and a set of reaction conditions. Experiments, which are predominantly used to identify reaction outcomes, are expensive, time-consuming, and require experienced chemists. It would therefore be beneficial for computational tools to identify the major product, any side-products, and validate retrosynthetic predictions. Optimising reaction conditions, such as catalysts and solvents, is also an important part of synthetic planning. Changing a set of reaction conditions, even slightly, could result in the formation of a different major product or a failed reaction. Integrating CASD with high-throughput screening and robotic equipment holds much promise for the future of reaction optimisation.

Advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning methods and availability of big data have provoked renewed interest in CASD. In this chapter, we will outline sources and representations of reaction data, give a brief description of machine learning methods focused on synthetic chemistry, and provide detailed approaches to CASD with contemporary examples and comparisons.

## 7.2 The Nature of the Chemical Data

### 7.2.1 Data Sources

Large amounts of data are required for training machine learning algorithms. Typically, supervised learning methods (see Section 7.3) are used in this area; these require labelled data. This means the ground truth associated with each input is required, whether that be the reactants, products, or yield data. Reactions are often extracted from reaction databases, cleaned, and re-written in a machine-readable format.^([7](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit7),[8](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit8)) The lack of a conventional approach for data extraction has resulted in different types of information, managed in different ways, used as the input to the machine learning methods. Databases are noisy and can contain duplicate and even erroneous reactions. These should be removed in the cleaning process. Recorded reactions that generated multiple products can be managed in two ways. The highest yielding (*i.e.* major) product can be kept and the others discarded,^([8](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit8)) or the reaction can be split into multiple single-product reactions.^([9](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit9)–[12](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit12)) Atom-to-atom mapping is often required in retrosynthesis and forward synthetic planning tools, usually to identify reaction centres. Atom map indices are used to label all atoms in the reactant species that are mapped to the atoms in the product species as shown in [Figure 7.1](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#fig1). Reactions with incorrect or incomplete indices should be removed. Other reaction information, for example stereochemistry, has historically been difficult to incorporate due to sparse availability, difficulty in encoding into the molecular descriptors, or difficulty in incorporating into the model.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00169-f1.jpg)

Figure 7.1 An example of an atom mapped reaction.

Reaction data reported in scientific journal publications and patents can be accessed through commercial repositories, such as Reaxys and SciFinder. Synthetic chemists use these tools to retrieve relevant experimental procedures, chemical literature, and patents. However, extracting large quantities of reaction data for data analysis or to train machine learning models requires a specific licence. Although rare, academic research groups have extracted ∼12.5M single-step reactions from Reaxys and built models for forward reaction prediction,^([13](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit13),[14](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit14)) retrosynthetic route design^([14](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit14),[15](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit15)) and the prediction of reaction conditions.^([16](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit16)) Nonetheless, to compare models an open-source dataset is required where access is not an issue.

Open-source patent data from the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) is the alternative dataset of choice when commercial licences are not available. US patents from 1976 to September 2016 were parsed by Lowe.^([17](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit17)) Reactants, products, reagents, solvents, quantities of molecules used, yield, temperature, time, preparation and workup steps were extracted using text-mining.^([18](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit18)) This common benchmark dataset contains ∼1M single-step reactions. Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES)^([19](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit19)) strings (see Section 7.2.2) represent the molecules in each atom mapped reaction. The USPTO dataset is useful for building synthetic design models, as it consists of many popular chemical reactions, particularly ones used in medicinal chemistry. Subsets of the dataset have been pre-processed and split into training, validation and testing sets. The USPTO\_MIT subset of *ca.* 480K reactions has been used in reaction prediction.^([20](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit20)) For the retrosynthesis task, the filtered dataset of 50K reactions (USPTO\_50K) have been classified into ten reaction types (see [Table 7.1](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#tab1)).^([21](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit21)) This enables models to be compared based on individual reaction types. The USPTO dataset contains prophetic examples which are predicted experimental methods and results that have not been carried out.^([22](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit22)) Prophetic examples are allowed in US patents as long as they are not written in the past tense. Models based on patents that include prophetic examples should be considered with caution, as synthetic routes may not have been predicted based on experimentally valid examples.

 

Table 7.1 The ten reaction types in the USPTO\_50K dataset.^([21](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit21))

| Reaction class || Reaction name || Size (%) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || Heteroatom alkylation and arylation || 30.3 |
| 2 || Acylation and related processes || 23.8 |
| 3 || C–C bond formation || 11.3 |
| 4 || Heterocycle formation || 1.8 |
| 5 || Protections || 1.3 |
| 6 || Deprotections || 16.5 |
| 7 || Reductions || 9.2 |
| 8 || Oxidations || 1.6 |
| 9 || Functional group interconversions || 3.7 |
| 10 || Functional group addition || 0.5 |

Reaction data published in journals and patents are biased toward high yielding reactions; low yielding and failed reactions are rarely reported. The latter may include reactions where all of the starting material remains or reactions leading to the formation of unexpected products. Supervised learning models built on published data are therefore limited, as counter-examples are required in training for optimum performance. The absence of failed data has been overcome by generating negative examples. Here, reaction templates (see Section 7.4) are used to generate chemically plausible “wrong/false” products.^([13](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit13),[15](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit15),[23](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit23))

Electronic Laboratory Notebooks (ELNs) are used in the pharmaceutical industry by chemists to document their experimental procedures, conditions, and notes. They also store other useful data including yields and spectra. ELNs contain failed reaction data and hence can be utilised to enhance supervised learning models, without generating artificial negative data. The restricted reactant space covered in ELNs contains common reactions used by chemists. The reactions are considered to be of high quality, reproducible, and reliable. Unfortunately, ELNs are not accessible to the public, nor in commercial databases due to confidentiality reasons. However, with access, the reaction data within ELNs has been used to build reaction prediction^([24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24)) and retrosynthesis models^([8](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit8),[24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24)) as well as to predict reaction conditions.^([25](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit25))

### 7.2.2 Molecular Descriptors

For a machine learning algorithm to learn from chemical structures, those structures must be represented in a way that an algorithm can process. Molecular descriptors are based on the structural, physiochemical, electronic, or topological nature of molecules. The type of descriptor used affects the performance of the algorithm as it has to capture the relevant information required.

One-dimensional descriptors represent molecules as a list of structural fragments. They are fast, easy to calculate, and simple to compare. An example is molecular fingerprints. These are vectors composed of binary digits that correspond to the presence or absence of specific substructures. This encoded information only defines one-dimensional features of the molecules. Molecular fingerprints can also contain two-dimensional information relating to atom connectivity by encoding the neighbourhood of each atom. Three-dimensional conformer information can also be encoded. A type of fingerprint called Morgan circular fingerprints has been used to predict reactant precursors by comparing the similarity of target molecules with products in a knowledge-base.^([9](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit9)) A reaction fingerprint, calculated by the difference between the sum of the products and the sum of the reactants fingerprints, has been developed to classify reaction types.^([26](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit26))

Two-dimensional descriptors encode the topology (*i.e.* connectivity) of a molecule. For example, molecular graphs contain nodes that correspond to the atoms, and edges that correspond to the bonds that connect the atoms. The nodes are labelled by atom type and the edges are weighted based on bond type. Molecular graphs are fast to compute and easy to interpret, as molecules with identical graphs are identical molecules. Another type of two-dimensional descriptors are line notations that describe a molecule as a sequence of characters. The most widely used line notation is SMILES and its extensions, SMARTS (SMILES arbitrary target specification) and SMIRKS (a reaction transform language). SMILES strings are defined as follows.

*   Atoms are written as their atomic symbols.
*   Single, double, triple and quadruple bonds are written as “-”, “=”, “#” and “$” respectively, although single bonds are usually omitted.
*   Atoms in aromatic rings are encoded using lower case letters.
*   Reactions can be written by splitting the reactants, reagents, and products with a “>” symbol.

For a single molecule, multiple SMILES strings may be valid, as the string can start from any atom within the molecule. This should be accounted for when building models, by either canonicalizing the SMILES strings or building a model that understands which different SMILES strings are equivalent. SMARTS strings are an extension of SMILES which include additional logical operators to allow searching for generic substructures. SMIRKS are another extension that describes generic reaction transforms. These line notations can be used as a direct input to machine learning algorithms.^([27](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit27)–[29](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit29))

Another type of descriptor employs properties found using quantum calculations. Examples include NMR shifts, electrostatic charges, HOMO/LUMO energies, vibrational frequencies, and intensities. Quantum chemical calculations have been used as descriptors in the prediction of yield.^([30](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit30)) However, density functional theory (DFT) calculations are computationally expensive.

## 7.3 Machine Learning Methods

Machine learning algorithms can be divided into many categories depending on the given task. This section will concern itself with two of the most popular, namely supervised and unsupervised learning. In supervised learning, the relationship between input-output pairs is modelled, to build a predictive model. The input data can be represented with various valid descriptors, examples range from a vector of numeric values to molecular graphs (see Section 7.2.2). Supervised learning models process the input data and return output data as a numerical or binary value. The key aspect of supervised learning is that the values of outputs are already known and can be used as examples to guide the learning process.

If the output data is a continuous or quantitative value, modelling its relationship with an arbitrary set of inputs is known as regression. Defining *X*\={*x*[i]}^(*N*)[*i*\=1] as the set of *N* input data points, *Y*\={*y*[i]}^(*N*)[*i*\=1] as the set of corresponding output data points and *F* as the unknown relationship between the two, regression estimates *F* based on the evidence that *y*[*i*]\=*F*(*x*[*i*]) for *i*\=1,…, *N*. The unknown function, *F*, does not have to represent a direct relationship between the input and output; it could represent a probability distribution over input-output pairs. However, the methods to infer *F* are the same and it is these that we are concerned with. Standard regression techniques assume that *F* belongs to a set of functions of similar structure and can therefore be parametrised based upon this structure. For example, one could assume that *F* is linear and parametrised by a vector *β*, thus *y*[*i*]\=*β*^(*T*)*x*[*i*] for *i*\=1,…, *N*. However, this can be restrictive if the relationship being modelled is not sufficiently described by the assumed form. To overcome this, many machine learning approaches make no such assumptions and, instead, infer *F* solely based upon the supplied data.

One popular approach to regression would be to use an artificial neural network (ANN). This is a model that can approximate an arbitrary relationship between the input-output pairs and is defined by a matrix of parameters *W* called the weights. During the learning process, the ANN uses the “Backpropagation” algorithm^([31](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit31)) in conjunction with a gradient-based optimisation scheme (for example, gradient descent) to produce an estimate *F̂* of *F* that minimises the error in its predictions. Each prediction *ŷ*[*i*] is a function of the input *x*[*i*] and the weights *W*, so *ŷ*[*i*]\=*F̂*(*x*[*i*], *W*). Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss function (which quantifies how accurate a prediction is) with respect to each weight. The gradient-based optimisation scheme then utilises this information to adjust *W* so that the error in prediction between *ŷ*[*i*] and *y*[*i*] is reduced. This process is repeated numerous times to allow the ANN to learn a set of weights that best describe the relationship. A more mathematical, yet still approachable, introduction to ANNs can be found in the review by Higham and Higham.^([32](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit32))

We have described a method to model the relationship between input and output data, where the output is a real number. Another supervised learning problem considers the output as a binary value *i.e. y*[*i*]\=1 or *y*[*i*]\=0. This is known as classification. Whilst ANNs can also be used for classification, another effective model is the Support Vector Machine (SVM).^([33](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit33)) SVMs classify through the use of a hyperplane (a generalisation of a straight line to any number of dimensions) that best separates the dataset. If a data point resides on one side of the hyperplane, it is classified one way. If it lies on the other side of this hyperplane, it is classified the other way. This can be formalised by writing any hyperplane as the set of points *x* satisfying *w*^(*t*)*x*−*b*\=0. Thus, any hyperplane is defined by *w* and *b*, which are identified by training an SVM classifier. Assuming the input data is linearly separable (it can be divided into two non-intersecting sets with a hyperplane), training an SVM selects two parallel hyperplanes of the form *w*^(*t*)*x*−*b*\=1 and *w*^(*t*)*x*−*b*\=−1 by minimising the cost function shown in (7.1).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00169-t1.jpg)(7.1)

The constraint *y*[*i*](*w*^(*t*)*x*[*i*]−*b*)≥1 ensures that both hyperplanes separate the data whilst also maximising the distance between them, which is usually referred to as the margin. To maximise the margin, it is necessary that each of the two hyperplanes must pass through at least one of the data points. Such data points are known as “support vectors”, hence the model's name. The SVM determines the hyperplane that “best separates” the data by maximising the margin. The resulting classifying hyperplane takes the form *w*^(*t*)*x*−*b*\=0 and lies exactly halfway between the two. [Figure 7.2](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#fig2) illustrates this. A new data point *x̂* is classified as 1 if *w*^(*t*)*x̂*−*b*≥0 and −1 if *w*^(*t*)*x̂*−*b*≤0. The previous description was based on the assumption that the input data are linearly separable, but this often is not the case. To account for this case, one needs to incorporate slack variables into the SVM formulation. These variables allow certain data points to reside on the wrong side of the best separating hyperplane by adding a penalty to the cost function, as shown in [eqn (7.2)](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#eqn2).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00169-t2.jpg)(7.2)

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00169-f2.jpg)

Figure 7.2 An example of a set of linearly separable data points. Also shown is the optimal hyperplane that separates them. The highlighted points are the support vectors.^([33](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit33))

Here, the slack variables *ξ*[*i*] are greater than zero if a data point *x*[*i*] resides on the incorrect side of the hyperplane. A penalty of ![inline](images/bk9781788017893-00169-t3.jpg)is added to the cost function to account for this. *C* is a user-defined parameter that balances the number of incorrectly classified points against the best fitting hyperplane. A more thorough treatment of this can be found in the article by Bennett and Campbell, which also includes the extension to non-linear decision surfaces.^([34](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit34)) Furthermore, a number of other algorithms can be used to perform classification and these have been the subject of many reviews.^([35](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit35),[36](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit36))

Unsupervised learning is an approach in which we are only provided with input data and the aim is to find global (describing a property of the whole dataset or distribution) patterns within this. We distinguish this from data mining, which is a similar area of research that is more concerned with local (describing a subset of the whole dataset) patterns in the data. With no prior knowledge of the pattern, the method identifies them by searching for and exploiting commonalities within the data. A standard approach to this task would be to partition the data into sets of “similar” data points, or clusters. A clustering algorithm therefore creates a number of clusters and each data point is uniquely assigned to the cluster that it is most similar to. A simple, yet effective, algorithm to perform such a task would be *k*\-means.^([37](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit37)) Initially, *k* data points are randomly selected to be the cluster centres. Each cluster is formed by the subset of data points closest to the respective cluster centre. The cluster centres are recalculated as the mean of the points assigned to the cluster. All data points that are not cluster centres are reassigned to their closest cluster and this process repeats until the clusters no longer change. Whilst it can be used for classification and regression (see Erman, Arlitt and Mahanti^([38](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit38))), the process of identifying clusters is mainly used to better understand the dataset in question. Although *k*\-means is guaranteed to find a clustering of the data points into *k* clusters, it is up to the practitioner to determine if anything meaningful can be inferred from the clustering. Another popular unsupervised learning algorithm is Principal Component Analysis (PCA). This is a dimensionality reduction algorithm that reduces a set of possibly correlated variables into a set of linearly uncorrelated variables called the principal components. Each principal component is calculated in such a way that it retains as much variance as possible. The first principal component retains the largest possible variance and all subsequent components retain the largest possible variance given that they are orthogonal to the previous principal components. This results in a set of variables that best represent the data; PCA is commonly incorporated into data visualisation. By plotting the first two principal components, one can visualise a low-dimensional representation of the original dataset. This is one of the more traditional algorithms to perform dimensionality reduction. We point the reader to the review by Maaten, Postma, Herik for an overview of more recent approaches that aim to overcome the limitations of traditional PCA.^([39](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit39))*k*\-means is one of the simpler clustering methods and we encourage the reader to inspect the review by Fung for a more thorough overview of clustering methods.^([40](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit40))

Having chosen an algorithm and built a model, the next point of concern is to evaluate how well it performs. Whilst performance can be measured in a number of meaningful ways, a key issue is to understand how well it generalises. Analogous to how a school teaches its pupils a topic and then tests them on related, but unseen questions, we “teach” the model using a set of data and test it on similar, but previously unseen data. This allows us to assess whether the model has learnt anything useful and evaluate how well it has learnt. In such analyses, one first splits the dataset into a training and test set (a 70:30 split is common). A model is built using only the training set and is used to make predictions on the test set. The key idea here is that the model has never before seen the test set, so it is using the knowledge it has learnt from the training data to make its predictions. This approach allows us to state the generalisability of the model to unseen data points. However, this may not be an accurate assessment of generalisability, as it is dependent on which data points belong to the train and test set. *K*\-Fold Cross Validation (*K*\-Fold CV) is a procedure to overcome this. Instead of splitting a dataset into a train and test set once, *K*\-Fold CV performs the split *K* times. Initially, it divides the dataset into *K* sets (or folds) of approximately equal size. It takes the first fold to be the test set and the remaining *K*−1 folds to be the training set. The model is trained on the training set and makes predictions on the test set. This process is repeated using each fold once as the test set (ensuring that each data point belongs to the test set once). [Figure 7.3](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#fig3) illustrates this. A score that evaluates how close the model predictions are to the actual values can be calculated for each train/test split, from which an average can be taken to get an overall score. Further details about *K*\-Fold CV, as well as a number of other methods to estimate model accuracy and generalisability, can be found in the study by Kohavi.^([41](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit41)) Although *K*\-Fold CV is a quick and easy way to reduce over-estimation of model accuracy, the data is split into *K* sets randomly. Therefore, it could lead to an unreliable over-estimation of model performance if there is a distributional shift in the data. If the training and test sets are very similar, machine learning models can exhibit high accuracy due to memorising the training set (overfitting the data).^([42](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit42),[43](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit43)) In the case of synthetic route design (see Section 7.4), care needs to be taken in the construction of training and test sets. In particular, one should be mindful that if highly similar reactions are present in both the training and test set, one may make an overly optimistic estimate of the generalisation achieved by the algorithm. Conversely, if the test set reactions are too dissimilar to those in the training set, one will be trying to make predictions beyond the scope of what one might reasonably expect the algorithm to learn.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00169-f3.jpg)

Figure 7.3 An example of how K-Fold Cross Validation works. Here, *K*\=5.

Now we can quantify how good our model is, it is worth considering how to pick the best model from a set of models. Generally, we should only compare models performing the same task *e.g.* two regression models. Let's assume we have the results of *K*\-Fold CV for two different regression models. The next step in picking the best model would be to use a statistical test to determine whether the difference in performance is solely due to chance. One such test is the *t*\-test, with a null hypothesis of “the difference in the means is equal to zero”. This test can be used to evaluate whether the difference between the means of two datasets is statistically significant, and we could easily apply it to the results of our two *K*\-Fold CV procedures. Performing such a test would allow us to accept or reject the null hypothesis. As α is defined as the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is in fact true, the test indicating a rejection of the null hypothesis implies that we are (1−*α*)×100% certain that the difference in the means is not zero. Taking alpha to be 0.05, another way to state this is that the probability of observing these two *K*\-Fold CV results and their difference being due to chance is 0.05. This is an important point because things would change if we were to compare three models, which would involve three separate hypothesis tests. Assuming our confidence for each test is α, the probability of one of the differences due to chance is now 1−(1−0.05)³\=0.1426 and is approximately three times as likely. To account for this, we use the Bonferroni Correction which states that, when testing *N* hypotheses, our confidence for each test must be equal to ![inline](images/bk9781788017893-00169-t4.jpg). This is one of many corrections that are applicable to multiple hypothesis testing, see the paper by Goeman and Solari^([44](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit44)) for a wider overview and the article by Demšar^([45](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit45)) for a thorough treatment of many statistical tests related to machine learning.

## 7.4 Synthetic Route Design

Designing synthetic pathways can be divided into two categories that are inverse processes. The first category, forward reaction planning, requires prior knowledge of reactant precursors to predict possible products of reactions. Retrosynthesis is the second, working backwards from a target molecule, predicting possible bond disconnections to obtain simpler reactant precursors. This step happens recursively until commercially available reactant precursors are reached. The overall synthetic pathway of a target molecule is a series of reaction steps. Single-step retrosynthetic design is far more complex than forward reaction prediction as there is no single correct answer. This is due to functional groups present in the output (reactants) being absent from the input (products). In the example Buchwald-Hartwig reaction shown in [Figure 7.4a](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#fig4), the halide leaving group is not present in the product. Multiple precursors and different reactant types may be plausible for a single bond disconnection. For example, the C–N bond in the target shown in [Figure 7.4](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#fig4) can be synthesised by a Buchwald-Hartwig reaction with various halides or a Chan-Lam reaction. Without defining the reaction type, multiple bonds could be disconnected, particularly in larger molecules. In reaction prediction, all relevant functional groups are present in the input (reactants). This significantly reduces the number of possible reaction types that may occur and hence reduces the number of possible outputs in comparison to retrosynthesis.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00169-f4.jpg)

Figure 7.4 An example of forward synthetic planning (a) and retrosynthesis route design (b) and (c).

The most prominent approach to synthetic route design is the use of pre-defined heuristics to encode reactions. Heuristics, also known in this context as reaction templates, define a single chemical transformation from reactant(s) to product(s), or *vice versa*. Basic reaction templates contain the atoms and bonds involved in bond-making/breaking (the reaction centre) and any neighbouring atoms that may influence the reaction. Additional information may not be included due to data availability and inconsistency.^([8](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit8),[23](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit23)) More complex templates can include reaction conditions, reactivity conflicts, protection requirements as well as stereo-^(46) and regioselectivity.^([47](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit47),[48](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit48)) In multi-step retrosynthesis, the aim is to find the minimal number of reaction templates that need to be applied to a target molecule to reach commercially available reactant precursors. There is an inevitable trade-off between generalisation and specificity when defining reaction templates. If the templates are too generalised, the model will not be able to perceive any potential reactivity conflicts and may result in improper use. On the other hand, overly specific templates result in poor generalisability to unseen molecules.

Reaction templates are written in a user-friendly syntax, usually specific to the developers. Early programs manually hand-coded reaction templates.^([49](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit49)) This method suffered from three major issues: (1) Expert synthetic chemists with years of experience were required to code each reaction. (2) This labour-intensive task was not scalable to a large number of chemistries and incomplete template libraries covering a limited scope of reaction classes were often a result. (3) The complexity of reactions is not straight-forward due to reactivity conflicts and dependencies on reaction conditions and hence was difficult to codify. Despite these limitations, the commercially available program Synthia (formally Chematica) has proved that, with sufficient time investment, hand-coded reactions can be used successfully for the retrosynthesis prediction task.^([47](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit47),[48](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit48),[50](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit50)) A more efficient and less time-consuming process for defining templates is to extract reaction data automatically from the literature. Providing the reactions in the dataset are atom mapped, the reaction centre can be identified.^([8](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit8),[15](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit15),[46](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit46),[51](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit51)–[54](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit54)) Tools, such as the Reaction Decoder Tool (RDT), are available to calculate atom map indices if they are not known.^([52](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit52),[53](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit53)) A toolkit has also been developed for handling stereochemical information when defining reaction templates.^([54](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit54)) It is far easier to maintain automatically extracted template libraries and they have been employed in reaction prediction^([14](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit14),[55](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit55)) and retrosynthesis.^([14](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit14),[15](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit15),[56](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit56))

Contemporary template-based methods consist of two components: a pre-defined template library and a scoring function. These components can be combined in two different ways. The first is to exhaustively apply all possible reaction templates to obtain potential reactants or products and then rank the generated candidates.^([23](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit23)) The second is to rank the reaction templates and only apply the most relevant templates to the input molecule to generate candidate species.^([14](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit14),[15](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit15),[46](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit46)) ANNs have been applied to both candidate and template ranking.^([14](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit14),[15](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit15),[23](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit23)) The similarity-based approach is slightly different to contemporary methods, as there is no pre-defined template library. This method is used exclusively in retrosynthesis. The target molecule is compared to the products in a knowledge base, reaction templates are extracted from the most similar reactions and are applied to the target to generate reactant candidates. The similarity of the candidates is compared to the precedent's reactants and used in combination with the product similarity score to rank the reactant precursors. This similarity-based approach differs from purely template-based methods as it is fully data driven.

Although template and similarity-based methods are easily interpretable, as they align with the way a synthetic chemist thinks, they have several limitations. The constant maintenance of template libraries is time-consuming and can be challenging when including new chemistries. Automatic extraction of templates from datasets is heavily dependent on atom-mapped reactions, which are not always completed or correct. Also, common atom-mapping tools are based on predefined expert rules. Reaction templates only focus on the local environment of reaction centres and, therefore, important groups in the global environment may be missed. Template-based methods are not able to make accurate predictions outside of their template library and hence cannot discover novel chemistries.^([14](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit14)) However, these methods are useful in aiding synthetic chemists with everyday retrosynthesis tasks.

The alternative to template-based methods is template-free methods. These methods are fully data driven and trained end-to-end without the construction of predefined reaction heuristics. Therefore, template-free methods are scalable to large datasets at a fraction of the computational cost and are generalisable to novel chemistries. To date, template-free models have either been graph-based or sequence-based. Graph-based models follow the same two-step procedure as those that are template-based in that reaction centres are identified to generate reactant precursors or products, depending on the task. Predictions generated from this approach are easily interpretable as the approach is analogous to that of a synthetic chemist. Reaction centres have been identified to generate product candidates using a convolutional neural network on molecular graph descriptors.^([20](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit20),[55](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit55)) Graph-based models have only focused on reaction prediction and not retrosynthesis.

Sequence-based models have a different approach to the above-mentioned methods. Here, the problem can be thought of as a machine translation task, whereby a language (*e.g.* English) is entered into a model that translates the text into another language (*e.g.* Spanish). When applied to reaction prediction and retrosynthesis the molecules can be represented by text notation, such as SMILES strings (see Section 7.2.2). In reaction prediction, the reactant SMILES strings are translated into a product SMILES string and *vice versa* for retrosynthesis. Sequence-to-sequence models have an encoder-decoder architecture consisting of two recurrent neural networks and an additional attention mechanism.^([10](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit10),[27](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit27),[29](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit29)) In this type of model each token in the SMILES string is assumed to be related to its neighbour and hence influences the nature of the neighbouring token. For each SMILES token, these models will only learn the local surrounding tokens and not tokens that are far away in the sequence. A transformer-based architecture has been adapted for the machine translation task.^([57](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit57)) These models differ from sequence-to-sequence models, as they do not contain recurrent neural networks. They have a fully attention-based encoder-decoder architecture. As the recurrent component is missing, the model is able to correlate individual tokens in the SMILES string regardless of their location. Unlike the sequence-to-sequence models, transformer models are able to capture long range interactions between tokens. Transformer models have shown success in both forward reaction prediction^([28](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit28)) and single-step retrosynthesis.^([11](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit11),[12](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit12),[24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24),[58](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit58)) Sequence-based models have some advantages over two-step graph-based models. They do not require atom-mapping, atom features nor any chemical knowledge. The global environment of the molecules is also implicitly incorporated into the model. The major drawback to sequence-based methods is SMILES invalidity. The models do not directly learn the terminology of the SMILES notation, so these cannot be guaranteed to predict valid SMILES. The attention mechanisms present in all the template-free methods discussed enable the models to be interpreted. Attention weights of the atoms (*i.e.* the SMILES tokens) can be used to identify which aspects of the input species influence the output species.

The performance of synthetic route design models is a balance between accuracy, reliability, and adaptability. Model accuracy can be calculated as the percentage of test set predictions where the ground truth was ranked within the top-*n* per cent of the predicted molecules for the given target. For example, the top-1 accuracy is the percentage of predictions where the correct molecule was ranked in the top-1 per cent. A model should be able to estimate the reliability of its predictions. The calculation of confidence scores should be implemented into model evaluation to identify when the model is likely to fail.^([24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24),[28](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit28)) It is important to know how adaptable a model is. A model may have high accuracy scores, but can it generalise across chemical space? For example, if trained on patent data can it accurately predict synthetic routes to molecules in ELNs that cover a different range of chemical space?^([24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24)) These are important points to consider when evaluating synthetic route design models.

### 7.4.1 Retrosynthesis

#### 7.4.1.1 Single-step Retrosynthesis

A combination of template-based and template-free models have been developed for the single-step retrosynthesis task. A target molecule is entered into the model which then disconnects a bond and generates possible reactant precursors. A benchmark dataset of 50 000 reactions extracted from US patents, herein named the USPTO\_50K (see Section 7.2.1),^([21](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit21)) has been used to train and test single-step retrosynthesis prediction tools (see [Table 7.2](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#tab2)). A template-based model was built by Liu *et al.* as a baseline model.^([10](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit10)) The reaction templates consisting of the reaction centre, neighbouring atoms, and the reaction class were automatically extracted from the training data. For each target molecule, all templates in the same reaction class were applied to generate reactant candidates that were subsequently ranked. The similarity-based approach described previously, another type of template-based method, outperformed the baseline and the template-free sequence-to-sequence model developed by Liu *et al.* in every reaction class.^([9](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit9),[10](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit10)) The similarity-based model does not focus on finding only the major product but ranking all possibilities. As a result, it has the highest top-5 per cent accuracy of 81.2% when the reaction class is known prior. This approach is limited beyond the scope of the knowledge base and will always disfavour creative disconnections.

 

Table 7.2 The top-n accuracy for the Baseline^([10](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit10)) and Similarity^([9](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit9)) template-based models as well as the Seq2seq,^([10](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit10)) Transformer – Lin *et al.*,^([12](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit12)) SCROP,^([11](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit11)) MT^([24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24)) and Transformer – Karpov *et al.*^([58](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit58)) template-free models.

Sequence-based, template-free models (Transformer – Lin *et al.*,^([12](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit12)) SCROP,^([11](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit11)) MT^([24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24)) and Transformer – Karpov *et al.*^([58](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit58))) with a transformer architecture can overcome these limitations and have shown to be state-of-the-art even when the reaction class is unknown (see [Table 7.2](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#tab2)). As previously mentioned, a drawback to these methods is the prediction of invalid SMILES. The standard transformer architecture does not learn the grammar of the SMILES notation. Therefore, a predicted SMILES string may be grammatically invalid, but the grammatically correct version may be the ground truth. The self-corrected retrosynthesis predictor (SCROP) has an additional component to the other transformer models.^([11](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit11)) Once a reactant SMILES is predicted, a transformer-based syntax predictor is used to automatically correct the SMILES string if it is not syntactically plausible. The addition of the syntax predictor improves the SMILES invalidity rate (see [Table 7.3](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#tab3)), remaining under 2.0% for the top-5 per cent of SMILES strings. The SMILES invalidity rate of the SCROP^([11](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit11)) model is also lower than the Seq2seq^([10](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit10)) and Transformer – Lin *et al.*^([12](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit12)) models. The Molecular Transformer (MT^([24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24))) model does not report a SMILES invalidity rate for comparison. The SCROP^([11](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit11)) model achieves the highest top-1 accuracy of 59.0% when the reaction class was known.

However, it is more realistic that the reaction class is unknown. Model training and testing of the Similarity,^([9](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit9)) Transformer – Lin *et al.*,^([12](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit12)) SCROP,^([11](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit11)) MT^([24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24)) and Transformer – Karpov *et al.*^([58](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit58)) models were performed without prior knowledge of the reaction class. Removal of the reaction class resulted in a drop of 11-16% in the top-1 per cent accuracy (see [Table 7.2](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#tab2)). All the transformer-based models have comparable top-1 accuracies.

#### 7.4.1.2 Multi-step Retrosynthesis

The aim of CASD software is not only to predict the reactant precursors of a target molecule but also to break down the precursors recursively until they are commercially available. This multi-step retrosynthesis task can be thought of as a synthesis tree. A synthesis tree will have a branching factor - the number of possible steps that can be taken from a particular molecule - and a depth - how many steps until the path is terminated. Pathway termination will occur if the precursors found are commercially available or if a predefined depth constraint is reached. For retrosynthesis, the branching factor is usually large and the depth low. The number of possible synthetic routes drastically increases with the number of steps in a pathway (depth). CASD tools require intelligent algorithms to identify the most promising branches and avoid exhaustive calculation of all possibilities. Unfortunately, choosing the optimum predicted reaction at every step may not lead to the most efficient pathway. The effect of each decision will not be known until the cost of the entire pathway is calculated. This cost could be related to the price of starting materials, the number of steps, waste generated, greenness, ease of product purification, sustainability, safety hazards, or environmental hazards. CASD tools generate synthesis trees to minimise a cost function that is often user-defined.

Commercially available CASD programs include InfoChem's ICSYNTH,^([46](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit46)) Wiley's ChemPlanner™ (formerly ARChem Route Designer)^([51](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit51)) that has integrated into CAS’ SciFinder^n and Synthia™ (formerly Chematica), a trademark of Merck KGaA.^([47](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit47),[48](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit48),[50](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit50)) These programs are based on reaction templates. Synthia™ contains a template library of *ca.* 60 000 reaction templates, hand-coded by expert synthetic chemists. Along with reaction transforms, the templates also encode possible incompatibility groups, protecting groups and reaction conditions. ICSYNTH and ChemPlanner™ automatically extracted templates, consisting of the reaction centre and neighbouring atom/groups, from reaction databases. ICSYNTH also provides software to generate template libraries from in-house data that can be used independently or alongside the supplied libraries. Scoring functions, based on user-defined criteria, evaluate each synthetic step and guide the search to commercially available substrates. Synthia™ and ICSYNTH filter the predictions to remove any unwanted structures. Additional heuristics are defined in Synthia™ to penalise non-selective reactions, strained intermediates, and unlikely structural motifs. In ICSYNTH, the predicted structure is compared to a predefined list of unacceptable structures. ChemPlanner™ uses a similar approach to filter out functional group incompatibilities. Synthia™ and ChemPlanner™ account for regiochemistry and electronic effects. Synthia™ can also handle stereochemistry and steric effects. Each program generates synthesis trees with references to supporting literature and the cost of starting materials.

Segler and Waller have published their neural-symbolic model, composed of three neural networks (expansion policy, in-scope filter and rollout phase) combined with Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) to guide the multi-step retrosynthesis search.^([15](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit15)) Reaction templates were extracted from 12.4 million reactions published before 2015 in Reaxys. The expansion policy and in-scope filter together are known as the expansion procedure, which is based on a knowledge base of 301 671 reaction templates containing reaction centres. The expansion procedure was applied to each target molecule to predict the reactant precursors for a single step. Here, the target molecule was represented by fingerprints and inputted to the expansion policy to prioritise the reaction templates. The top *k* templates were applied to the target to generate reactant candidates. The in-scope filter classified the reactions as feasible or not, to filter out any unfeasible reactions. The rollout policy, based on 17 134 reaction templates (containing reaction centres and neighbouring atoms), calculated tree position values. The expansion procedure and the rollout policy are incorporated into the MCTS algorithm to forms the 3N-MCTS model. Predicted pathways generated by the model for drug-like compounds could not be distinguished from literature routes according to a double-blind AB test. While the 3N-MCTS model can account for stereochemistry, it does not consider the prediction of reaction conditions in pathway generation.

### 7.4.2 Reaction Prediction

Retrosynthetic routes, either predicted by chemists or machine, are not guaranteed to be experimentally feasible. To validate the routes, one option is to test all the possibilities experimentally, which requires experienced synthetic chemists, a substantial amount of time, and high costs. An alternative validation technique is forward reaction prediction. Here, the reactants, reagents and possibly reaction conditions are known, and the aim is to predict possible products. It is important to include reaction conditions in the model as slight changes in solvent or temperature can result in a large change in yield or the formation of a different major product. Quantum chemical calculations can be used to identify the major product, but the calculations are computationally expensive and limited to smaller molecules. Machine learning and artificial intelligence can be applied to large systems at a low computational cost.

The benchmark dataset for reaction prediction is the USPTO\_MIT dataset (Section 7.1) composed of *ca.* 480K reactions.^([20](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit20)) State-of-the-art in reaction prediction are template-free models (see [Table 7.4](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#tab4)). The graph-based Weisfeiler-Lehman Difference Network (WLDN^([55](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit55))) model outperformed the sequence-to-sequence (S2S^([27](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit27))) model with an increase of 5.3% top-1 per cent accuracy. The WLDN model identifies the reaction centre from a reactant pool consisting of reactants, reagents and solvent species using a Weisfeiler-Lehman Network, a type of graph convolutional neural network. Another graph convolutional neural network (WLDN) then ranks the candidate products generated by focused enumeration. A sequence-based transformer model, the Molecular Transformer (MT^([28](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit28))), outperformed the graph-based model (WLDN) by 4.8% in the top-1 per cent accuracy. The reported accuracies are for the USPTO\_MIT dataset that was pre-processed to distinguish between reactants and reagents, prior to model training and testing. Removing the distinction results in lower model accuracy, 5.6% lower for the WLDN model and 1.8% for the MT model.

To assess the adaptability of the MT model, the MT and WLDN models were trained on the USPTO\_MIT data and tested on reaction data within ELNs from Pfizer.^([24](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit24)) The two datasets cover different regions of chemical space, which ensures the elimination of control bias from analogous reactions in the reported model accuracies. The MT model predicts the correct molecule within the top-1 per cent 69.0% of the time when predicting outside of its trained chemical space (see [Table 7.4](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#tab4)). The transformer-based architecture is currently the highest performing model type for both forward reaction prediction and single-step retrosynthesis.

### 7.4.3 Optimising Reaction Conditions

Identifying reaction conditions requires the expert knowledge and experience of a synthetic chemist. A reaction may be carried out under a variety of reaction conditions, but the most common conditions selected are those used for similar reactions that proved to be successful. Selection based on similarity can be insufficient, as reaction outcomes are influenced by a number of reaction parameters. Reaction conditions are therefore challenging to anticipate, especially because small changes in reaction parameters can result in quite different reaction outcomes or failed reactions. Chemists are required to find a combination of catalyst(s), reagent(s), solvent(s), temperature and pressure that work. Predictions from CASD programs and reaction prediction methods can only be validated experimentally if corresponding reaction conditions are also predicted. Therefore, incorporating condition prediction into such tools is crucial.

The prediction of reaction conditions is an under-explored area that has mainly focused on the optimisation of a single reaction condition or single reaction class. A binary classification model has been implemented for the prediction of the type of catalyst and solvent used in Michael additions.^([59](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit59)) A similarity-based approach was employed for the identification of catalysts for catalytic hydrogenation reactions, a type of deprotection reaction. The greatest interest has been in catalyst prediction and optimisation. Catalysts are important as they can increase rates of reactions and, in asymmetric catalysis, allow for the selectivity of one stereoisomer. Efforts to predict the selectivity of asymmetric catalysts have the potential to change how catalysts are designed, when one stereoisomer is favoured.^([60](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit60)–[63](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit63))

It is desired that reaction condition prediction tools allow for the prediction of all reaction conditions. A neural network has been built to predict catalyst(s), solvent(s), reagent(s) and temperature for a range of chemical reactions, which can be applied on a large scale.^([16](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit16)) The combination of machine learning with an automated synthesis and testing module is the future of reaction condition optimisation.^([64](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit64)) Computer-assisted synthetic planning and a robotic flow chemistry platform have been built for the execution of predicted synthetic routes to small molecules. This is a step closer to fully automatic synthetic chemistry.

## 7.5 Real-life Applications

CASD programs (see Section 7.4.1.2) that predict multi-step synthetic pathways to molecules may have high validation scores, but chemists will remain cautious until there is evidence supporting their true value. Applications thus far are primarily focused on drug-like targets and bioactive molecules.

InfoChem, in collaboration with AstraZeneca, has evaluated the performance of ICSYNTH (see Section 7.4.1.2) to act as an idea generator.^([46](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit46)) The ability of the program to predict routes to medicinal targets, present in AstraZeneca's commercial drug projects or the literature, was assessed. Predicted pathways were compared to the literature, brainstorm proposals and in-house experience of chemists working on the projects. Without prior knowledge of the brainstorm proposals, ICSYNTH rediscovered known chemistries, returned brainstorm suggestions and provided new unreported synthetic routes. Due to its unbiased nature, it also identified an unconventional transformation that leads to a non-intuitive solution to a problem.^([46](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit46)) ICSYNTH is able to generate ideas to complement synthetic chemists.

In a case study, synthetic routes proposed by ChemPlanner™ (see Section 7.4.1.2) were verified experimentally.^([65](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit65)) Synthetic routes to medicinally relevant targets were compared to routes developed by chemists. ChemPlanner™ identified almost all routes designed by chemists, although not all were identified as the best routes due to the scoring functions within the program. Alternative routes with fewer steps and lower costs were also suggested. Therefore, ChemPlanner™ can assist synthetic chemists in designing synthetic routes, saving them time and money.

Synthia™ (see Section 7.4.1.2) uses network theory, high power computing, AI, and expert chemical knowledge to design retrosynthetic pathways.^([47](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit47)) It can design novel synthesis routes to medicinally and industrially relevant targets. The program found synthetic routes to the selection of eight commercial bioactive substances and natural products.^([47](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit47)) The target products were chosen where previous attempts at synthesis were low yielding, not scalable, or failed. The predicted pathways were evaluated experimentally. Synthia™ designed routes that improved yields and saved money and time. It also designed a successful pathway to one of the targets that had no known synthetic routes. An extension of Synthia™ enables one to avoid patented routes.^([48](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit48)) It is important not to breach existing patented routes when designing pathways to novel molecules. A bond preservation method identifies bonds, which are essential to patents and prevents their disconnection in retrosynthesis. To validate this method, three commercial drugs linezolid, sitagliptin, and panobinostat were evaluated by Synthia™. Predicted pathways were generated with and without the patent bond constraints. Without constraints, Synthia™ suggested similar routes to the patents. However, by selecting the bonds that are not to be broken, the program could navigate around them and identify alternative routes.

## 7.6 Conclusions

In the pharmaceutical industry, progression from early-stage drug candidates to preclinical trials is performed in the quickest and the most cost-efficient manner. Synthetic chemistry has facilitated both drug discovery and development. Medicinal chemistry is a significant part of drug discovery, the aim being to design and synthesise novel small drug candidates for testing medicinal chemical hypotheses. For a single biological target, many analogues of lead compounds are synthesised on a small scale for screening, to identify structure–activity relationships. Medicinal chemists require reliable synthetic pathways that will deliver material for test quickly. Consequently, medicinal chemists are biased towards robust reactions when designing routes to novel molecules.^([66](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit66)) The use of artificial intelligence and machine learning in CADS programs removes this personal bias in its predictions and therefore can broaden the medicinal chemists’ toolbox.

Process chemistry is the key in drug development, whereby active pharmaceutical ingredients are scaled up and reactions are optimised. Process chemists usually work on a single target molecule, as opposed to many analogues. Synthetic routes to target molecules are optimised to meet SELECT (safety, environmental, legal, economics, control, and throughput) criteria.^([67](#BK9781788017893-00169.xhtml#cit67)) Synthetic accessibility of molecules is one of the several criteria that influence which compounds are selected to be synthesised in medicinal chemistry and is an important concept in process chemistry. It is desirable to know whether a compound is synthesisable prior to performing the reactions experimentally. The closest to knowing is to predict synthetic pathways with high confidence. CASD programs could assist medicinal and process chemists in accelerating synthetic planning timelines, reducing the number of steps in a pathway, reducing costs, and suggesting alternative, unconventional pathways.

There are clear advantages for synthetic chemists to incorporate CASD into their everyday working lives. However, poor model interpretability has created suspicion among synthetic chemists. As a result, there is limited implementation of the tools. The so-called black-box tools will not be accepted unless they can be justified by literature or preferably, experimentally. Early and strong engagement with synthetic chemists will facilitate more rapid development of CASD with wider acceptance and uptake from the community.

There are other challenges that also need to be addressed to achieve advancement in CASD. Reaction data and code sharing are at the top of the list. Open-source large datasets containing counter-examples are required for training algorithms to perform optimally. Reaction data need to be of high quality and reproducible, containing no prophetic examples. There is a call for open sharing of machine-readable data and to define publication standards in order to incorporate this. Open sharing would allow for fair benchmarking of different methods. Rigorous validation methods for the assessment of model generalisability need to be established to ensure that reported results are not misleading.

CASD programs are aimed to assist synthetic chemists in the decision-making process for designing pathways. They are not intended to replace synthetic chemists; chemical intuition is still needed. The combination of robotics with CASD is the future of automated reaction optimisation. Such units would improve productivity in synthetic laboratories but will not replace the bench chemists.

Constraining Chemical Networks in Astrochemistry

SERENA VITI[\*](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#affc)^([a](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#affa),[b](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#affb)) AND JONATHAN HOLDSHIP^([a](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#affa),[b](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#affb))

^b Leiden Observatory, Leiden University, PO Box 9513, NL-2300 RA Leiden, The Netherlands
