## 8.1 Introduction

The space between the stars, the interstellar medium (ISM), is far from empty. The ISM is populated with interstellar clouds and filaments, made of gas (∼99%) and dust (∼1%). These clouds and filaments are the birth sites of stars.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit1),[2](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit2)) Modelling the physical and chemical processes leading to the formation of stars and, hence, planets is a highly non-linear, very time-dependent, problem, involving a multi-layered interconnection between the physics and the chemistry of the gas and the dust. Despite the many advances driven by state-of-the-art telescopes, we are still far from solving the ‘star formation problem’: stars form in molecular filaments or clumps, cold (∼10 K) and relatively dense (>10⁴ particles cm^(−3)) regions of the interstellar medium, where most of the gas is molecular. These regions also contain higher-density cores. The first two stages of the formation of solar-like systems involve highly non-linear physical and chemical processes that are hard to corroborate by astronomical observations alone. In the first stage, some cores can become gravitationally unstable and initiate star formation. This collapse is controlled by the presence of molecules, which cool the gas and allow gravity to overcome hydrostatic equilibrium. During this pre-stellar core phase, due to the high density and low temperatures in the cores, species from the gas phase ‘freeze’ onto the dust grains present and form an icy mantle. The gas and surface compositions during these two stages exhibit a complicated time dependent, non-linear chemistry that strongly depends on the physical environment.^([3](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit3)) Little experimental information is available for the interstellar ices. What is the unprocessed ice composition? What are the efficiencies of the viable surface reactions? And how do the energetics of the ISM (cosmic rays, UV radiation, shocks) influence the processed ices?

Examples of key issues involve even the simplest molecules: the CO molecule sticks efficiently to surfaces at temperatures below ∼25 K and is abundant in the ices. Some of this CO can be converted to other species, and the observation of CO[2] and CH[3]OH in ices^([4](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit4)) suggests that this *processing* does occur. H[2]CO, CH[3]OH, and glycolaldehyde are involved in the surface hydrogenation of CO, and determining their chemistry in star-forming regions is vital for studies of prebiotic chemistry.^([5](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit5)) Some ices return to the gas phase when the gas temperature rises above 20 K. At lower temperatures, non-thermal desorption processes can still return molecules from solid to gas-phase.^([6](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit6)) However, these non-thermal mechanisms ‘compete’ with the freeze-out. Gas-phase chemistry is better constrained than surface chemistry; nevertheless, many uncertainties still remain on the formation and efficiencies of routes for some of the most complex species (routinely called Complex Organic Molecules or COMs by astronomers) observed in space.^([7](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit7),[8](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit8)) In summary, the composition of the gas and icy mantles varies according to a time-dependent process, which is highly dependent on the conditions of the gas and dust in any particular cloud.

In the second stage, *i.e.* when the protostar is born, the gravitational energy is converted into radiation and the envelope around the central object, the future star, warms up. The molecules frozen on the grain mantles during the previous phase acquire mobility and likely form new, more complex species. When the temperature reaches the mantle sublimation temperature of ∼100 K, the molecules in the mantles are injected into the gas, where they react and form new, more complex molecules. Simultaneously, a fraction of matter is violently ejected outward in the form of highly supersonic collimated jets and molecular outflows. When the outflowing material encounters the quiescent gas of molecular cloud, it creates shocks, where the grain mantles are (partially) sputtered and the refractory grains are shattered. Once in the gas phase, molecules can be and are observed *via* their rotational lines. Again, as during the first stage, the interaction of gas and dust, and hence the gas composition, varies within very short timescales (less than one hundred years), and the effects of chemistry and dynamics are interlocked in a complex non-linear fashion.^([9](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit9))

In both stages, molecules provide an essential tool for the analysis of the chemical and physical conditions of star- and planet-forming regions. Each stellar or planetary evolutionary stage is characterized by a chemical composition, which, *if properly interpreted*, leads to the determination of the physical processes of its phase.

This brief description of the multi-million years of star formation cycle highlights our challenge: the interconnection and non-linear correlation of the many parameters with each other or with extra, unknown ones, makes determining and specifying the parameter network within chemical models a highly challenging task.

Of particular importance is the reliability of the chemical reactions datasets. Databases of chemical reactions and rate coefficients for both gas and solid-phase reactions are the *key* input to all chemical models. While there are some gas-phase databases online, in reality each research group creates a personal version of such databases, especially as there is no accepted standard for databases; in addition, there is no database containing a complete set of solid-phase reactions. We explore the completeness and reliability of such databases in the next section.

## 8.2 Completeness and Reliability of Chemical Reactions Databases

Typically, chemical models of the ISM in use today employ databases of mainly 2-body (sometimes 3-body) chemical reactions; these contain long lists of gas and solid-phase chemical reactions. In the gas-phase, for each reaction, three constants are provided that are then used to calculate the rate coefficient. The first constant (usually α) represents the rate at 300 K and the other two constants (β and γ) give the temperature scaling of that rate. For photo-reactions, an equivalent set of constants gives the rate in an unshielded interstellar UV field and the extinction dependence of that rate. These three constants will have their own associated uncertainty. Depending on the physical conditions, between 20 and 50% of the reactions may not have been experimentally studied. In some cases, chemical reaction rates are therefore highly speculative.

For reactions occurring on the dust grains, the pathways, efficiencies, and branching ratios are even more uncertain than for the gas-phase reactions, due to the lack of experimental data. Surface reactions are, therefore, highly speculative and consequently are often not included in astrochemical models.

Reducing the degree of uncertainty for all the reactions would require an unfeasibly large number of laboratory experiments. Yet, chemical models fully rely on these databases, making their accuracy a prime problem for Astrochemistry. In the next two sections, we will describe elaborately the two categories of databases: gas-phase and surface reaction networks.

### 8.2.1 Gas-phase Networks

All the astrochemical models developed through the years calculate the abundances of hundreds of species involved in thousands of chemical reactions. Gas-phase reactions are the backbone of chemical networks as they are the primary routes for the formation and destruction of most molecules. Hence, a poor understanding of the rate coefficients can lead to large errors in the abundances of the main molecules observed in the ISM.

The range of kinetic temperatures and gas densities over which we need accurate rate coefficients will depend on the region of space that we need to model, but it can be from 10 K to >1000 K and from 100 to 10^(14) particles cm^(−3), respectively. Chemical reactions, under these conditions, can be studied in the laboratory or theoretically. However, each experiment, or study, takes at least a few months to complete. Often then, rate coefficients are estimated from other already known rate coefficients. More importantly, even if every reaction were to be experimentally or theoretically investigated, it would be impossible to do so under the whole range applicable to the ISM and many extrapolations are therefore performed. Measures have been taken by the community to compile databases where some quality assurance is performed. For example, the Kinetic Database for Astrochemistry (KIDA)^([10](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit10)) is a public gas-phase network, which provides all the rate coefficients from various sources and evaluates their accuracy where possible. We refer the reader to^([10](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit10)) for a detailed explanation of this network. However, even the best efforts at transparency and completeness such as KIDA fall short of providing the user with a complete, accurate, and reliable gas-phase network that includes all the possible species involved in the complex chemistry routinely observed in the ISM. This is especially true for complex organic molecules, which are species that contain 6 or more atoms, are present in the ISM mostly with low abundances and yet are key for our understanding of prebiotic chemistry in space.^([7](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit7)) Gas-phase networks including the formation and destruction of COMs are far from complete^([11](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit11),[12](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit12)) and astrochemical models have been struggling to explain the observed abundances of COMs. While most current models tend to favour grain surface over gas-phase chemistry in COMs formation, several studies have now shown that COMs may indeed form in the gas phase but that, due to the incompleteness of gas-phase networks involving COMs, the relative contribution of gas-phase *versus* surface reactions cannot be quantified.

### 8.2.2 Grain-surface Networks

There is no doubt that dust grain chemistry plays a pivotal role in the formation of key abundant species observed routinely in the ISM *e.g.* H[2]O, CH[3]OH, and NH[3] which are primarily formed through solid state chemistry.^([13](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit13),[14](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit14)) Although debate exists on whether gas-phase reactions contribute to the formation of COMs, it is clear that the latter are at least partly formed on the surface of the grains.^([7](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit7),[8](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit8),[15](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit15))

We know that dust grains act as ‘catalysts’ meaning that – on their surface – surface reactions and energetic radiation can synthesize molecules as complex as prebiotic species^([16](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit16),[17](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit17)) starting from very simple molecules (*e.g.* CO and N[2]) and atoms (H, C, O, N, S *etc.*) deposited from the gas when the temperature of the medium is close to 10 K. In the last couple of decades, many experiments have been performed to evaluate surface chemical reactions (see the review in ref. [18](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit18)).

Molecular hydrogen was the first molecule to be studied on dust surfaces.^([19](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit19)) Many experiments since then have been performed to study the formation of more complex molecules *e.g.* ref. [20](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit20)–[22](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit22) as well as the ice morphology and ice mantle mechanisms *e.g.* ref. [23](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit23) and [24](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit24). However, all these experiments are performed within a constrained range of laboratory conditions, which differ from those found in the ISM: for example, atomic fluxes, ice temperatures, ice morphologies, and mixture ratios, energetic processes in the laboratory will differ from those found in the ISM. Hence formation, desorption and destruction routes and rates for surface molecules as derived from experiments may not always be exhaustive to the needs of the chemical modellers. In other words, experimental data for interstellar ices are limited, as the experimentation process is neither simple nor fast. As a consequence, most chemical models either include very simple surface reaction networks or ones where most of the reactions are essentially guesswork.

## 8.3 A Bayesian Approach

In astrochemistry, it is not common to use Bayesian methods as a means of deriving posterior probability distributions (PPDs) for model parameters from observations. The first study to do so^([9](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit9)) used Bayesian inference to derive parameters such as the gas density and cosmic-ray ionization rates within a dark molecular cloud from observations of species in the gas and ices using chemical models. This study particularly highlighted the nature of the problem at hand, namely that astrochemical problems are typically non-linear, ill-posed inverse problems where solutions may not be unique or may not depend continuously on the observational data. In one study,^([9](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit9)) a Bayesian approach based on the use of the Metropolis–Hastings (MH) algorithm (an example of a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm) was adopted and they used a simplified version of UCLCHEM (a time-dependent gas–grain chemical model, now open source: [https://uclchem.github.io/](http://https://uclchem.github.io/)) to explore a nine-dimensional parameter space for molecular clouds. They ran two identical sets of eight MCMC chains differing only in the way the prior distribution information was set, with the first set having a non-informative prior information in the form of an acceptable range of possible values for observed ices, while in the second the prior include all the observational constraints from observations, including gas-phase abundances. Of particular relevance to this review, it is interesting to see how the different prior distributions have affected the resulting Posterior Probability Distributions (PPD) for one of their dimensions: the branching ratios for some key chemical reactions pathways *e.g.* those that control how much of the oxygen that freezes on the grains turns into H[2]O or OH. With noninformative uniform prior, the high-density regions of the PPD cover excessively large sections of the distribution, meaning that the branching ratio could not be constrained enough. With informative priors, the high-density region in the PPD is reduced and gives a clear indication that the production of water over OH is favoured. This example showed for the first time in Astrochemistry that branching ratio parameters can be successfully estimated through Bayesian MCMC methods.

A more recent work^([25](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit25)) used the above methodologies as a proof of concept in an attempt to infer rates of reactions for a limited surface network, and in doing so provided the means to derive reduced networks in the context of observational constraints. In this work, a simple chemical model was developed that considers only the solid state chemistry in the ice mantles of dust grains in a dark molecular cloud. The simplified model is a time-dependent single-point model that generates a time series of solid-phase molecular abundances as a function of the physical conditions of the molecular cloud and the chemical parameters of the defined chemical network. This network only included surface reactions and mainly hydrogenation of common gas-phase species. We report these reactions in [Table 8.1](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#tab1).

They find that when observational constraints directly constrain the abundance of a species involved in a reaction, the range of likely values for the rate of that reaction can be sufficiently narrowed for use in chemical models. Therefore, this method represents a method by which reliable reaction rates can be obtained for use in modelling until laboratory measurements or theoretical work supersede them.

Although this approach has many strengths, it requires a large amount of computational power. In both of the above examples, the chemical model used for the inference was greatly simplified in comparison with a typical model used to interpret observations. Where the model itself is not the subject of the inference (as it is in the work of ref. [25](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit25)), we might use machine learning to map from model inputs to outputs in order to do more efficient parameter inference on the input parameters.

## 8.4 Machine Learning Techniques for Complex Networks

Ultimately, chemical modellers need to be able to rely on *complete* and accurate chemical reaction networks. Reducing the degree of uncertainty for such networks requires cutting edge Artificial Intelligence techniques combining Artificial Neural Networks, Bayesian Inference methods, and advanced Monte Carlo sampling algorithms. While we are still quite a way from achieving these, ML techniques have now started being used in Astrochemistry.

A neural network was used to emulate a full chemical model.^([26](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit26)) By creating a training set from the outputs of a full model (UCLCHEM^([†](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#fn1))) for a wide range of input physical parameters, they were able to train a neural network to predict these outputs. This allows for the computation of chemical abundances required to interpret observations in milliseconds rather than the minutes of CPU time required to run a full chemical model. Consequently, computationally intensive parameter inference can be performed using a close approximation of a full chemical model without taking an infeasible amount of CPU time.

Such neural networks would have uses beyond the direct interpretation of observations. Many radiative hydrodynamical simulations use highly approximate radiative-chemical treatments to provide the cooling rates for the simulated gas. This is a necessity when a full chemical model would add to the computational burden of an already intensive model. However, evaluating a neural network is generally a small task and as such, more accurate chemistry could be inserted into physical models in the form of pre-trained neural network emulators.

The use of machine learning techniques on chemical networks could be of particular importance for the reduction and accuracy of networks of complex organic molecules, in particular those that are as yet undetected in the ISM. For example, the ‘holy grail’ for astrochemists is to find amino acids in space. Amino acids are important organic compounds that play a key role in the formation of proteins. In the protein production process, amino acids join together to form polymer chains, which represent the structural units of proteins. It is believed that the formation of amino acids may indeed have occurred in the ISM, as they have been firmly detected in meteorites.^([27](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit27)) This is supported by laboratory experiments where amino acids are found to form on the surface of model dust grains by UV-photon and ion irradiation of suitable precursor molecules under astrophysically relevant conditions.^([28](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit28),[29](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit29)) Despite great efforts towards their detection, a firm detection of amino acids in the ISM is still – unfortunately – eluding us.

One possible solution to this is to use ML tools to identify weak signals from the amino acids in spectroscopic telescope data. When detecting molecules, strong peaks in the spectra from an observed object are identified by matching their frequency to known emitting frequencies of molecules. If the emission is weak it may not be detected by a human, or the statistical significance of many weak lines may be missed. A classification model trained to categorize spectra as containing a particular molecule or not, based on the spectral noise and the emission profile at various frequencies, could give confident detections in cases that a human would miss. In the case of previously undetected molecules, such as amino acids, a training set can be produced by creating many synthetic spectra. Further, such an analysis could be performed on thousands of targets with little effort which has made it an interesting prospect for the exo-planetary community aiming to identify molecules in planetary atmospheres.^([30](#BK9781788017893-00195.xhtml#cit30))

Another solution is to focus our search by determining the optimal conditions for observing amino acids. It is likely that, if present, such amino acids must form on the mantle of dust grains. It is therefore essential we determine the optimal conditions under which simple amino acids, such as glycine and alanine, can form on the dust icy mantles and can subsequently be released into the gas phase.

Key prerequisites for understanding how and where glycine and alanine form are the determination of the surface reactions that lead to their formation as a function of (i) kinetic temperature; (ii) gas density, (iii) structure of the gas, (iv) presence and abundance of other molecular species on the ices, and (v) UV and cosmic ray ionization rates, among other factors. To date, no large-scale predictions of the formation routes of glycine and alanine have been made, as a function of the parameters above.

A possible method to achieve this may be based on advanced and cutting edge techniques developed in the information sciences, ML and statistical disciplines. It should be possible to devise and apply a combination of statistical and ML techniques to perform large scale chemical models, involving large datasets of gas- and surface-phase chemical reactions to derive the physical and chemical conditions under which every surface chemical reaction is viable. A technique worth investigating is probabilistic graphical modelling, a branch of ML that studies how to use probability distributions to describe a particular problem whose ‘model’ has many uncertainties.

Ultimately, for any well-defined species set (COMs, amino acids, ice species *etc.*), we need to be able to simultaneously investigate the paths and efficiencies of their formation and destruction over a large physical (densities, temperatures, radiation fields, and cosmic ray ionization rates) and chemical (rate coefficients) parameter space, and discover if, where and under what conditions these species are abundant in space.

## 8.5 Conclusion

Machine Learning and probabilistic methods for solving typical astrochemical problems is a fast-growing field. As larger chemical reaction networks and more complex models are being employed in astrochemistry, the need for intelligent data mining algorithms will increase. It is clear that there are large uncertainties, as well as lack of information on formation and destruction routes, in gas and especially surface reactions and rate coefficients. To date, these uncertainties have only been tackled by laboratory experiments and quantum mechanical calculations. However, the complexity of the reaction networks, the lack of much prior information in the form of observed ices, and the length of each laboratory experiment, make a parameter exploration (in terms of gas densities, gas temperatures, UV, and cosmic ray fluxes for example) unfeasible. Initial ‘experimentation’ with ML algorithms has been proven to be an efficient avenue to tackle this challenge.

CHAPTER 9

Machine Learning at the (Nano)materials-biology Interface

DAVID A. WINKLER^([a](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#affa),[b](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#affb),[c](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#affc),[d](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#affd))

^a La Trobe Institute for Molecular Science, La Trobe University, Bundoora 3046, Australia

^b Monash Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Monash University, Parkville 3052, Australia

^c School of Pharmacy, University of Nottingham, Nottingham NG7 2QL, UK

^d CSIRO Data61, Pullenvale 4069, Australia

Email: [d.winkler@latrobe.edu.au](mailto:d.winkler@latrobe.edu.au)

## 9.1 Machine Learning Overview, Challenges, and Opportunities

Currently, machine learning (ML) is one of the most exciting computational techniques in science, technology, and medicine. The reason for the excitement is that, unlike traditional computer programs that have to be programmed precisely with every operation required to achieve a goal, ML methods can learn from examples in a similar way to humans. The same ML program can be trained to model and predict many different types of experiments and scenarios and can take into account heterogeneous data types like experimental conditions, physical and chemical properties, and processing history of samples.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit1)) ML models can generate models of continuous properties like water solubility, biological activity, and materials strength, but also categorical data (good/bad, active/inactive, nontoxic/moderately toxic/very toxic *etc.*). Newer types of ML can also generate very good features, *i.e.* mathematical representations of intrinsic properties of molecules, materials, images *etc.* that generate improved models, as the quality of features is paramount when constructing ML models.^([2](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit2))

Not surprisingly, artificial intelligence (AI) methods, largely ML, are generating a lot of new and potentially disruptive science across broad research and application domains.^([3](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit3)) There is an exponential increase in the number of publications that employ ML; many of these are in top-level journals, like Nature, Science, Cell and PNAS and their families of journals. However, ML is not new. The first neural network, the perceptron, was developed in 1958. A simple statistical modelling antecedent, quantitative structure–activity (or property) relationships (QSAR/QSPR), arose in chemistry at a similar time. Shortly after, neural networks were used to model relationships between chemical structures and other molecular and physicochemical properties of organic molecules and some useful property, especially biological effects. There was a steady progress in this field, but several important roadblocks hindered more rapid progress and wider application of these ML methods. The main issues were very limited computational technologies, lack of data to train ML models, a lack of clarity on how to generate mathematical entities that encode useful information, lack of understanding on how to reduce the dimensionality of ML modelling problems (feature selection), and even long-standing academic arguments on the best way to measure how predictive an ML model is.^([4](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit4)) Despite these limitations, a lot of useful research was conducted in this period; the method generated new drug candidates and predicted their possible toxicities and metabolic liabilities, and many of the limitations of low availability of computational resources were eased as computing power underwent spectacular development in subsequent decades.

At the moment, there is a happy coincidence of (or perhaps a deliberate push towards) advanced development in computational technologies and algorithms (*e.g.* deep learning (DL)), automation and robotics generating very large data sets suitable for training ML models, and development and/or application of a much broader range of powerful ML algorithms with unprecedented capabilities. What has also changed in chemical applications of ML is that we have found very good solutions to many of the vexing roadblocks in the QSAR/QSPR method (a model for ML in chemistry). Deep learning methods such as autoencoder/decoder, adversarial, and convolutional neural networks, for example, have simplified the problem of generating mathematical descriptors to train ML models. Indeed, these methods can now take simple representations of molecular entities (*e.g.* SMILES strings, linear text representations of organic molecules) and generate relevant descriptors internally. We have also adopted powerful new descriptors like fragment and signature descriptors^([5](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit5)) that generate very good models. Unlike older and more arcane descriptors (*e.g.* those generated by descriptor generating packages like Dragon^([6](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit6))), they are much easier to interpret in terms of molecular interactions and mechanisms. There is now a much wider use of efficient sparse feature selection methods (*e.g.* LASSO) that remove poor and uninformative descriptors, making models faster to train, easier to interpret, and more predictive.

These developments have driven a substantial expansion of ML into new areas such as forward and retrosynthetic reaction prediction,^([7](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit7)) prediction of thermodynamic and dynamic stability of materials, prediction of protein structures from sequence,^([8](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit8)) prediction or properties and performance of porous and 2D materials,^([9](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit9)) for energy applications, and many others.^([10](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit10)) Very recently, these techniques are being applied to autonomous evolutionary design of robots,^([11](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit11)) neatly completing the circle where robotics have allowed the generation of large amounts of data, which is then used to train models that can generate new robot architectures. This chapter will not discuss these applications as many are well covered in other chapters in the text.

Data availability has grown massively with rapid developments in robotics, automation, and omics technologies. Copious and diverse data representative of the domain of the problem being studied are essential for data-driven modelling methods like ML and DL. However, the size of possible accessible materials space (∼10^(100), essentially infinite) clearly shows that experiments alone, no matter how fast or well planned (*e.g.* using design of experiments), cannot cover such spaces adequately. More efficient methods are required to identify ‘islands of utility’ in the vast sea of materials possibilities. This strongly suggests that ML methods need to couple synergistically with evolutionary algorithms that can explore very large search spaces very efficiently. This will be discussed in detail later in this chapter.

## 9.2 Scale and Importance of Problem/Special Issues with Complex Materials

Like ML and big data, the fields of materials science, regenerative medicine, and biomaterials are undergoing unprecedented expansion. They are taking advantage of new automated methods of synthesis, characterization, and testing of materials.^([12](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit12)) Much of the most interesting research is occurring at the boundary between materials and biology *e.g.* biomaterials, tissue engineering, stem cell control, implantable and indwelling devices, nanoscale smart delivery systems, 2D materials for wearable sensors, robotics, and prosthetics.

However, ML modelling of complex materials has special problems compared to small organic drugs or drug-like molecules. Nanomaterials exhibit distributions of shapes and sizes, their surfaces change dynamically depending on the environment in which they are embedded, and the materials are often not well characterized. Similarly, polymers are also not well characterized, they are polydisperse, crosslinked, their structures are not precisely known *etc.* There is a strong need for systematic studies on how properties of these materials affect the behaviour of systems constructed from them. Clearly, characterizing complex materials mathematically for use in training ML models is problematic. Materials-specific descriptors are largely not available or if they are, are quite arcane and uninterpretable. However, new DL methods such as encoder-decoder networks and general adversarial neural networks will significantly improve this deficiency, as they can generate internal descriptors ‘on the fly’ from chemically simple representations.

There are massive opportunities provided by contemporary ML technologies. They are providing, for the first time, the opportunity to tackle scientific, medical, social, and technological problems that have been out of reach due to their complexities. We now describe several areas in materials science where ML has provided novel solutions to very complex problems. The aim is to show how ML is now being used; the focus is on applications that are useful and interesting rather than those that are cutting edge but obscure.

## 9.3 Machine Learning Examples in Materials

We provide a few examples of where ML has been used to solve important problems in the energy and environmental arena. This section, which is brief because it is covered by others, shows recent research into ML modelling of porous and 2D materials properties.

Porous materials like metal organic frameworks (MOFs), zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs), and covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are attracting much interest because of their diversity, tunability, and potential energy-related applications such as carbon capture, hydrogen and methane storage, electrocatalysts for carbon dioxide electro-reduction and water splitting reactions and related applications. There are millions of porous materials that could be synthesized that reside in large porous materials databases; however, it is not known which of these are stable and synthesizable. For every reported successful synthesis of an MOF, there are undoubtedly hundreds or thousands of failed reactions that have been attempted. ML could use knowledge of successful and failed reactions to predict and optimize the syntheses of new MOFs. MOF synthesis involves the self-assembly of metal ions and organic linkers in a 3D periodic network. However, our understanding of this self-assembly process is still too poor to predict which combinations will be able to be synthesized or which synthesis conditions will be optimal. Moosavi *et al.* recently used ML to capture chemical intuition from a set of successful and unsuccessful experiments to synthesize a metal–organic framework.^([13](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit13)) They used a random forest ensemble learner to evaluate the importance of variables in the synthesis of a MOF made from copper ions and 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylic acid, thereby generating a material with unprecedented surface area. Moghadam *et al.* subsequently applied ML to predict the mechanical stability of MOFs that are suited to their applications.^([14](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit14)) They first conducted high-throughput molecular simulations for 3385 MOFs containing 41 distinct network topologies, which were then used to train an ML model to predict the mechanical properties of MOFs. Their model trained using five accessible descriptors, could rapidly estimate the bulk moduli of new or existing MOFs, which are representative of the critical pressure these materials can withstand under typical operating conditions, a valuable tool for the MOF community.

In the energy applications area, Thornton and co-workers reported the use of ML to design zeolite catalysts for CO[2] reduction.^([15](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit15)) They employed statistical and machine learning (QSPR) modelling techniques to identify quantitative relationships between the zeolite structural characteristics and the adsorption properties for CO[2] and hydrogen simulated by accurate but computationally demanding grand canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) calculations. Robust structure–property relationships were found that linked structural descriptors such as pore size, surface area and void fraction to zeolite performance. Useful catalysts were identified from the computational screening of >300 000 zeolite structures. Several of the top candidates were very promising energy-efficient templates for catalysis with predicted performance 50% higher than conventional reactors.

They subsequently showed how ML can be used to leverage GCMC calculations of hydrogen adsorption by nanoporous materials to identify their performance limits.^([16](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit16)) Hydrogen is an attractive transportation fuel with zero carbon emissions, but it is difficult to store. MOFs have shown promise as physical adsorbents of hydrogen. They exploited the Nanoporous Materials Genome, containing over 850 000 materials, and GCMC calculations results used to train an ML model to explore the limits of hydrogen storage. The also incorporated limited evolutionary optimization that used ML models of the fitness of materials to accelerate the discovery of higher performance examples in successive rounds of optimization. [Figure 9.1](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig1) shows the results of selected GCMC calculations used to train neural net models of the fitness landscape for nanoporous materials, and improvements in performance over three optimization cycles. Maximum net capacity at room temperature was achieved with pore sizes of around 6 Å and void fractions of 0.1, while at cryogenic temperatures pore sizes of 10 Å and void fractions of 0.5 are optimal. The top candidates were commercially attractive cryo-adsorbents, with promising storage capacities at 77 K and 100 bar of 40 g L^(−1), a promising alternative to liquefaction.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00206-f1.jpg)

Figure 9.1 Selected GCMC calculations (grey filled circles), ML predictions (light grey points), and experimental data (black points) for net deliverable energy as a function of void fraction at 77 K, cycling between 100 and 1 bar, for the complete genome (∼850 000 porous materials). GCMC calculations were used to train neural net models of the fitness landscape for nanoporous materials that were used to generate improvements in performance over three optimization cycles. Experimental data are from the literature, the dashed line represents the predicted bare tank performance, and the solid dark line is the fitted Langmuir model. Reproduced from ref. [16](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit16), [https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.chemmater.6b04933](http://https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.chemmater.6b04933), with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2017.

2D materials are another very strong research area of contemporary research. These materials are essentially 1 atom thick; layered materials derived from them exhibit novel and useful electro-optic properties. They are also being developed as components of wearable and implantable electronics such as continuous sensors. Their properties can be predicted using computationally expensive quantum chemical calculations. Recently a flurry of papers has shown that ML models can be used to predict properties of large libraries of 2D and layered 2D materials orders of magnitude faster than QM calculations, with similar accuracy.

There are ∼2000 2D materials known or predicted to be synthesizable, and they exhibit a wide diversity of potentially useful properties. For example, a recent study^([17](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit17)) identified 1825 2D materials that could be exfoliated from known inorganic compounds. Hybrid layered 2D materials (two layers of different 2D materials) are of great interest for photovoltaic and photonic applications, as they have much larger scope for being tuned in application-specific ways. Known 2D materials can theoretically generate ∼2 million bilayer structures, and around a billion trilayers. Clearly, such a massive number of hybrid materials cannot be generated and tested experimentally and, even though DFT calculations can predict their properties, the computational demands make it also infeasible to predict the properties of more than about a hundred materials. ML methods can be used to leverage a relatively small number of accurate DFT calculations of hybrid 2D materials properties into a much larger material space. For example, Tawfik *et al.* reported the prediction of the interlayer distance and band gap for almost 1500 bilayer heterostructures. Their models could predict the interlayer spacing for hybrid materials in a test set with a mean error of 4% and an RMSE of 0.2 eV for the band gap. Use of hybrid DFT and ML methods allow predictions to be made for large numbers of materials much faster than those from DFT calculations alone.

## 9.4 Machine Learning Examples in Nanomaterials

Materials in nanoparticulate form often exhibit useful (but also potentially detrimental) biological properties compared to the same material in the bulk phase. This is largely due to the extremely high surface to volume ratio of small particles compared to larger ones. Materials surfaces interact directly with biology so are very important. Nanomaterials have shown great promise in delivering drugs and gene therapies to target tissues in the body, and as imaging agents for diagnosis. ML methods have been used quite widely to understand the relationship between nanoparticle physicochemical properties and how they affect biology. Computational models of nanoparticle behaviour are very difficult to devise for several key reasons: nanoparticles exhibit a distribution of sizes and shapes, so are more difficult to characterize than small molecules; they are much larger than molecules, so it is not clear how to encode their chemical properties in meaningful ways; in biological systems they become coated by complex layers of proteins (the corona) that significantly affect the types of biological responses that they generate; experiments to map their distribution *in vivo*, uptake through lungs, GI tract, and skin are very difficult; and although *in vitro* assays are easier they often do not correlate well with *in vivo* responses.

ML methods can simplify some of these difficulties and they do not require a complete understanding of mechanisms involved in nanoparticle biological responses. They have been an important element in understanding the potential adverse biological properties of nanomaterials used commercially. The aim is to use ML models as part of a ‘safe-by-design’ paradigm to generate commercially useful materials with minimal adverse effects. For example, Le *et al.* described an experimental and computational approach for the development of nanoparticles that are safe-by-design.^([18](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit18)) They generated a library of 45 ZnO nanoparticles with varying particle size, aspect ratio, doping type, doping concentration, and surface coatings and measured cell damage in human umbilical vein endothelial cells or human hepatocellular liver carcinoma cells. They successfully generated quantitative and predictive ML models mapping nanoparticle properties to cell viability, membrane integrity, and oxidative stress. [Figure 9.2](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig2) shows the results of ML models for these potentially adverse biological effects of nanomaterials as function of the size, shape, core material, doping, and coating type.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00206-f2.jpg)

Figure 9.2 Performance of ML models for LDH level (a measure of cell membrane integrity, right) for a range of ZnO-based nanomaterials with different sizes, shapes, core materials, doping, and coating types (left). Reproduced from ref. [18](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit18) with permission from John Wiley and Sons, © 2016 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim.

The most important factors driving cell damage were the concentration of nanoparticles the cells were exposed to, the type of surface coating, the nature and extent of the ZnO core doping, and the aspect ratio of the particles. Oksel *et al.* also reported several ML models of nanoparticle biological properties and recently described the application of random forest ML methods to modelling nanoparticle properties.^([19](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit19)) They found RF methods generated models that were easier to interpret in terms of ranges and limits of nanoparticle properties that most influence any adverse effects of nanomaterials.

As ML methods are data-driven, one of the main issues with them is obtaining sufficient high-quality experimental data to train them. This is particularly difficult with nanomaterials, as there are still relatively few high throughput synthesis and characterization studies on these materials, and they are more difficult to study experimentally. This urgent need was identified in recent reviews on the application of ML methods to predicting the adverse properties of nanomaterials^([20](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit20),[21](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit21)) and in a paper calling for more systematic studies of these properties.^([22](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit22))

Amphiphilic, self-assembling nanomaterials such cubosomes and hexosomes are a promising class of drug delivery materials (see [Figure 9.3](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig3)). However, they are tricky to design as the types of nanophases they assemble into can be dependent on the temperature, time, drug loading and drug physicochemical properties, amongst others. Only specific nanophases are useful as delivery vehicles. Predicting the effects of these complex parameters on the resultant nanophase was considered intractable until recently. Le at al. showed how ML methods can accurately predict which of several (sometimes coexisting) nanophases will form for a given set of conditions.^([23](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit23),[24](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit24)) They validated their ML models predicting nanophases by a subsequent *de novo* synthesis of loaded amphiphilic nanoparticles and experimental determination of the resulting nanophase using small angle x-ray scattering on the Australian synchrotron (see [Figure 9.4](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig4)). The predictions were 90% accurate. They subsequently showed how ML models could accurately predict the time evolution of nanoparticulate amphiphilic drug delivery systems.^([25](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit25))

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00206-f3.jpg)

Here, we show example structures of the inverse-bicontinuous diamond QIID (Pn3m), gyroid QIIG (Ia3d), and primitive QIIP (Im3m) cubic phases. Reproduced from ref. ![image](images/bk9781788017893-00206-f4.jpg)

Figure 9.4 ML models predicting the existence of individual phases (inverse-bicontinuous diamond QIID (Pn3m) cubic (blue, to the left of [Figure 9.4A](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig4) and B), hexagonal HII (yellow, filled circles), gyroid QIIG (Ia3d) cubic (red), primitive QIIP (Im3m) cubic (purple, to the right in [Figure 9.4C](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig4) and D), and fluid isotropic FI (brown)) for a range of new drugs incorporated in the nanophases. Amphiphiles used to generate the nanoparticles were (A) phytantriol and (B) monoolein nanoparticles. These particles were loaded with new drugs at 25 and 37 °C. Circles indicate incorrect predictions for the nanophases determined subsequently by small angle X-ray scattering at the Australian Synchrotron. The predictions were 90% accurate. This showed how ML models could accurately predict nanophase behaviour as a function of amphiphile, drug type, drug loading, and temperature. Reproduced from ref. [23](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit23), [https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/mp3006402](http://https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/mp3006402), with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2013.

siRNA can also be used for therapeutic purposes and ML has been used to design siRNA libraries and more effective materials to deliver these highly charged molecules. A 2011 review described the various ML methods used to assist with the rational design of siRNA sequences and delivery systems.^([26](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit26)) For example, Huesken and coworkers trained a neural network on 2182 randomly selected siRNAs targeted to 34 mRNA species using a high-throughput reporter gene system.^([27](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit27)) The ML model predicted the activity of 249 siRNAs in an independent test set with a modest r² value of 0.44. This ML model was used to design a genome-wide siRNA library consisting of two siRNAs per gene. This collection of 50 000 siRNAs identified genes involved in the cellular response to hypoxia. The dramatic increase in the capability of ML methods subsequently has reignited interest in this important area. The prediction of efficacy of siRNA sequences for gene silencing has improved significantly and ML methods are making much better predictions on the efficiency of nanoparticulate gene delivery systems. For example, more recently Han *et al.* used deep learning methods to improve the accuracy of prediction of siRNA efficacy. Their DNN extracted hidden features from sequences and thermodynamic properties. The model predicted siRNA efficacy slightly better, with an *r*² value of 0.53. Subsequent experiments showed that their model was more accurate than several other siRNA prediction methods. Anderson's team at MIT reported the effects of a small library of nanoparticles synthesized from lipid-modified aminoglycosides and siRNA.

## 9.5 Machine Learning Examples in Biomaterials and Regenerative Medicine

Biomaterials are an important element of regenerative medicine that promises hitherto inaccessible treatments for injury and disease. Biomaterials can replace damaged tissues, stimulate the growth of nerves, provide environments for implanted cells in cell therapies aimed at generating essential hormones such as insulin, replace bone damaged by accidents or disease, precisely deliver drugs and gene therapy agents to diseased tissues, and hide otherwise biologically incompatible implanted components such as pacemakers and cochlear implants from the body's immune response. Given the almost infinite variety of chemically accessible materials to choose from, it is essential to conduct experiments to select them using high throughput techniques, and to employ powerful computational methods such as ML and evolutionary algorithms to extract design rules from large data sets and to explore materials space as efficiently as possible. To date, the materials most widely used for these purposes are polymers and nanomaterials.

Given the rapid growth in implantable and indwelling medical devices, it is particularly important to design or discover materials that resist bacterial attachment and biofilm formation, and those that reduce or eliminate the foreign body response (FBR) that often causes device failure. FBR to an implanted device generates a fibrous capsule that insulates the device or implanted cell therapy from the body, compromising function. Clearly, materials surfaces and interfaces are often the main drivers of biological response, so the ability to analyze, modify and model the chemistry and topography of surfaces is very important for the development and optimization of new biomaterials. However, interactions between surfaces and biology are poorly understood at the molecular and mechanistic level.

ML methods have been used to model the propensity of polymers to support the growth of pathogenic microbes. Clever generation of large arrays of different polymers using dip pen and inkjet printing methods has provided the means for measuring the responses of diverse cell types to the polymers. Building on the seminal work from the Langer group at MIT, Hook *et al.* described this experimental technique in a recent publication.^([12](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit12),[28](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit28)) They found relationships between the degree of attachment of three important hospital pathogens, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and uropathogenic Escherichia coli, and surface chemistry (as determined by experimental surface analysis) for several hundred diverse polymers. Subsequent ML modelling of these data using surface analysis data as descriptors, or computational generated molecular descriptors for the monomers, resulted in robust and predictive models of pathogen attachment.^([29](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit29)) A subsequent study showed how a single ML model could simultaneously predict the attachment of all three pathogens,^([30](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit30)) making it much simpler to conduct virtual screens of thousands of accessible but not yet synthesized polymers to identify those with low general pathogen attachment (summarized in [Figure 9.5](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig5)).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00206-f5.jpg)

Figure 9.5 A single ML model simultaneously predicts the attachment of three important hospital-acquired pathogens,^([30](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit30)) Measured and predicted attachment (estimated using the log of the GFP fluorescence, logF) of the multi-pathogen attachment model employed computed molecular descriptors. Reproduced from ref. [30](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit30) with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2018.

As ML models of biomaterials (and drugs too) have historically been trained using efficient but rather arcane (hard to understand) descriptors, they subsequently showed how a specific type of molecular fragment descriptor could generate models that were easier for experimental materials scientists to interpret.^([31](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit31)) A similar ML modelling approach was used to find relationships between the attachment of stem cells to polymer libraries.^([32](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit32),[33](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit33)) More recently, ML methods have been used to model a library of 141 homopolymers and 400 diverse copolymers for their abilities to support attachment, proliferation, and differentiation of human dental pulp stem cells.^([33](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit33)) In this study, a Bayesian regularized neural network with a sparsity inducing Laplacian prior was used to model the three stem cell responses separately. Computational models were generated, relating polymer properties to cellular responses. The models correctly predicted the attachment of stem cells 92–95% of the time, proliferation 85–92% of the time, and differentiation 82–85% of the time. The models also identified several key functional groups that support specific cell responses.

Surface analysis methods like time of flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) and Raman spectroscopy are very important for understanding how biomaterials interact with biology. This is because the surfaces of bulk materials and nanomaterials are the primary sites of contact with cells and other biological entities. ToF-SIMS impacts materials surfaces with atoms or clusters of atoms to fragment the constituent molecules, providing a kind of fingerprint that is specific to the materials surface. Surprisingly, analysis methods for the large data sets that surface analysis methods generate have involved relatively simple statistical methods like principle components analysis (PCA). When used as mathematical descriptors that encode surface chemistry, ion peaks from ToF-SIMS, for example, are also very useful for generating quantitative relationships between surface chemistry and biological responses.^([12](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit12),[28](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit28)) Recently, we and others have employed more sophisticated informatics and ML methods to analyze these data sets and have shown that much more information can be obtained this way. For example, a recent study found that self-organizing maps (SOMs), a specialized form of neural network used for nonlinear clustering of complex data, are more effective at extracting information from data from ToF-SIMS experiments on polymers than principal components analysis (PCA), which is commonly employed.^([34](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit34),[35](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit35))[Figure 9.6](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig6) shows how SOMs can distinguish between nylon samples with very similar chemical structures, a task that PCA cannot achieve. The nonlinear neural network clustering methods could detect small quantities of materials such as antibodies better than traditional methods but could also discriminate between materials with high degrees of chemical similarity.^([34](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit34),[36](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit36))

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00206-f6.jpg)

Figure 9.6 Discrimination between nylon samples with very similar chemical structures using Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs). The 10×10 supervised Kohonen network (SKN) was calculated for positive ion ToF-SIMS data. False-colouring is used to clarify sample locations on the network according to their sample group – see online version of the figure: (red, Nylon-6; green, Nylon-11; navy, Nylon-12; cyan, Nylon-6(3)T; pink, Nylon-6/6; yellow, Nylon-6/9; and dark green, Nylon-6/12). This ML model had a 98% class assignment accuracy. Reproduced from ref. [34](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit34) with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2018.

We and others have also shown the importance of using modern sparse feature selection methods to remove chemical features from models that do not drive biological responses. These methods remove (set to zero) any features that are less relevant to the biological response using a variety of mathematical methods; the most widely used are the LASSO regression and multiple linear regression using an expectation algorithm and a sparse Bayesian prior.^([37](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit37),[38](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit38)) This makes models more interpretable, and also improves the predictive power of them because optimally sparse models generalize the best to new data. These methods have been very effective in identifying small numbers of genes in gene expression microarray data that correlate with biological responses. Tens of thousands of genes on a microarray can be reduced in a context-dependent way to a handful of those most relevant. For example, Autefage and co-workers used gene expression data from experiments in which mesenchymal stem cells were driven down the osteogenic (bone) pathway by strontium ions leaching from an implanted biomaterial. These implants have been shown to slow the loss of calcium in bone, reducing fractures and osteoporosis. Subsequent analysis using sparse feature selection identified a small number of related fatty acid and steroid biosynthesis genes as being important in osteogenesis. Subsequent experimental testing of these predictions using qPCR, lipid raft and gene expression measurements validated the importance of these hitherto unknown pathways for strontium-induced differentiation of MDS down the osteogenic pathway.^([39](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit39)) In another study, stem cells were caused to divide symmetrically or asymmetrically using a variety of chemical and physical methods. In symmetric division, they divide into two stem cells and in asymmetric division they divide into one stem cell and one progenitor cell. This division process was a long-standing unexplained problem in stem cell biology. Subsequent analysis of the gene expression microarray profiles identified 5 potential markers for the symmetry of stem cell division. Experimental validation using fluorescent antibodies for these gene products shows that these genes were indeed markers of symmetry of division (see [Figure 9.7](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig7)).^([40](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit40)) Some of these markers are now sold commercially by Asymmetrex.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00206-f7.jpg)

Figure 9.7 Experimental validation using fluorescent antibodies for these gene products shows that these genes were indeed markers of symmetry of division. The top row shows the positions of cell nuclei marked by DAPI stain, the lower panels show the marker H2A.Z that only identifies one of the two cells when asymmetric division has occurred (lower right two panels) and both cells when symmetric division occurs (lower left two panels). Reproduced from ref. [40](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit40) with permission from Elsevier, Copyright 2015.

## 9.6 Materials for Cell Therapies, Bioreactors, and Implantable Cells

Cell therapies (implanting of therapeutic cells into the body) are important medical interventions *e.g.* bone marrow transplants for leukaemia (current) and islet cells for diabetes (future). Key to the success of these therapies is the ability to culture large quantities of cells in artificial bioreactors.^([41](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit41),[42](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit42)) Materials science and ML methods are playing increasingly important roles. For example, ML methods successfully modelled the relationships between bioreactor parameters such as initial cell type and seeding density, cytokine concentrations, reactor types, media *etc.* on subsequent cell fold increases (how many times the initial seed concentration of cell increased).^([1](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit1)) This study by Winkler and Burden modelled the increase in total number of cells and 5 different stem cell or progenitor cell types belonging to the haematopoietic (blood) differentiation pathway. Data from over 300 bioreactor experiments were successfully and quantitatively modelled using MLR and sparse Bayesian neural network methods. Apart from predicting the fold increase for each cell type within a factor of two (three for nucleated cells), their sparse feature selection methods also identified the most important chemical factors and bioreactor parameters driving each type of cell expansion, very useful information for controlling the specific types of cells the bioreactors generate.

## 9.7 ML and Evolutionary Methods

Although ML is attracting most of the attention, as we stated in the Introduction, the estimated 10^(100) possible accessible materials mean that even the most optimistic predictions of the capabilities of high throughput experimentation and ML modelling suggest that these methods cannot possibly explore more than a minute fraction of this effectively infinite space unaided. Evolutionary algorithms (EA) are one of the most efficient ways to explore very large search spaces. It is therefore logical that evolutionary methods be employed to explore materials spaces better to discover entirely novel materials and to optimize those already discovered. There have been a limited number of studies on using evolutionary methods to ‘evolve’ materials, primarily catalysts and phosphors, as these represent ‘low hanging fruit’, more easily represented as materials ‘genomes’. Applications of evolutionary methods to bioactive compounds and materials discovery are only now emerging, and progress is summarized in recent reviews.^([43](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit43),[44](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit44))

White light LEDs that have made possible energy-efficient lighting potentially lowers greenhouse gas emissions. These devices rely on phosphors, often made by high-temperature sintering of rare earth oxides. Phosphors are useful to demonstrate how materials ‘genomes’ are generated and the basic operation of *in silico* simulated Darwinian evolution. Phosphors can be very simply presented by a ‘genome’, for example, a vector containing the relative mole fractions of each rare earth oxide component. After sintering, phosphor brightness and colour are measured (equivalent to species fitness in Darwinian evolution) and the best phosphors are ‘bred’ to generate a new and higher fitness population of phosphors. Mutation operations such as elitism (passing on the best phosphors into the next generation unchanged), changing the concentration of one rare earth (point mutations), and splitting the genomes of two phosphors and combining the parts into new ones (crossover operators) are applied to the fittest materials in a given cycle of evolution. This evolutionary loop is iterated for a number of cycles, until a specified performance level is reached, or the algorithm fails to generate improved examples. In this way, Sharma and co-workers^([45](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit45)) steadily improved the fitness (brightness and colour) of mixed metal oxide seven-dimensional library (MnO–Na[2]O–Li[2]O–MgO–ZnO–CaO–GeO[2]) by evolution to find a promising green phosphor for use in backlit liquid crystal display applications. (see [Figure 9.8](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#fig8)). They synthesized only a few hundred phosphors but explored a much larger space of phosphor composition to find locally optimum materials.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00206-f8.jpg)

Figure 9.8 By iterating around this evolutionary loop for five cycles, Sharma *et al.* improved the fitness of the phosphors (brightness and green colour). The upper and lower panels are replicates. Reproduced from ref. [45](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit45) with permission from John Wiley and Sons, Copyright © 2009 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim.

Consequently, it is very likely that the next disruptive technology to be adopted by materials scientists after ML will be genetic technologies. This is likely to play out in two ways: more efficient searching of materials spaces using high throughput experiments coupled with EAs, and even more effective searching using synergistic combinations of ML and EA. The latter involves building ML models of the fitness landscape from experimental data in successive initial rounds of high throughput experiments and using these to replace experimentation in later stages of the search. It has been shown that such ‘adaptive’ evolution (an in-silico equivalent of the biological Baldwin Effect) allows systems to evolve more quickly than those that do not use it.^([46](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit46),[47](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit47))

Evolutionary methods also make possible, for the first time, the possibility of autonomous discovery methods, fully automated invention machines with no ‘human in the loop’. In broad terms, such a machine would consist of a general purpose synthesis robot, automated characterization instruments for quality control and to measure a specified fitness, an evolutionary program that could select the fittest members of an initial population of molecules or materials and mutate them into a new population, and a method for specifying the new molecules to be synthesized to the robotic synthesizer. Several groups are developing autonomous chemists and autonomous materials scientists. Some of these are focused on automating organic synthesis,^([48](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit48)) and others materials discovery.^([49](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit49)) There is major work towards universal organic synthesis machines, a prerequisite for an autonomous organic chemist, at the Max Planck Institute for Colloids and Interfaces in Potsdam. The US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) has funded several international initiatives. to help remove barriers to autonomous synthesis systems. The research teams are pursuing both hardware and software solutions for automation.^([50](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit50)) MIT is using preloaded cartridges to automate synthetic steps such as heating, mixing and separating chemicals.^([51](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit51)) They trained an ML model on millions of reactions from the Reaxys database and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. The ML model learned to apply retrosynthetic transformations, identify relevant reaction conditions, and to estimate reaction feasibility. It was taught to generalize from specific known chemical reactions to new substrates. A team at the University of Glasgow led by Prof. Lee Cronin have developed a Chemputer, a modular desktop-sized robotic synthesizer that compiles text-based synthetic instructions into machine instructions to drive synthesis robots costing £25 000–30 000 (US$33 000–39 500) each.^([52](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit52)) This approach has successfully synthesized generic versions of common drugs in an order of magnitude faster than conventional manual synthesis methods. His online platform, Chemify, allows chemists to download Chemputer assembly instructions.

## 9.8 The Path Forward

ML is passing through at least the second of the well-known hype cycles. Claims of ML's capabilities are often exaggerated, but it is clear that there are also many examples across broad fields of science, technology, medicine, manufacturing, and business of spectacular outcomes. ML is a disruptive technology that will change the world as we know it in the next few decades. It has the potential to remove much of the tedious, repetitive, and sometimes dangerous work of chemical and materials researchers, freeing them up for more creative endeavours. The main roadblocks to future development are:

*   the ability to describe complex materials mathematically to train ML methods,
*   a paucity of data to train deep learning models,
*   a better understanding of how to reduce bias in ML models learning from examples,
*   development of chemical synthesis languages that will completely specify reactions to improve reproducibility and allow robots to be programmed with synthesis information,
*   development of synthesis machines with broad applicability (*e.g.* by breaking down molecule or materials syntheses into a finite number of unit operations),
*   and optimal synergy between automation, ML, and evolution.

ML and AI will also generate profound changes to the workforce, with even intellectual jobs such as accounting, law, and some aspects of medicine being impacted. As foreshadowed, the combination of AI, ML, robotics, and evolutionary methods will potentially unleash new ways of doing science that can accelerate our understanding of materials properties, their interactions with biology, and the discovery of novel molecules with highly novel and useful properties. As well as robots helping design and synthesize new molecules and materials, we are likely to see materials evolving collaboratively with robot morphologies and controllers to generate new fit-for-function robots,^([11](#BK9781788017893-00206.xhtml#cit11)) another neat ‘closing of the loop’ in technology.
