As seen in [Table 11.8](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab8), the variables that contributed most to Dim1 were MW, HBD, HBA, PSA, and NATOMs. logD contributed most to Dim2, and ROT and NRING contributed the most to Dim3. We conclude that Dim1 explains flexibility, Dim2 explains lipophilicity, and Dim3, due to the negative relationship between ROT and NRING, represents cell permeability.

The distribution of the score >4 targets is shown to be more spread along Dim1, and the range of the targets with score ≤4 seems more pronounced on Dim2 (see [Figure 11.3](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig3)). Positioning of compounds along Dim2 is governed largely by logD (and by high values of PSA, HBA, and HBD), which influence compounds in a positive (upward) and negative (downward) direction, respectively ([Figures 11.2](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig2) and [11.3](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig3)). In addition, logD influences the positioning of targets negatively (leftward) along Dim1 and positively (rightwards) by (MW, NATOM, and ROT) along Dim1. A larger portion (70%) of the targets with high scores >4 cluster in the upper right (quadrant A) of the PCA plot ([Figure 11.3](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig3), see also [Table 11.9](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab9)) and to a lesser extent (22%) are in the lower right region (quadrant D), 6 of which (75%) are oral targets (see [Table 11.9](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab9)). For the non-violator targets with scores ≤4, 35% and 37% cluster in the upper left (quadrant B) and lower left (quadrant C), respectively – with equivalent percentages being oral or non-oral low score targets in each quadrant B and C (see [Figure 11.3](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig3), [Table 11.9](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab9)). PCA analysis successfully identified a group of disease targets with a specific score function range and position of ADMET descriptors in different quadrants. Indeed [Table 11.9](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab9) confirms a significant association between the score 4 logD classes and the quadrants for all targets (P<0.0001) and also for targets stratified by both score 4 status and oral status (a significant score 4 status by oral status interaction effect, P<0.0001).

#### 11.3.2.1 Results of the Analyses Based on the PCA of the MPs and the Raw Target Data

[Table 11.10](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab10) reports the RF and ANN models on the raw target data and demonstrates that RF performed better than ANNs for the score 3 variant models, but that the ANN score 4 logD model was optimal overall, with AUC (95% CI) of 0.89 (0.77, 1.00). The neural network plots for the 4 models based on the raw target data for the score C logP and score C logD (*C*\=3 and 4) partitions are given in [Figure 11.4](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig4). [Table 11.11](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab11) shows that overall the ANN classification was superior to the RF models for score 3 and score 4 logD models, with the ANN target based PCA with partition *C*\=4 achieving best classification, with AUC (95% CI) of 0.92 (0.81, 1.00). Similarly, for the molecular parameter PCs, the ANN method performed better than RF classification, with the score 4 logD being optimal with AUC (95% CI) of 0.95 (0.87, 0.94) (see [Table 11.11](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab11)). [Figure 11.5](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig5) displays the ANN plots for the drug target PCA constructs based on score 4 logP and score 4 logD models. [Figure 11.6](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig6) shows the RF plots for the drug target PCA constructs based on the score 3 logP and logD variants.

#### 11.3.2.2 Mapping Variable Importance from ANN Analyses to the PCA Loadings of the Target Data

For the superior ANN score 4 logD model based on the raw target data given in [Table 11.10](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab10), the corresponding variable importance measures, in decreasing order of magnitude, were attributable to PSA, logD, NRING, HBA, MW, NATOMS, ROT, and HBD with a corresponding variable importance vector of 21.65, 19.53, 13.18, 11.48, 11.06, 9.5, 7.52, and 6.08, (see also Table 4 of Hudson *et al.*^([14](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit14))). This revealed the stronger contribution in the ANN classification of both PSA and logD, compared to MW as is traditionally assumed. From [Table 11.8](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab8), which reports the PCA loadings of the PCA dimensions founded on the target data studied in this chapter, we note that the variable importance measures above, mirror, in part, the sequence of high absolute values of the PCA loadings on the variables (see [Table 11.8](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#tab8)) for the dimensions as follows: adding strength to the value and interpretation of the PCA dimensions to classify targets into high *versus* low scorers as shown in [Figure 11.3](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig3):

*   **Dim2:** PSA (loading=−0.24), logD (0.61), NRING (0.45)
*   **Dim1:** HBA (0.41), MW (0.41), NATOM (0.39)
*   **Dim5:** ROT (−0.37), HBD (0.60).

## 11.4 Conclusion and Discussion

This chapter demonstrates how PCA and score functions of violations can be used to identify the hidden pattern of druggable molecules and disease targets. Our novel PC analytic MP and target constructs showed that molecules and targets lie in particular locations (quadrants) in molecular space and as stratified by our scoring function cutpoints. Overall violations above 4 mirrored poor targets, which could be plainly differentiated and located in reduced PCA dimensional space (see [Figure 11.3](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig3)) as can also be seen in both the 2D raw MP and 2D target data maps (see [Figures 11.7](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig7) and [11.8](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#fig8)) which, in addition, delineate the bRo5 and eRo5 regions. We found that in the full data set analysed, 614 molecules actually lie within the bRo5 space, all of which satisfied the Ro5 criterion, of which 23% had a score ≤4 in contrast to 77% exhibiting high scores >4. While 1174 molecules follow the traditional Ro5, only 34 (3%) satisfied the eRo5 criteria, of which 11 molecules were outside the Ro5 region, 6 of which 6 (18%) had a low score (≤4), while 82% were high scoring >4 violators.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00251-f7.jpg)

Figure 11.7 Molecular parameter 2D maps: black=Ro5 (with extension) region, blue (to the right of the Figure)=bRo5 region, and red (lighter colours to the left of the Figure)=eRo5 region.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00251-f8.jpg)

Figure 11.8 Target median data 2D maps: black=Ro5 (with extension) region, blue (to the right of the figure)=bRo5 region, and red (lighter colours to the left of the figure)=eRo5 region (points in the plots are medians for each target).

The RP and ANN rules to classify the high score target and the low-score molecular violators, based on both MPs and the PCA constructs, confirmed the value of logD's inclusion in the scoring function, validating Zafar *et al.*^([11](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit11),[12](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit12)) and supporting the recently established cutpoints.^([14](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit14),[15](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit15)) Overall, the RF models and ANNs showed different variable importance profiles. The ANN models performed better than RFs, and the use of logD rather than logP was confirmed. Earlier work^([15](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit15)) had also shown that the most important MPs that influence classification, determined by RF methods, were MW, NATOM, logD, and PSA. By contrast, the ANN target models indicated that PSA and logD were highly important, more so than the traditional parameter MW. Overall, our score 4 partitions using logD were better at classification as shown in all RF and ANN analyses.

Our simple scoring functions of counts of violations partitioned chemospace well, identifying both good and poor druggable molecules and targets. Moreover, ligands with 4 or more violations, were shown to be associated with specific disease targets, *e.g.*, Anti- Bacterial, Antineoplastic, Antihypertensive and Anti-allergic, within which most molecules had a non-oral delivery mode. The Anti-Bacterial target drugs (score 4=6) were shown to have high values for all MPs, consistent with the results of Giordanetto *et al.*,^([65](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit65),[66](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit66)) who reported that compounds that fall into the bRo5 space (higher MW and PSA) include the Anti-bacterial target. Interestingly, the value of HBA, HBD, and PSA were also high for Anti-Bacterial target drugs (10, 3.5 and 180.82, respectively) with these descriptors representing important hydrogen bond or electrostatic features. We note that these descriptors also displayed high loadings in PCA space. Target drugs with a low median score were *e.g.,* Adrenergic, Dietary, Analgesics, Anaesthetics, Adjuvants, Anti-convulsants, Antimetabolites and Antidepressants, most of which were non-oral. Notably, the Dietary target drugs had low values for the molecular descriptors, with a lowest score 4 of 1.0, lowest median MW and also negative medians for both logP=−2.45 and logD=−2.81.^([14](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit14),[15](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit15))

Two decades have passed since the Ro5 piloted the concept of “drug-like” properties. A recent examination of oral drug parameters approved before and after the original Ro5 analysis has demonstrated that while some parameters such as calculated logP and HBD have remained constant, cutoffs for parameters such as MW and HBA have increased substantially over the past 20 years, thus bringing into question whether MW is a “drug-like” property.^([67](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit67)) Understanding the internal relations in the chemical database remains a key feature for the exploration of the chemical space to further develop new substances with predefined properties. Visualisation of the target chemical space by mapping from multidimensional descriptor space into a reduced dimensional space is still a challenging task in chemo-informatics and computational medicinal chemistry. Deep learning (DL) algorithms and neural networks now offer ways forward. For example, a parametric Stochastic Neighbour Embedding t-SNE approach, which yields a neural-network-based function to map new portions of data, has been suggested recently to aid the interpretation of structurally conditioned biological properties of chemical compounds.^([68](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit68)) Likewise, the exploration of chemical space by core analysis,^([69](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit69)) feature optimisation in high dimensional chemical space by DL,^([70](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit70)) and chemical space exploration guided by DL^([68](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit68)) have been indicated as new approaches. We refer the reader also to a recent review on DL methods in drug discovery^([16](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit16)) and a comparative analysis of machine learning algorithms for the prediction of potential druggable drugs by DrugMiner.^([34](#BK9781788017893-00251.xhtml#cit34))

## 12.1 Introduction

Functional organic materials are prevalent in many fields, including electronics,^([1](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit1)) porous materials,^([2](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit2)) polymers,^([3](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit3),[4](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit4)) and ionic liquids.^([5](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit5)) We define the scope of organic materials here as materials formed from small or polymeric molecules constituted of only light elements. We do not include pharmaceutical drugs and biological materials as these are covered elsewhere, although we will note similarities in the problems faced and the approaches that can be used to tackle them. The discovery of new materials has previously been dominated by serendipity, but there is now a clear need to accelerate their discovery to help tackle the problems facing humanity, such as climate change and the depletion of the Earth's natural resources. The focus of this chapter is the application of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to accelerate the discovery of new organic materials by assisting in the prediction of their structure and properties and guiding their optimisation for target applications (see [Figure 12.1](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#fig1)).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00280-f1.jpg)

Figure 12.1 A schematic summary of the materials discovery workflow in the age of AI, which is driven by the data from (a) curated databases and the scientific literature. From the available data, (b) complex and multivariable structure–property relationships can be inferred using AI. Here, brute force structure generation and/or prediction may feed into property predictors or inverse design may be applied, which predicts top candidates for a target property prior to structure prediction. The (c) resultant search space can then be explored experimentally using AI-designed experiments (d) to efficiently explore phase space, leading to optimised materials, as well as improvements to material databases, search spaces, and the preceding AI models through feedback mechanisms.

Organic materials often offer advantages over their inorganic counterparts in their improved sustainability, increased processability, reduced toxicity of the final material, and often lower cost, all of which are crucial to the scale-up of material production. Furthermore, organic compounds are relatively easy to modify through a vast array of robust synthetic routes, allowing for the fine-tuning of material properties. For example, in the development of semiconductors and other electronics, there is currently a push to replace inorganic, silicon-based materials with organic materials.^([6](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit6)) From a modelling perspective, one major difference between organic materials and their inorganic counterparts is that they are normally a combination of separate molecules, be it small molecules or polymers, rather than a single entity. As such, one can in principle represent an organic material either as an isolated molecule, ignoring, perhaps beyond a mean-field approximation, the effects of the environment of the molecule, such as intermolecular packing in the case of solids, the solvent in the case of dissolved molecules, or even interfaces, or treat the whole condensed system. There are many clear examples in the literature for systems where a ‘molecular representation’ is employed. However, for this representation to be accurate and effective, the material's properties need to be dominated by that of the individual molecules. For example, for porous molecular cage materials, because the individual molecule's structure defines the solid-state pore topology, the potential for molecular separations can be determined from the single molecule.^([7](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit7)) Similarly, for conjugated polymers that form amorphous solids, a comparison between DFT calculations on isolated polymer chains and experimental photoelectron spectroscopy on polymeric solids^([8](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit8)) suggests that isolated polymer chains might be a good representation of the solid for predicting their optoelectronic properties. Conversely, for polymers of intrinsic microporosity (PIMs),^([9](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit9)) where intermolecular voids arise from the inherent poor packing of the polymer chains, a molecular representation will be clearly inadequate for predicting the emergent porosity, and a ‘condensed-phase representation’ is required. The choice of representation is relevant to both the generation of training data and the kind of descriptors used for machine learning. As will be discussed in more detail below, for some properties, computational limitations mean the only (efficient) way of calculating them is inherently molecular, while completely different types of descriptors are used for molecules and condensed phases.

The search space for new organic materials does not only include the chemical space of the constituent molecules, which is estimated to consist of 10^(60) molecules,^([10](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit10)) but must also consider different ways of assembling individual molecules into materials, their resultant bulk properties, and the effect of experimental variables such as synthetic protocol.^([11](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit11)) With previous knowledge in a field, an experimental chemist can decrease this search space significantly. However, an inherent bias towards small changes within ‘known’ regions of phase space is a hindrance to a thorough exploration of phase space for the optimal material for an application. Computational methods and algorithms offer cheaper and more complete ways of searching phase space for the optimal materials.^([12](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit12)) A crucial aspect of exploring phase space using computational methods is the ability to predict the material properties of interest for each candidate accurately. Here, it is common to replace the complexity of multiple length and timescales with simplified models that are defined by existing structure–property relationships.

Computational optimisation has been applied in the field of drug discovery for many years because clear structure–property relationships exist.^([13](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit13)) In the case of early computer-aided drug discovery, only the molecular structure, which was used to calculate simple molecular properties (for example Lipinski's rule of five),^([14](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit14)) was necessary to advance the drug discovery process. Similarly, in the field of crystalline, inorganic materials, the existence of well-defined structures simplifies the determination of structure–property relationships, because in many cases the relatively well-defined electronic structure of the crystalline material contains the required information about the properties of interest.^([11](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit11),[15](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit15)) However, because weak non-covalent interactions mostly define the bulk structure of many organic materials, the link between structure and organic material properties is not always clear. Therefore, the development and understanding of structure–property relationships is a complex, multiscale and multivariable problem. Given sufficient data, AI can be applied to understand multiscale structure–property relationships and remove the need for approximations and simplifications, which significantly advances the ability to predict material properties. Such a capability will drive the implementation of inverse design procedures, which determine the optimal candidate materials and efficiently explore the material search space based on the optimisation of material function, without the need to test a myriad of possible candidates.^([16](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit16),[17](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit17))

It is possible to apply AI approaches to all aspects of a modern materials discovery pipeline, from candidate generation and data extraction to analysis and property prediction, offering the opportunity to drastically speed up the discovery process without a significant loss of accuracy. Additionally, AI presents a pathway toward the automation of materials discovery, at a significantly faster rate and lower cost than human-driven discovery. A significant barrier in the application of AI approaches is the quantity and quality of existing data, the lack of negative data,^([18](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit18)) as well as the choice of representation of chemical and physical systems.^([17](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit17))

## 12.2 Extracting Data from the Literature

From the perspective of using AI approaches to predict new materials and their properties, it is crucial to have a large quantity of high-quality, machine-readable data for training. Within the entirety of the scientific literature, there is a massive amount of experimental and theoretical data in the form of unstructured text, figures or tables in journal articles, technical documents, and patents.^([19](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit19),[20](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit20)) The manual collection and curation of this data into a machine-readable database becomes intractable on a large-scale. Fortunately, the scientific literature is often written in a formulaic way, which allows for the application of text-mining algorithms to automatically extract data. However, the ambiguity and variability in many conventions in different scientific domains limit the universality of established dictionary and rule-based approaches to text mining.^([19](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit19)–[21](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit21)) The current trend for large-scale information extraction is the use of machine learning (ML)-based (or hybrid) text-mining workflows because they are much more flexible than hard-coded methods.^([19](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit19),[22](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit22)–[24](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit24))

Recently, Cole and co-workers developed ChemDataExtractor (CDE), open-source software for the automatic extraction of chemical information.^([25](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit25)) CDE implements supervised and unsupervised ML models throughout the entire natural language processing (NLP) and named entity recognition (NER) workflow (see [Figure 12.2](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#fig2)). NER is used to find named entities within the text, which can include chemical species, processes, synthetic conditions, material properties, and characterisation methods, and can be performed using ML^([23](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit23)) and hybrid ML, dictionary, and rule-based approaches.^([19](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit19)) A significant challenge of text mining is reliably creating a unique identifier for each entity, *i.e.* matching synonymous terms, which is called entity normalisation. Weston *et al.* performed tokenisation using CDE, NER using a neural network (NN) and entity normalisation using word embeddings (a machine-learned map of each word onto a dense vector space based on their co-occurrences in text) on the materials science literature toward a structured and accessible database of materials.^([22](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit22)) Similarly, Tshitoyan *et al.* learned a word embedding using text from scientific abstracts and used this to uncover relationships between materials and their potential properties.^([24](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit24)) As a result of its inbuilt flexibility, CDE is useful in many subdomains. In the field of organic materials, Cole and co-workers applied the CDE to the discovery of optimal organic dye pairs for co-sensitised solar cells.^([26](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit26)) They text mined 9431 dye candidates into a database that linked chemical structure with optical adsorption peak and molar extinction coefficient. From this initial database, a high-throughput screening workflow was applied to identify suitable candidate dye pairs and improved power conversion efficiency of the resultant top candidates was experimentally validated.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00280-f2.jpg)

Figure 12.2 Natural language processing pipeline. Text is split into sentences and then into individual tokens. The part-of-speech tagger and entity recogniser outputs are combined to assign a single tag to each token, which is then parsed using a rule-based grammar to produce a tree structure. This tree structure is interpreted to extract individual chemical records for this sentence, which are then combined with records from throughout the document to resolve data interdependencies and produce unified records for depositing in a database. Tags shown: NN=noun, CD=cardinal number, VBZ=verb (third person singular present), DT=determiner, NNS=noun plural, IN=preposition, JJ=adjective, CC=coordinating conjunction, CM=chemical mention. Reproduced from ref. [25](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit25) with permission from American Chemical Society, Copyright 2016.

## 12.3 Building Block Libraries

Developing diverse precursor libraries is an important part of the materials screening process,^([27](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit27)) as it defines the chemical space available for examination. While molecular structure libraries such as ZINC,^([28](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit28)) GBD,^([29](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit29)) and PubChem^([30](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit30)) offer a large amount of diverse, synthesisable molecules, they are unfocused, making an exhaustive search of all precursor candidates infeasible, and many molecules in them are not designed with materials in mind. Enumeration of existing molecular libraries, through adding known useful functionalities or systematic processes, is a common method of extending building block libraries. However, hard-coded transformations often limit the chemical space spanned by precursor libraries,^([27](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit27)) potentially missing compounds that occupy favourable regions of property space. As part of the Harvard Clean Energy Project, a precursor library was created by enumerating compounds based on combining 26 molecular building blocks using pre-defined chemical transformations, to generate a library of over 1 000 000 molecules.^([31](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit31)) Additionally, Gómez-Bombarelli *et al.* designed a library of 1.6 million candidate materials for light-emitting diodes based on donor-bridge-acceptor molecules, systematically incorporating additional functional groups into the library according to chemical intuition.^([32](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit32))

## 12.4 Predicting Properties

### 12.4.1 Training Data

Any application of ML requires training data for the model, the quantity and quality of which directly influence the types of algorithms that can be used and the likely accuracy of the trained model. Regression, *e.g.* Gaussian process and kernel ridge regression (KRR), and decision tree models can be trained with relatively small training datasets, but neural networks require much more data. Both algorithms offer advantages; however, deep neural networks typically outperform traditional ML techniques in property prediction.^([33](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit33)) The training data itself can be obtained from experiment or from theory and computation. In the context of property prediction, experimental data-sets are typically rather limited in size; for example, Kim *et al.* trained models to predict the glass temperature and density of polymers using 451 and 173 experimental data points, respectively.^([34](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit34)) Hence experimental training data is often used in combination with regression and decision tree methods. Computational chemistry derived training datasets can be much larger, up to millions of data points, and can be obtained from a range of methods, including semi-empirical, density functional theory (DFT) and quantum chemistry calculations. DFT calculations are the norm, but modern semi-empirical methods, *e.g.* the xTB family of semi-empirical methods developed by the Grimme group,^([35](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit35),[36](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit36)) can give results with a similar accuracy for a fraction of the computer time and hence allow for the generation of (much) larger training data-sets than feasible with DFT.^([8](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit8),[37](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit37)) Conversely, if one wants to train an ML model to predict data with similar accuracy to quantum chemistry calculations, then one must train it with data from quantum chemistry calculations, which is possible, but time-consuming.^([38](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit38)–[40](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit40))

Despite the ongoing progress in database creation for organic materials, there still remains an absence of data compared to other domains, such as in the fields of drug design or inorganic materials, in which automated calculation workflows have fuelled the growth of several inorganic material property databases, such as NOMAD^([41](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit41)) and the Materials Project database.^([42](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit42)) In the organic materials domain, there are several data repositories, focussing on specific material applications (see [Table 12.1](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#tab1)). Many datasets contain computational calculation results such as Khazana,^([43](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit43)) the Harvard Organic Photovoltaic Dataset,^([44](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit44)) the Open Spectral Dataset,^([45](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit45)) the dye-sensitised solar cell database^([46](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit46)) and the Organic Materials Database.^([47](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit47)) From these repositories, new material design principles have been established using both ML^([48](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit48)) and data-mining techniques.^([49](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit49)) Olsthoorn *et al.* used the smooth overlap of atomic positions (SOAP) kernel method of crystal structure featurisation to predict the band gap using KRR on data from the Organic Materials database.^([50](#BK9781788017893-00280.xhtml#cit50)) The predictive model was then used to screen the Crystallographic Open Database, containing 30 713 organic crystal structures, and identified 15 candidates that were predicted to have a suitable band gap for solar cells.
