CHAPTER 13

A New Era of Inorganic Materials Discovery Powered by Data Science

YA ZHUO, ARIA MANSOURI TEHRANI AND JAKOAH BRGOCH[\*](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#affa)

Department of Chemistry, University of Houston, Houston, TX 77204, USA

\*Email: [jbrgoch@central.uh.edu](mailto:jbrgoch@central.uh.edu)

## 13.1 Introduction

Empiricism has been the central force driving science forward, allowing us to gain and generate extensive knowledge and understanding about our surroundings. As our comprehension increased, numerous scientific theories in the form of numerical expressions were eventually developed that could describe or replicate various ideas or ‘real-world’ observations, such as the establishment of Newton's Laws. However, scientific complexity has increased seemingly exponentially, and simple mathematical expressions are not always capable of solving many of the modern scientific problems. Fortunately, the advent of computers, and the ideas propelling computational modeling and ultimately data science have transformed how researchers approach scientific questions. This evolution has been nicely categorized in four paradigms, as shown in [Figure 13.1](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#fig1).^([1](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit1))

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00311-f1.jpg)

Figure 13.1 The four paradigms of science: empirical, theoretical, computational, and data-driven.

Chemistry began like all branches of science with qualitative, empirical observations and the development of chemical intuition followed by the construction of quantitative theories to explain these observations, like laws of thermodynamics. The eventual creation and implementation of advanced experimental approaches stemming from this second paradigm marked a significant revolution, allowing a better understanding of the observations. Inorganic, solid-state chemistry specifically was one of the subfields extensively strengthened by the introduction of improved synthesis techniques and advanced characterization techniques. The creation of methods to solve complex crystal structures or perform physical property measurements and data analysis over the past couple of centuries has led to the generation of significant amounts of data, most of which are now compiled in structured databases. For example, the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD),^([2](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit2)) the Pauling File (now Pearson's Crystal Data; PCD),^([3](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit3)) the Materials Platform for Data Science (MPDS),^([4](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit4)) the NIMS Materials Database (MatNavi),^([5](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit5)) and the American Society for Metals datasets like the ASM Phase Diagram Database,^([6](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit6)) among numerous others, have endeavored to provide well-curated data sets that contain information on known (inorganic) crystal structures and measured physical properties. A majority of these data have been submitted directly by the research groups that generated the results, which is an excellent example of successful scientific ‘crowd-sourcing’. Some of the databases have also been expanded through the laborious task of manually extracting data from the peer-reviewed literature.

The transition to the third, computational paradigm has been propelled by the outstanding accomplishments of computational materials chemists and spurred by their access to these sizeable crystallographic data sets. Numerous computational approaches have been developed over time, ranging from semi-empirical methods to *ab initio* methods. Density functional theory (DFT), as a subset of *ab initio* calculations, is arguably the most widely used among the inorganic materials community. Although it was first proposed in the 1960s, the recognition of its importance came only in the 1980s as the result of the increase in computational capacity and continuous theoretical refinement and expansion of the methodologies.^([7](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit7)) Indeed, DFT has made tremendous strides in determining the electronic structures of inorganic solids^([8](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit8),[9](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit9)) even though limitations still exist.^([10](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit10),[11](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit11)) For example, these calculations frequently require high-performance computing clusters, which are not always accessible or available. Also, DFT struggles to calculate disordered crystal structures and highly correlated systems, although DFT+U can improve the outcome.^([12](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit12)) DFT is usually able to accommodate only a limited number of atoms, typically a few hundred at most currently, which prevents researchers from modeling longer length scale interactions, such as microstructures, at the *ab initio* level. Nevertheless, the expansion of computational power has allowed DFT to obtain the electronic structure for thousands of inorganic solids as well as be implemented in an automated, high-throughput format where considerable computational resources are employed to ascertain the electronic structure of a vast number of compounds. Supported by the launch of the Materials Genome Initiative (MGI)^([13](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit13)) in 2011, the outputs from these high-throughput computational projects have been compiled in massive on-line databases providing accessible, robust, and trustworthy computational (DFT) results. Some of the most well-known examples are the Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD),^([14](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit14)) Materials Project (MP),^([15](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit15)) and Automatic-Flow for Materials Discovery (AFLOW).^([16](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit16)) These databases are quite extensive, containing basic information like electronic structures, calculated elastic tensors, thermodynamic properties, and even predicted phase diagrams.

The MGI was arguably the catalyst not only for the creation of these large high-throughput computational databases but also for encouraging the transition to the fourth paradigm where these enormously useful repositories are employed directly for research. The accessibility to such high-quality data has compelled investigators to think about the best pathway to utilize this ‘big-data’, which has been bolstered by subfields such as data analytics or informatics that are focused on understanding the principles behind data and the practice of information processing and the engineering of information systems. From these initial ideas, data science and machine learning have emerged as the principal methodology to analyze data sets, identify chemical trends, and suggest new opportunities to advance materials chemistry. The goal is to accelerate materials discovery by recognizing previously unknown correlations in a compound's composition–structure–property-processing relationship, as well as uncovering new qualitative and quantitative rules for materials development. Moreover, advanced experimental and computational techniques with their ever-growing rates of data acquisition and storage capabilities required new procedures for quickly assessing and analyzing the large collected data sets. Machine learning techniques and big data approaches have also provided an avenue to improve these methods by employing algorithms that can model the relationships between materials properties and related factors, even in high-dimensional data. Data science can also help decipher the intrinsic characteristics of materials and then reveal new hypotheses regarding the conditions that lead to successful products, which are much more challenging and critical for materials discovery.^([17](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit17))

Given the potential provided by data science and its recent prevalence in inorganic materials chemistry, this chapter reviews some of the recent successful strategies where machine learning was essential for materials discovery and design. It also analyzes the challenges that the community is facing and those that should be overcome in the near future. It is anticipated that this chapter can introduce a new perspective toward data-driven materials chemistry research. In the rest of this chapter, we first introduce the formal description of machine learning as it pertains to inorganic materials chemistry, including discussing the commonly used steps in machine learning, and then survey the current research status with respect to the applications of machine learning with a focus on inorganic materials discovery. In particular, we highlight notable examples of synthetic process optimization, crystal structure prediction, and physical property prediction achieved using a variety of machine learning strategies. Finally, the most pressing challenges and research opportunities in this field are examined.

## 13.2 Workflow for Materials Discovery *via* Machine Learning

Artificial intelligence in computer science is the intelligence demonstrated by a machine aimed at mimicking ‘cognitive’ functions that humans associate with the human mind, such as ‘learning’ and ‘problem-solving’. Attempts have been made to approach the problem of acquiring knowledge by a machine through various symbolic methods, as well as methods based on connection principles, such as neural networks and perceptrons. The term ‘machine learning’, coined in 1959 by Arthur Samuel, grew out of the quest for artificial intelligence as a scientific endeavor. Its emphasis is more on logical and knowledge-based methods than on symbolic approaches. The goal of machine learning is to tackle solvable problems of a practical nature by developing methodologies and models derived from statistics and probability theories. Benefitting from the development of various learning algorithms over the years, machine learning has shown outstanding success in clustering, classification, regression, and other related tasks. Examples of applying machine learning specifically to inorganic materials chemistry can be traced back to the mid-1990s when approaches like neural networks were first employed to predict the melting point of binary intermetallic compounds and the mechanical behavior of fiber/matrix interfaces in ceramic-matrix composites.^([18](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit18)–[20](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit20)) The increasing availability of digitized information in the form of the materials-specific databases, and the ability to distribute data in a digital format has allowed machine learning to finally flourish. As a result, a substantial amount of research addressing various topics such as property prediction, new materials discovery, and materials design, has been published.

Regardless of the specific problem under study, a machine-learning problem can be broken into the following steps: data collection, data representation, data reduction, model construction, and model evaluation (see [Figure 13.2](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#fig2)). In the following subsections, a detailed explanation of each step as they relate to machine learning in inorganic materials chemistry is presented.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00311-f2.jpg)

Figure 13.2 The general machine learning workflow.

### 13.2.1 Data Collection

The foremost prerequisite for any machine-learning task is the availability of a significant number of data in a machine-readable format that can be used as a ‘training set’. Access to the chemical information is arguably the most pressing need that scientists must overcome to grow this research area. Fortunately, the large crystal structure databases like ICSD and PCD, the physical property databases like MPDS and MatNavi, and electronic structure databases like AFLOW, OQMD, or the Materials Project, have provided access to viable training data. Users can even efficiently extract information from some of these large data sets through the open Materials Application Programming Interface (API) and the open-source Python Materials Genomics (Pymatgen) materials analysis package.^([21](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit21),[22](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit22)) Additionally, considerable scientific knowledge is present in figures, tables, and textual paragraphs. For example, laboratory notebooks contain extensive information that can be valuable as an input data set.^([23](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit23)) Peer-reviewed publications also contain troves of information; however, these data are challenging to analyze using traditional statistical analysis or machine learning methods. Several studies have used supervised natural language processing (NLP) to improve access to the information contained within research articles by text mining the scientific literature.^([24](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit24)–[29](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit29)) In one specific example, researchers encoded materials science knowledge present in the published literature as information-dense word embeddings (vector representations of words), which can capture the underlying structure of the periodic table and structure–property relationships in materials without human labeling or supervision.^([30](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit30)) Extracting and gathering all of the necessary training data in a single location is the essential first step to any machine learning project.

### 13.2.2 Data Representation

Once a set of training data is available, the next step is to create numerical representations of this information that can be interpreted by computers, which are known as features, descriptors, predictors, or attributes. In the context of inorganic materials, features are mainly based on property-related compositions and crystal structures. The former captures a diverse range of physical and chemical properties of the compounds. These are developed based on the fractions of elements present in a chemical formula or through a series of mathematical expressions describing a variety of elemental properties. For example, Ward *et al.* used this kind of feature set to accurately predict a diverse set of properties, including the formation energy and bandgap energy of crystalline materials as well as the glass-forming ability in metal alloy systems, with tremendous success.^([31](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit31)) Even so, only using compositional features prevents the descriptions of compounds that form polymorph crystal structures. As an example, graphite and diamond would produce identical compositional features in machine learning; yet, their mechanical properties are distinctly different. Systems that have invariance in their compositional features, but a large discrepancy in the corresponding properties, are something that current algorithms simply cannot appreciate. One solution is to incorporate structural features or augment the compositional features to distinguish between graphite and diamond. In terms of structure descriptors, different from molecular systems, which can easily lend themselves to descriptions as graphs, the conventional description of inorganic crystal structures employs primitive translation vectors and fractional coordinates of the atoms so that a crystal can be represented in an infinite number of equivalent ways by choice of different coordinate systems. This type of representation is not unique and thus not a suitable set of features for the learning process. Representations based on partial radial distribution function (PRDF),^([32](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit32)) Voronoi tessellations,^([33](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit33)) or property-labeled materials fragments^([34](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit34)) are among the promising approaches to tackle the problem of structure. Currently, multiple materials informatics packages have been developed and are widely available, such as Pymatgen,^([21](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit21)) Matminer,^([35](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit35)) and MatErials Graph Network (MEGNet)^([36](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit36)) to generate features with minimal effort.

It is essential that the representations uniquely characterize each material in a data set and relate to the essential physics and chemistry that influence the property of interest.^([37](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit37),[38](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit38)) Unfortunately, there is not a unified feature set that is effective across inorganic materials chemistry. Caution must, therefore, be exercised when selecting features. For example, the density of a crystalline compound is expected to relate to the density of the constituent elements. Including the average density of the constituent elements as a descriptor, a machine-learning algorithm could recognize the correlation between this value and the density of the crystal and then build a predictive model. Nevertheless, the mean density of the constituent elements neither uniquely describes a composition nor perfectly represents the density of the compounds. Therefore, additional descriptors must be included to create an appropriate feature set for this problem. However, the choice of descriptors is rarely simple; for instance, one possible feature to include in this problem might be crystal structure information that reflects the atomic packing scheme, but it is never clear. To overcome this conundrum, most researchers will create an excessively large feature set that includes all possible features and use data reduction techniques to determine the specific features related to the desired prediction. It is also imperative to examine the final set of features to ensure the reduced set represents experimentally or chemically reasonable information. Take the prediction of Li ion conductivity as an example.^([39](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit39)) Although ionic conductivity is expected to be influenced by several intrinsic and extrinsic factors, only ion diffusivity, average volume, transition temperature, and experimental temperature are of experimental interest. Therefore, it is necessary to ensure that these experimentally relevant factors remain in the learning process and are not removed during feature selection.

Finally, a typical good feature set should be universal, although this is not strictly necessary when performing analysis within a well-constrained chemical space. Features also have to be able to be reversed back into a description of the material in cases such as inverse design, in which the desired target property is used as inputs to predict the composition and structure.^([40](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit40))

### 13.2.3 Data Pre-processing

Data pre-processing usually requires a majority of a data scientist's time and is one of the most critical steps in machine learning. Analyzing data that has not been carefully pre-processed can produce misleading results. For instance, if a dataset includes a significant portion of irrelevant, redundant information, or noisy and unreliable information, then the knowledge gained by the algorithm during the training step may be questionable. This problem is often more significant in materials chemistry as the datasets are not, in most of the cases, ‘big data’ and usually range between a couple of hundreds to thousands. Therefore, within such relatively small datasets, each datum can be infulential to the performance of the model. Data pre-processing can usually influence the outcomes of the model or the ability to interpret the results. Proper pre-processing is, therefore, critical to the accuracy of the machine-learning model. Typically, pre-processing tasks include data cleaning, transformation, and reduction, as illustrated in [Figure 13.3](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#fig3). In the following, we will expand on the discussions and meanwhile present the most well-known algorithms for some steps of data pre-processing as they pertain to inorganic materials chemistry.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00311-f3.jpg)

Figure 13.3 Data pre-processing tasks and some commonly used approaches.

#### 13.2.3.1 Data Cleaning

Most techniques in machine learning rely on data sets that are complete and noise-free. However, real data are usually incomplete, noisy, and inconsistent, which can make analysis problematic. These imperfections in scientific data are often the result of complex issues like instrument limitations or technical problems at the time of data collection, as well as simple problems like the duplication of data or human error. Therefore, a cleaning step is essential to convert the original information into a trustworthy data set.

The occurrence of missing values is pervasive in the acquisition processes. A missing value is a datum that has not been stored or gathered due to non-existence, a flawed sampling process, cost restrictions, or limitations in the acquisition process. Incomplete data are usually an unavoidable problem, but they tend to cause severe difficulties for researchers because handling missing values, particularly in materials science, is generally difficult. Inappropriate treatment of the missing values can lead to inadequate knowledge extraction, strong biases, and wrong conclusions.

Many approaches are available to tackle the problem imposed by missing values. The simplest is to discard the instances that contain a missing value. However, this approach is beneficial only when a data set is quite large, and multiple values are missing within a tuple. Otherwise, it may produce a bias in the learning process as a result of producing an even smaller data set. The seminal works on data imputation stem from statistics and rely on probability functions. For instance, it is possible to use maximum likelihood procedures, where approximate probabilistic models are employed to fill the missing values. It is also possible to predict the missing value by developing a regression or classification model based on a complete data set for a given feature.

Another problem associated with the data set can be noise generated from faulty data collection, or data entry errors, among other sources. Data mining algorithms assume that any data set is a sample of an underlying distribution with no disturbances. In specific machine-learning problems, noise can have a significant impact on the input features. The situation is made worse when the noise affects the output targets or both inputs and outputs, as this means that the bias introduced will be more significant. To remove noise in data, two approaches are commonly applied. The first is to use data polishing methods to correct the noise, especially if it affects the labeling of an instance. Even partially correcting noise is beneficial to the model; however, this requires knowledge of the data set and is usually limited to correcting small amounts of noise.^([41](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit41)) The second approach is to use noise filters, like variable-by-variable data cleaning, to detect and remove noisy instances in a data set. An advantage of using noise filters is that they are straightforward to implement and require minimal knowledge about the data set. Noise identification and elimination are still active areas of research and development.^([42](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit42),[43](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit43))

#### 13.2.3.2 Data Transformation

Transforming the cleaned data in an appropriate form suitable for the learning process is the next step. Mandatory transformations must be done for data compatibility. For example, a classifier was constructed to distinguish metals from insulators. Because machine-learning models are based on mathematical equations, it can sometimes be problematic if categorical strings such as ‘metal’ or ‘insulator’ are fed directly into the computer. Instead, these are generally converted into machine-readable numerical values before modeling, *e.g.*, encoding metals and insulators as the integers ‘0’ and ‘1’, respectively. Often features are also not available as numerical values but are instead categorical; it is mandatory to convert these features to numerical representations.

Optional quality transformations may also improve model performance. The continuous features in a data set are often at varying scales; for instance, the melting point covers a broad range from a few kelvin to thousands of kelvin. A standardizer could be used to translate this information to a scale where 0 represents the average melting point for the data set, and −1/+1 represents one standard deviation from the average. In general, learning algorithms benefit immensely from standardizing the data. Robust scaling or transforming is more appropriate if outliers are present in the data set. Many popular machine-learning estimators may behave poorly if the individual features do not follow a standard distribution, which is usually considered to be a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and unit variance. For example, elements used in the objective function of a learning algorithm, such as the l1 and l2 regularizers of linear models or the RBF (radial basis function) kernel of Support Vector Machines, assume that all features are centered at zero, and have variance in the same order. If a feature has a variance that is orders of magnitude larger than others are, it might dominate the objective function and make the estimator unable to adequately learn from other features. Practically, there is an almost unlimited number of ways that a data set can be transformed. To provide one example, transformation based on a logarithm function is a commonly used method of dealing with an exponential data series.

Discretization is another action sometimes needed in the pre-processing step. For example, in the process of inducing decision trees and deriving decision rules, the importance of one set of features tends to be overestimated if it contains too many continuous values.^([44](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit44)) Discretization, which partitions continuous numerical features into discrete values, is a useful process to address this problem. Discrete values are closer to a knowledge-level representation than continuous values, making data more understandable and easier to use, thereby improving predictive accuracy. Numerous discretization methods have been proposed and tested. Feature binarization converts numerical features to binary features with the assumption that data follows a Bernoulli distribution. A bucketizer discretizes a set of continuous features into bins. Generally, most discretization methods can be grouped into *top-down* (splitting) and *bottom-up* (merging) methods.^([45](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit45)) Top-down methods start with an empty list of cut-points and recursively split data into smaller intervals. As an example, Maas *et al.* examined candidate cut-points against an error function and explored a search space of boundary points to minimize the number of wrong predictions in a classification problem.^([46](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit46)) Conversely, bottom-up methods start with the complete list of all continuous values as cut-points and iteratively merge neighboring intervals. One example is Khiops, where data can be discretized based on the global optimization of chi-squared.^([47](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit47)) Although many methods have been developed, the selection of the interval borders and the correct arity for the discretization of a numerical value range remain open questions.

#### 13.2.3.3 Data Reduction

Data mining is a technique that is utilized to handle vast amounts of data. Working with a large volume of data makes the analysis more difficult, leading to reduced accuracy, low efficiency, and increased cost. Performing data reduction is valuable because it can improve model accuracy by reducing the number of misleading data, save storage space, and lower computing needs. The critical challenge in proper data reduction is to produce a condensed representation that is smaller in volume yet retains the integrity of the original data set. Additionally, data reduction can help simplify a model. The complexity of the model increases with the increasing number of features potentially causing overfitting, because as a machine-learning algorithm is trained on a large number of features, it gets increasingly dependent on the data. Avoiding overfitting is one of the primary motivations for performing data reduction, with the added benefit that the resulting models tend to be more straightforward.

A few methods are often used to reduce the volume of data. Principal component analysis, or PCA, is a statistical method that reduces the numbers of features by lumping highly correlated features together regardless of the importance of the meaning of these features. With each iteration, orthogonal transformation converts the features into principal components, which are a set of linearly uncorrelated values. Feature selection is another useful procedure to reduce the data volume by identifying and removing irrelevant and redundant features. Straightforward feature selection methods are low variance filter, which aims to remove less informative features that are characterized by having a low variance, as well as a high correlation filter, which discards features that have a correlation coefficient higher than a threshold, meaning other features carry similar information. Algorithms associated with a stopping criterion are also employed to generate a subset of features and to evaluate the performance of a proposed subset. A stopping criterion can be: (i) including (or excluding) any feature does not produce a better subset; and (ii) an optimal subset is obtained according to the evaluation function. Without a proper stopping criterion, the selection process may run exhaustively or forever through the space of subsets. The genetic algorithm (GA) is a well-known approach for feature selection. It generates a feature subset that is only composed of the ‘winning’ features in the race between being included in a subset or excluded from a subset.^([48](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit48),[49](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit49)) Research has also shown the possibility of using a particular learning algorithm as a pre-processor to discover useful feature subsets. Recursive feature elimination (RFE) is a heuristic method to remove irrelevant features. First, an external estimator is trained on the original features, and weights are assigned to each feature. Then, comparison of the weights indicates the least important features and recursively prunes these features from subsequent sets until a desired number of features is reached.

Dimensional reduction techniques have become popular for producing condensed feature representations to speed up model construction. Many of these ideas have also been implemented by materials chemists to establish process–structure–property relationships and for exploratory data analysis to understand trends in multivariate space.^([50](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit50)) For example, Dey *et al.* used PCA to identify the features that cause outliers in the task of predicting the bandgap energy for chalcopyrite compounds.^([51](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit51)) Agrawal *et al.* employed a ranking-based feature selection to get insights about the relative predictive potential of the input features for the problem of fatigue strength prediction of steels.^([52](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit52))

### 13.2.4 Model Construction

The data are ready for modeling once appropriate data pre-processing has been completed. A model bridges the finger-printed features to the target property through mathematical functions. A range of algorithms are available, among them, some use actual functional forms that relate input to output, *e.g.*, support vector machine, whereas others do not, *e.g.*, decision tree. Moreover, the amount of input data strongly dictates the choice of learning algorithms. For example, tens to thousands of data may be adequately analyzed using algorithms such as kernel ridge regression or Gaussian process, but a much larger data set (>hundreds of thousands or millions) may be necessary for artificial neural networks or deep learning. In some cases, a single algorithm may work poorly, but the use of several estimators built within a single learning environment may improve model generalizability and robustness; this is called an ensemble method and includes methods such as bagging and boosting. In addition, intelligent optimization algorithms, such as genetic algorithms (GA) and particle swarm optimization (PSO) are sometimes employed to optimize the model hyper-parameters.^([53](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit53),[54](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit54)) Regardless of approach or methodology, one of the most significant distinctions is that learning can be supervised and unsupervised depending on whether or not the outputs are labeled.

#### 13.2.4.1 Supervised Learning

A significant amount of practical machine-learning problems in materials science rely on supervised learning. It requires that the ground truth, or the knowledge of what the output values for the samples should be, is prior available. The goal of supervised learning is to produce a mapping function from the input features (*x*) to the output targets (*y*) so that the model can predict an output *y* when given a new input *x*. Supervised learning models predict output values within a discrete set or a continuous set. The former is seen in classification problems, *e.g.*, categorizing a material as a metal or an insulator, whereas the latter is the output from a regression model, *e.g.*, predicting a material's bandgap energy. There is a variety of supervised learning algorithms that can be applied depending on specific tasks. The selection of an appropriate algorithm is critical in model construction because it dramatically influences the prediction accuracy and model generalizability. Each approach has its unique features, and no one algorithm is suitable for all problems. In the following, some commonly used algorithms in materials chemistry are outlined.

K Nearest Neighbor (KNN) is an instance-based algorithm used in both classification and regression.^([55](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit55)) It hinges on the assumption that similar things exist in close proximity and that the distances between points in a descriptor hyperspace can be calculated. The prediction is then determined based on the values of the K ‘nearest neighbors’ in the data, where K is an integer value specified by the user. In classification, the prediction is the most frequent label within the region of K nearest points, whereas in regression, the prediction is determined to be the average of the K nearest points.

Decision tree (DT) is a non-parametric algorithm that creates a tree-like flowchart to support each decision step.^([56](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit56)) It can handle both classification and regression tasks, although it is less appropriate for regression tasks. The model is trained by recursively partitioning the source set into subsets based on attribute value tests until members of the subset at one node all have the same value of the target, or splitting no longer adds value to the predictions. The tree depth determines the complexity of the decision rules and fitting. It is worth noting that an overly complex tree cannot generalize the data well. Mechanisms such as pruning, setting the minimum number of samples required at a node, or setting the maximum depth of the tree are, to some extend, necessary to avoid this problem.

Kernel methods are a class of algorithms for pattern analysis, whose best-known members are support vector machine (SVM), kernel ridge regression (KRR), and Gaussian process (GP).^([57](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit57)) Kernel methods work as a similarity function over pairs of data points, *i.e.*, it transforms two input data points into an output that quantifies how similar they are. Any kernel method solution comprises two components: a kernel function that performs the feature mapping and a learning algorithm used to discover the patterns in high dimensional feature space. Some popular kernel functions include linear, polynomial, sigmoid, while the radial basis function (RBF) is probably among the most used, as it has localized and finite response along the entire *x*\-axis. Kernel methods are modular in the sense that any kernel will work with any kernel-based algorithm.

Artificial neural networks (ANN) and deep neural networks (DNN) are computing systems that are intended to mimic the way that humans learn.^([58](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit58),[59](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit59)) They consist of artificial neurons arranged in input and output layers, as well as (in most cases) hidden layers. In a straightforward computation, hidden layers transform input signals into something that the output layer can use. Neurons and connections between neurons typically have weights, indicating the strength of the signal. Learning is the process of adjusting the weights to reproduce the training data as accurately as possible.

#### 13.2.4.2 Unsupervised Learning

Unlike supervised learning, unsupervised learning does not have labeled outputs, so its goal is to infer the inherent structure present within a set of data. The most common task within inorganic materials chemistry is clustering. Instead of directly predicting new values, clustering divides data into groups based on a similarity metric in a way that uncovers patterns and categories. Several algorithms are available today for automatically clustering data, such as *k*\-means clustering, Ward hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixtures, and density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN). Each algorithm partitions data based on a geometric metric; for example, the *k*\-means method aims to minimize the squared distances between data and cluster centers while Gaussian mixtures group data based on Mahalanobis distances to centers. Sometimes, additional parameters depending on the algorithm, *e.g.*, the number of clusters or distance threshold, need to be defined before performing a clustering analysis. Iterative algorithms may also require different trials to find an optimal grouping. The results of a clustering analysis can be used downstream. The advantage of using this approach is that materials in different clusters might bury some non-obvious physical characteristics, and a separate model thus can be constructed for each cluster. By using this approach, Meredig and Wolverton identified electronic structure features of dopant oxides and predicted zirconia dopant stability.^([60](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit60))

Unsupervised learning is also becoming popular in experimental data analysis, where the collected data set is used as the fingerprint. Shen *et al.* developed robust convolutional neural network approaches to reconstruct crystal orientations from electron backscatter diffraction patterns.^([61](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit61)) It is also possible to use this approach to quickly determine the presence of different crystallographic phases in a sample analyzed using high-throughput X-ray diffraction, allowing the automated creation of phase diagrams and identification of new phases.^([62](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit62)–[65](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit65)) Merging machine learning approaches with these types of studies will be critical to advance the field of materials chemistry and aid the discovery of new compounds and crystal structures.

### 13.2.5 Model Evaluation

In principle, errors of a model arise from three sources: model bias, model variance, and irreducible errors, with the total error being the sum of these. Bias comes from erroneous assumptions taken by the learner. High bias can lead to missing underlying relations between features and target outputs. Variance is the result of sensitivity to small fluctuations in the training set. High variance models have limitations on the flexibility to learn the true signal from the data. Irreducible errors exist in every model, even in well-trained ones, and they stem from the inherent variability in data due to systematic errors in laboratory instruments, calculation uncertainties, or simply from outliers or missing data. A poorly performing model usually indicates high bias or high variance.

A robust machine-learning model should have adequate prediction power on not only existing data but also unseen data. A widely used approach for evaluating the quality of a model involves partitioning the original data set into a training set for model construction and a test set for model evaluation. The data in the test set should be randomly selected and completely unseen from the model. It is advisable, especially for small data sets, to use multiple (>3) randomly selected training and test sets to ensure the robustness of the model. To avoid the introduction of additional deviations, sampling methods can be used to maintain the consistency of the data distribution to the highest possible extent. The model performance can be approximated by evaluating the extent to which the output data in the test set is accurately predicted. Cross-validation (CV), as a second approach for model evaluation, partitions the original data set into mutually exclusive subsets. For example, *k*\-fold CV divides the data set into *k* subsets of the same size, and the union set of *k-*1 subsets is taken to train the model, while the remaining one is used as the test set. This process is repeated for each subset. A particular case is when *k* equals the number of original data, called leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). LOOCV is a powerful CV approach to ensure a model's validity; however, it is not necessarily suitable for large data sets because it can take a long time for the cross-validating process, and it may also artificially underestimate the error for highly correlated data sets. Recently, leave-one-cluster-out cross-validation (LOCOCV) was proposed as a new measure of model performance geared toward materials discovery.^([66](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit66)) Instead of a standard LOOCV, LOCOCV first generates clusters and then removes the entire cluster in the cross-validation step. This approach offers a more realistic evaluation by estimating the ability of the model to extrapolate by removing entire groups providing information on the capability to extrapolate to entire classes of unseen materials.

## 13.3 Applications of Machine Learning in Inorganic Materials

The use of data-driven tools has the potential to result in significant materials advances, whether through the enumeration and analysis of experimental and computational data or the codification of chemical intuition. The purpose of building predictive models is not to replace experiment and computation, but rather to focus the effort in these research areas. In this section, we highlight a selection of research projects applying many of the machine-learning techniques that have been discussed here to advance the field as well as reduce the barriers to understand the compositions–structure–property-processing relationships in inorganic materials.

### 13.3.1 Machine Learning in Synthesis Optimization

Determining the optimal reaction condition or processing procedures to prepare an inorganic material has historically relied extensively on heuristics, theoretical analysis, and the accumulation of experience. As a result, the targeted production of new materials has always been a slow step in materials realization. A more productive approach might be to establish a comprehensive and accessible link between the specific material and the requisite preparation conditions to achieve the compound. Given the enormous complexities in the synthesis processes, machine-learning methods could be one of the most beneficial approaches to unify the different factors in the synthetic route and suggest the optimal conditions. One example where this has proved successful is in the study of Al–Zn–Mg–Cu series alloys. Fang *et al.* used least square support vector machine (LSSVM) models to optimize the aging temperature and aging time for targeting the product with high hardness and high electrical conductivity, followed by hybridizing nondominated sorting-based multi-objective genetic algorithm (MOGA) and LSSVM to make tradeoffs between hardness and electrical conductivity.^([67](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit67)) Ling *et al.* employed ensemble machine-learning algorithms to map functions between mechanical properties, such as tensile yield strength and shear strength, and processing steps, such as heat treatment and pressure treatment, in aluminum alloys and nickel-based superalloys.^([68](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit68)) Neural networks are also showing particular promise for predicting materials’ synthesis routes. Kim *et al.* developed a framework that compiled inorganic materials synthesis recipes across over half a million scholar publications through natural language processing and used these recipes to train machine-learning models to obtain insights into the critical parameters, such as calcination temperature, needed to synthesize specific, technologically relevant materials at a high level of automation.^([69](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit69)) In another study, failed or unsuccessful hydrothermal syntheses collected from laboratory notebooks, termed ‘dark reactions’, were analyzed using machine-learning models to determine the optimal reaction conditions for the crystallization of templated vanadium selenites.^([23](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit23)) Their model exceeded human intuitive strategies, and successfully predicted synthesis conditions for new organically templated inorganic product formation with a success rate of 89%.

Given the fact that numerous competing factors simultaneously govern the preparation of a material, it is sometimes complicated to directly model the complex kinetic processes with mathematical expressions by conventional methods. Fuzzy neural networks (FNN) offer an alternative to handle imprecision and uncertainties presented in synthesis procedures. It integrates the excellent learning capability of neural networks with fuzzy inference for extracting the initial rules of a fuzzy system. For example, Han *et al.* trained an FNN prediction model as well as a multiple linear regression (MLR) model for comparison to establish the relationship between processing parameters during hot working and heat treatment processing and the resulting mechanical properties of Ti–10V–2Fe–3Al titanium alloy.^([70](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit70)) The optimum processing parameters leading to the desired mechanical property can be accurately selected based on the fuzzy model. The FNN method achieved better prediction precision and showed much better agreement with experimental results than the MLR method.

In addition, merging intelligent models with simulation techniques turns out to be efficient in some complex systems. For example, neuro-fuzzy and physically based models were jointly used to predict the flow stress and microstructural evolution during the thermomechanical processing of aluminum alloys.^([71](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit71),[72](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit72)) The physically based components in the hybrid model facilitated extrapolation beyond process conditions, leading to better agreement with experimental data.

### 13.3.2 Machine Learning in Structure Prediction

Predicting the crystal structure preference of inorganic materials has always been of great interest. The crystal structure of any composition dictates the electronic structure and hugely influences its properties. Consequently, understanding the composition-crystal structure–property relationship in solids comprises a significant endeavor of inorganic chemists, emphasizing the importance of this subject. However, there is no practical method to predict the crystal structure of any given composition before synthesis. Often comprehensive characterization techniques such as single crystal structure diffraction are also required once a new compound has been prepared to solve the structure. To achieve the goal of predicting a structure *a priori*, correlations must be identified based on innate elemental properties, while many other factors such as temperature and pressure are influential. A simple yet fundamentally imperative correlation was identified by Pauling in which the coordination number of crystals was predicted based on the radius ratio of anions and cations.^([73](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit73)) Many other empirical correlations followed, laying the foundations to decode the intricate complexity of composition crystal structure relationships of inorganic materials. More recently, the emergence of *ab initio* computational methods such as DFT to numerically estimate the ground-state energy of extended compounds based on atomic coordination made a considerable impact on the community with regard to a prior crystal structure prediction. Clearly, it is not possible to compare the DFT ground-state energy of all possible crystal structure-types, even ignoring the possibility of a new-crystal structure-type, to indicate the most energetically favorable structure. To approach this problem, methods based on evolutionary algorithms have been developed, such as Crystal Structure Analysis by Particle Swarm Optimization (CALYPSO)^([74](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit74)) and Universal Structure Predictor: Evolutionary Xtallography (USPEX)^([75](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit75)) to potentially reach the ground state structure significantly faster. However, it is difficult to ensure that the calculated structure is at a global minimum rather than a local minimum of the energy landscape. Further, these methodologies are still extremely computationally expensive, especially for *k*\-nary (*k*\>3) compounds, which in many cases negates the purpose of the prior prediction.

Researchers have also implemented an alternative approach that combines data mining with first-principle calculations. A probability heuristic framework is constructed to suggest candidate structures of compositions to predict alloy formation of metallic binaries.^([76](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit76)) Regardless, DFT calculations have their limitations; the calculations are performed at zero kelvin while many compounds go through phase transformation at higher temperatures, and the calculations cannot account for statistical site-sharing of atomic positions in a straightforward manner, while correlation effects should be dealt with carefully in some compounds, *e.g.*, transition metal oxides or compounds containing f electrons.

Similar to the original correlation diagrams and analysis that Pauling and others created to unravel the correlations between crystal structure and composition,^([73](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit73),[77](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit77)–[80](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit80)) data-driven techniques are being implemented for the same purpose. Machine-learning algorithms are capable of constructing complex correlations, potentially in multi-dimensional space unattainable to humans, in big data sets. Therefore, it is a natural transition to implement these tools to predict crystal structures. Thus far researchers have utilized various machine learning methods to predict crystal structure types. For example, Oliynyk *et al.* used a random forest algorithm to model the possibility of AB[2]C compositions forming the Heusler structure.^([81](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit81)) Cluster resolution feature selection (CR-FS) in conjunction with support vector classification (SVC) was adopted to predict the crystal structure of AB and ABC compounds.^([82](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit82),[83](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit83)) Moreover, Balachandran *et al.* implemented a multi-faceted framework by combining group theory, machine learning, and DFT calculations to identify new noncentrosymmetric materials.^([84](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit84)) Additionally, researches have utilized machine learning techniques to assist in solving X-ray diffractions and the automatic classification of diffractograms.^([85](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit85)–[87](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit87)) These examples highlight the success of predicting whether a generic composition will adopt a specific structure type.

To construct a more general machine-learning model for structure prediction, a random forest classifier has been implemented, which is capable of predicting the structure-type for any composition.^([88](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit88)) The main issue in classifying structure-types is that crystal structures are, in fact, distributed in an extremely unbalanced fashion. For almost 25 000 unique compositions extracted from PCD there are around 10 700 entry prototypes with most of them corresponding to only a few (<10) structures. Not only there is an extreme imbalance concerning the structure-type distribution but also there are many instances of unusual or exotic structure-types that are extremely rare, which may disturb the learning process.^([89](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit89)) Therefore, one might not expect the algorithm to identify very exotic crystal structure-types correctly. To partially circumvent this issue, a cut-off, ranging between 10–150 instances, is determined. Any structure-type with fewer instances is therefore classified as ‘other’. The algorithm with a cut-off of 100 shows precision and recall of around 85% and 68%, respectively, indicating it is capable of identifying the structure-type of any composition with reasonable accuracy. Despite its usefulness, one should note that this model cannot distinguish if a combination of elements will crystalize or not, and the prediction of new instances could be, therefore, purely hypothetical. In another approach, a deep neural network was used based on atomic fingerprints as inputs. The researchers have focused on predicting the likelihood of various elements occupying atomic sites through a combinatorial approach. The reason for this implementation is that there are no examples of crystal structures that do not form, which must be included as negative results in the learning process. Moreover, to prevent the issue of elemental imbalance distribution of training data an oversampling method is utilized by increasing the number of the elements with low repetitions.^([90](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit90))

Finally, a crystal structure prediction engine was developed using Bayesian optimization algorithm.^([91](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit91)) Based on a combination of exploration and exploitation, the number of trials to reach the ground-state energy is significantly reduced, as shown for the cases of NaCl and Y[2]Co[17]. This methodology starts with a random generation of crystal structure that is relaxed using DFT calculations. These energies, in conjunction with relevant created descriptors, form the first set of training data. A Bayesian optimization algorithm then selects another set of candidates, which are optimized with descriptors being updated before the next set of selections until the global minimum is reached. Machine learning methods have also been used to develop interatomic potentials for inorganic material. One research project has constructed a dubbed Gaussian approximation potential-based random structure searching tool that leads to crystal structure prediction of inorganic solids. This methodology was applied to elemental phosphorus, correctly predicting its polymorphs.^([92](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit92)) These approaches demonstrate exceptional potential in future crystal structure prediction methods by significantly reducing the time required for methods such as first-principle evolutionary structure searches, ultimately enabling the future investigation of larger and more complex systems.

### 13.3.3 Machine Learning in Material Property Prediction

The application of machine learning in predicting inorganic materials’ physical properties involves determining the relationships between the properties, either computationally modeled or experimentally measured, and the feature set. Numerous research projects have already been carried out specifically for property prediction. For example, Isayev *et al.* combined data from *ab initio* calculations with quantitative materials structure–property relationship (QMSPR) models to predict several electronic and thermomechanical properties.^([34](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit34)) They first developed a calculation tool called property-labeled materials fragments (PLMF) to represent materials. Features generated with PLMF capture both structure geometry and local atomic properties. Using the gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT) method, a candidate material is classified as a metal or an insulator, followed by the prediction of bandgap value if the material is predicted to be an insulator. Regardless of the material's metal/insulator classification, another six GBDT models are then constructed to predict thermomechanical properties, including bulk modulus, shear modulus, Debye temperature, heat capacity at constant pressure, heat capacity at constant volume and thermal expansion coefficient. Hyper-parameters of all models are optimized with grid searches, and the model's generalizability is assessed with five-fold cross-validation.

Calculations done in a high-throughput manner have been critical for maximizing data availability, which makes the data collection process much more efficient. However, models that learn from computational data may have some shortcomings. Take bandgap as an example; high-throughput DFT calculations can obtain a large number of bandgap values at the PBE-level of exchange and correlation. However, these calculations show a systematic underestimation (∼40%) of bandgap compared with the experimental values.^([10](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit10),[11](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit11)) It is also often limited to ordered crystal structures and loses its reliability for highly correlated systems.^([93](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit93)) Therefore, any machine-learning model constructed using these DFT data are expected to underestimate the bandgap. At the same time, the predicted bandgap of site-mixing containing compounds or highly correlated compounds is less accurate than those ordered compounds. Alternatively, machine learning on a training set containing only experimentally measured bandgaps can be used to address many of those limitations.^([94](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit94)) The resulting model does not suffer from the DFT systematic error and achieves excellent agreement between the experimentally measured bandgaps and predicted bandgaps. The success of this experiment-based model is partially attributed to the relatively abundant availability of experimental data (∼4000 bandgaps) and, more importantly, the adequate selection of features. These data enable the model to capture the relative variation in bandgaps as a function of the features, eventually culminating in the prediction of bandgaps for new compounds. Unfortunately, in most cases, gathering a large amount of experimental data can be a difficult task for reasons such as the lack of reports or technical limitations in data extraction.

Conventional machine learning processes are not ideal for small data sets because the shortage in data can prevent the model fully capturing the inherent relationships between properties and features, resulting in a weak model, significant uncertainties in predictions, and thus selections of nonoptimal materials in a screening process. Fortunately, an adaptive procedure, called adaptive design or active learning, shows excellent potential for scientific problems where data are scarce. This strategy works as an iterative loop with feedback from experiments. It balances the trade-off between exploitation, where the goal is to search for materials likely to have the best property, and exploration, where the goal is to improve the quality of the model by searching the space that contains fewer sampling points and greater uncertainty. Adaptive design has been successfully applied in areas such as computer science,^([95](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit95)) engineering optimization,^([96](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit96)) cancer genomics,^([97](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit97)) and recently materials chemistry.^([98](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit98),[99](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit99)) For example, Xue *et al.* employed this adaptive design framework in the discovery of low thermal hysteresis NiTi-based shape memory alloys by using a limited number of 22 training examples.^([99](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit99)) An RBF embedded SVR regressor was first modeled to predict the thermal hysteresis with the uncertainties obtained from a bootstrap method, and then a knowledge gradient (KG) based selector used these predictions and their uncertainties to suggest the next material to investigate. By iterating the learning process nine times, 36 predicted compositions were synthesized and tested from a potential space of ∼800 000 compositions with 14 out of these 36 new compounds having a lower thermal hysteresis than any of the 22 compounds in the initial data set.

Predicting a material's properties with informatics techniques has also become a considerable research focus. Besides modeling materials’ physical properties, such as formation energies and melting points, machine learning can also be employed to predict functional properties, such as ionic conductivities for battery materials or critical temperatures for superconductors.^([39](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit39),[100](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit100)–[102](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit102)) In the example of predicting superconducting critical temperatures (*T*[c]), >30 candidate materials were identified.^([102](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit102)) The learning process happened in two stages: a classifier first categorized a material into either the high-*T*[c] class (*T*[c]\>10K) or the low-*T*[c] class (*T*[c]<10K); then a regressor predicted the values of *T*[c] for compounds that were categorized to the high-*T*[c] class. However, explicitly predicting the functionalities is not a straightforward action in problems where many internal or external factors greatly influence the target functional properties. For example, in the search for new intrinsically hard and superhard materials, explicitly predicting the hardness is hindered by the limited number of reports. Moreover, hardness is a load-dependent property, and the load is not always reported. Hardness is also related to microstructure, which is also often unknown. As an alternative, Mansouri Tehrani *et al.* employed bulk and shear modulus as proxies for hardness, which are two intrinsic properties easily extracted from high-throughput computational databases.^([103](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit103)) After building a model using SVM based on a combination of compositional and structural features, the elastic moduli of more than one hundred thousand compounds were readily predicted for the screening for high bulk and shear compounds, which indicates the high hardness. The selected top candidates, ReWC[0.8] and Mo[0.9]W[1.1]BC, were revealed to be extremely hard, reaching the superhard threshold at low indentation load after the experimental examination of these systems. Similarly, a material's Debye temperature can act as a proxy for photoluminescence quantum yield of inorganic phosphors.^([104](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit104)) Screening for compounds of high predicted Debye temperature and adequate bandgap has lead to the discovery of a highly efficient blue-emitting phosphor.

## 13.4 Challenges and Opportunities

Machine learning has become pervasive throughout chemistry and a majority of its subfields, including inorganic materials. It impacts the way that we do experiments, analyze data, and it is even altering the way that we teach. There are undoubtedly plentiful opportunities to use data-driven methods to advance materials research and development (R&D) and manufacturing; however, numerous challenges also remain. Materials discovery is based on understanding and interpreting multivariate correlations in terms of the fundamental physics, chemistry, and engineering. In the following, some general difficulties limiting the application of machine learning in materials chemistry are identified, while some promising strategies to address each problem are discussed.

### 13.4.1 Learning from Small Data Sets

Perhaps, the most frequently asked question by new researchers that are eager to use data science is whether their problem lends itself to such methods. No matter the specific problem, a prerequisite for machine learning is the existence of reliable data or the ability to generate at least a subset of the critical information in a uniform and controlled manner. In materials chemistry, however, we are often limited to hundreds or thousands, sometimes even fewer, high-quality data points. One of the biggest hindrances is a combination of a relatively small number of well-characterized and reliable materials, with the absence of effective aggregation of this high-quality data. There are several existing data infrastructures that are quite general, and they usually provide basic knowledge about compounds, *e.g.*, structure or fundamental physical and chemical properties, but these databases can be expensive to access. Some of these databases also do not allow bulk data downloads. For example, the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD) is an authoritative collection of crystallographic data containing tens of thousands of compounds, but it is not straightforward to download the data in a bulk manner.

Expanding data sets through data mining techniques is one route to address small data sets, but for some scientific problems, there may simply not be more data available. A promising solution in these cases is through the modification of the learning process. Adaptive design (also mentioned in Section 13.3.3) is one method that has shown fantastic capability, where knowledge is quickly accumulated iteratively.^([105](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit105)) Meta-learning is also useful for handling limited data sets because knowledge in this approach is gained within and across problems.^([106](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit106)) New developments in computer science such as Neural Turing machines (NTM),^([107](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit107)) transfer learning,^([108](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit108)) and imitation learning^([109](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit109)) are enabling the realization of this process. For example, a Bayesian program learning (BPL) framework has recently been demonstrated to outperform recent deep learning approaches and even achieve human-level accuracy on one-shot learning tasks with limited data.^([110](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit110)) The outstanding performance of these models provides exciting potential if applied to materials chemistry where data are usually scarce, exorbitantly expensive and slow to obtain.

### 13.4.2 Generating Efficient Data Representation

Generally, a more suitable representation of the input data leads to a better model, whereby the relationship between the input and output data can be more accurately learned. Essential research efforts are being directed toward the development of efficient features for encoding complex materials data. However, either compositional features or structural features emphasize the importance of leveraging domain knowledge, resulting in a significant impediment to the use of machine learning in problems where the physics driving behavior is yet to be understood. One solution would be to learn the properties of materials from their atomic identities. Jha *et al.* designed a deep neural network model using only the elemental compositions as features to learn the chemical interactions and similarities between different elements automatically.^([111](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit111)) This methodology purely relies on representation learning without using any domain knowledge about materials.

### 13.4.3 Enhancing Model Interpretability

The knowledge extracted by machine-learning algorithms is usually difficult to interpret even though the model has predictive power. Several reasons could cause for this shortcoming. First, the knowledge is not presented in a way that scientists are familiar with; for example, when employing the SVM model in a classification task, the optimal hyperplanes that are created to separate each class are usually in multidimensional space and too complex to visualize, which prevents additional analysis. The second reason is that scientists sometimes are uncertain of the information produced by the algorithm and cannot link the input to the output in any rational, direct way, which makes machine learning truly a ‘black box’. The question is how to turn a ‘black box’ into a ‘white box’. To date, research on enhancing machine learning interpretability mainly focuses on developing methods that run alongside the existing black box models to generate statistical explanations in a human-understandable manner.^([112](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit112)) These methods range from ranking input features importance to constructing entirely new models that closely approximate the original black box model while using a much simpler, easier-to-understand algorithm such as linear regression. A better understanding of the machine-learning model could potentially accelerate the discovery of scientific laws and principles.^([113](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit113))

### 13.4.4 Increasing Model Accessibility

Most currently available data informatics programs require users’ programming skills and knowledge about data science to analyze and manage data. Without this background, researchers may quickly become mired in jargon, arcane parameters, or unfamiliar syntax. As a result, data-driven materials chemistry can only be accessible to those who have appropriate experience in computer programming and data science. It is vital to democratize materials informatics. That way the community can benefit from the widespread access of large-scale materials data analysis. To achieve such a goal, software needs to be developed that is intuitive and easy to use for materials experts, even those who have never been trained in computer science and data science. Such tools have now been emerging for pervasive consumption by the materials community; examples include AFLOW-ML and MEGNet for machine-learning predictions of materials properties,^([36](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit36),[114](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit114)) Pourbaix diagrams generator on the Materials Project,^([115](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit115)) Citrine Informatics's thermoelectric materials recommendation engine,^([116](#BK9781788017893-00311.xhtml#cit116)) and many others. The continued development and deployment of models with friendly graphical user interfaces will provide exceptional computational tools to researchers with a range of skill levels at institutions around the world.

## 13.5 Concluding Remarks

As a branch of data science and one of the most powerful tools of data analysis, machine learning has gained unprecedented attention in all scientific disciplines. The number of reported applications is growing at an extraordinary rate, and materials chemistry is not different. There has been a steady shift from experimental and computational focused research toward data-driven studies with close collaboration between computational predictions and experimental validation. The objects under study, particularly in the field of inorganic materials chemistry, are extensive, including inorganic oxide materials, electrolyte materials, metallic materials, functional materials, and numerous others. The function of machine-learning algorithms in developing these materials ranges from optimizing synthesis conditions to predicting crystal structures and physical properties. The advantage of using advance machine learning strategies lies in their ability to make full use of the extensive data available, even failed data, and to speed up the materials research process. Machine learning methods have exhibited a great ability to solve problems such as regression, classification, and clustering. Recently, these approaches have also shown useful performance in materials design and experimental data analysis. Applications in material chemistry will continue to expand and will likely lead to even more significant developments. The application of one particular model is usually limited to one kind of material and one property; therefore, fabricating different models together could develop a unified framework to target the most promising compounds with the balance between several factors. This may also help research produce novel multifunctional materials. The success of applying data science no matter how promising, however, will rely on improved access to open-source and data sharing among researchers as well as the development of more advanced computer science techniques with a particular ability to deal with smaller data sets. There is no doubt that machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry, and we are in a new era for inorganic materials discovery.
