CHAPTER 14

Machine Learning Applications in Chemical Engineering

Y. YAN, T. N. BORHANI AND P. T. CLOUGH[\*](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#affa)

Energy and Power Theme, Cranfield University, Cranfield, Bedfordshire, MK43 0AL, UK

\*Email: [p.t.clough@cranfield.ac.uk](mailto:p.t.clough@cranfield.ac.uk)

## 14.1 Introduction

Chemical engineering can be broadly defined as the process of converting a raw material/energy into a useful product; no matter how complex the process, everything is designed, optimised, and controlled to ensure economic, safe, and environmentally considerate production. Chemical engineers are commonly associated with the petrochemicals industry, where pipes, tanks, reactors, and pumps are all readily visible, but this is just one application of chemical engineering and there is a great diversity of roles that chemical engineers play. Through the so-called fourth industrial revolution (Industry 4.0 – Internet of Things with integrated autonomous data processing), chemical engineers are being called upon to utilise the vast quantities of data generated by their processes to make the process plant ‘smarter’ in order to gain a financial advantage; the application of artificial intelligence (AI) is one way of achieving such a task.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit1))

AI is being exploited in a greater number of ways across all industries to find useful insights and understanding of data in order to drive up efficiency and process performance and is, therefore, understandably finding applications in chemical engineering. Recently, companies including BP,^([2](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit2)) ExxonMobil,^([3](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit3)) HSE,^([4](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit4)) and GE^([5](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit5)) have all invested significant sums into AI for chemical engineering applications in order to improve process safety and reliability, identify new connections and work flows, accelerate project lifecycles, and enable rapid use of the latest process data. Within all this investment, we should remember that AI is still only ‘narrow AI’, meaning it is very good at doing one particular task; it is very time-consuming to make representative models that build connections between unseen data or understand the overall plant/process integrations and dependencies. Furthermore, AI systems that have been publicised as being applied to chemical engineering facilities and processes quite often take on the role of data analytics and data insight, finding patterns in data that would take significantly longer for a human to find, rather than operating or optimising the plant's operation.^([6](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit6)) This is not to say that advanced data analytics is less important; in fact, most companies would relish the opportunity to identify that a pump or compressor is close to failure so that it can be replaced, rather than waiting for it to fail, shutting down the plant and then performing a cold start. However, AI in chemical engineering is rarely applied online to give real-time data analytics and process performance insights, which is where the future of AI in chemical engineering could, and should, be heading.

While the current influx of faster, more powerful computing has brought a surge of AI-themed excitement to all industrial sectors, including chemical engineering, AI is actually not that new. In the early days of machine learning (ML) computing (1980s), expert systems (ESs) and later genetic algorithms (GAs) were utilised in the chemical industry to aid with catalyst development and predicting thermophysical fluid properties.^([7](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit7),[8](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit8)) Over time, artificial neural networks (ANNs) have replaced other forms of AI because of their ability to adapt well to alternative problems, their ability to solve non-linear problems, and the wide availability of adequate training data. Machine learning is an all-encompassing term, so throughout we shall endeavour to keep the reader informed of the varieties and their differences, limitations, and benefits as we broach them.

In this chapter, we explore ML algorithms that have been applied to three areas in chemical engineering: modelling and simulation, process control, and estimation and prediction.

## 14.2 Modelling and Simulation

ML and AI have wide applications in modelling and simulation of chemical and process engineering.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit1),[9](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit9)) Here, we consider important unit operations involved in chemical and process engineering; the application of ML and AI for each of them is reviewed and discussed using selected published studies. It should be noted that in addition to modelling and simulation studies, AI has substantial application in optimisation problems related to chemical and process engineering that can be found in relevant books.^([10](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit10)) The general format of any AI model is illustrated in [Figure 14.1](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#fig1).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00340-f1.jpg)

Figure 14.1 General format of AI models.

### 14.2.1 Application of AI for Modelling and Simulation of Separation Units

#### 14.2.1.1 Distillation Columns

Modelling and simulation of distillation columns require accurate process models that contain governing equations and many relations to predict different parameters and physical properties. A number of distillation process models are available in the published literature, but the complexity of distillation processes has led to a number of assumptions that may limit the universality of the models. Most of the mechanistic models of distillation systems have assumed equilibrium cases for the stages. Such models deviate from reality, and so these will not give a true representation. To overcome this, the non-equilibrium or rate-based approach has been introduced. This involves chemical reactions and mass transfer equations for each phase, which adds to the complexity of the problem. Furthermore, such mechanistic models are computationally demanding, making them unsuitable for real-time optimisation. To overcome these problems, AI can be utilized to solve complex simulations for different distillation columns or other similar unit operations such as absorption and desorption columns.

Chetouani^([11](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit11)) used a multi-layer perceptron – artificial neural network (MLP-ANN) method to develop a model to simulate the distillation column in steady-state and non-steady-state conditions. Khayet and Cojocaru^([12](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit12)) modelled an air gap membrane distillation process using an ANN. The input variables to the ANN model were air gap thickness, the condensation temperature, the feed inlet temperature, and the feed flow rate of salt aqueous solutions, while the response or output was the performance index, which takes into consideration both the permeate flux and the salt rejection factor. The results obtained from the developed model showed good agreement with experimental data. Ochoa-Estopier *et al.*^([13](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit13)) represented the crude oil distillation column and its integrated heat exchanger network using an ANN. Using the ANN model, the authors determined the operating conditions that enhanced the overall process economics. Osuolale and Zhang^([14](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit14)) used ANN to model and optimise the exergy efficiency in distillation columns. They mentioned that mechanistic modelling of distillation columns for real-time optimisation is not applicable. For such cases the ANN model can be used, as the required computational time for the ANN is very short, which is helpful in real-time optimisation.

#### 14.2.1.2 Absorber and Desorber

Absorption and desorption are very important unit operations that play a vital role in different industries. One of the most well-known examples of these processes is CO[2] removal from different gas streams, such as flue gases, natural gas, and biogas using different types of solvents.^([15](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit15)) Similar to distillation columns, mechanistic modelling of absorption and desorption columns requires complex equation solving with many details.^([16](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit16),[17](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit17)) Black-box modelling using AI can be beneficial for such a complex system and researchers can predict the required outputs from black-box models with high accuracy more rapidly than using mechanistic modelling.

Some published studies used different AI tools to model absorption and desorption columns and in this section, we review some recent ones. Zhou *et al.*^([18](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit18)) developed four adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) models to describe the CO[2] capture process (absorption and desorption) using amines. They considered four different scenarios by changing different parameters as input and output. The ANFIS modelling procedure is illustrated in [Figure 14.2](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#fig2).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00340-f2.jpg)

Figure 14.2 ANFIS modelling procedure developed by Zhou *et al.*^([18](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit18)) Reproduced from ref. [18](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit18) with permission from Elsevier, Copyright 2013.

The authors reported that the problems presented in scenarios #1 and #2 could not be completely resolved unless changes were made to the definition of the input parameter sets. One important observation is that the parameter of steam flow rate through reboiler (FT-103C) is a critical component of the input parameter set. Hafizi *et al.*^([19](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit19)) compared adaptive neuro-fuzzy and ANN to model the flow rate of rich amine in CO[2] capture absorption columns and reported that the adaptive neuro fuzzy inference systems were more successful in predicting this parameter than the ANN model. Mohammadzadeh *et al.*^([20](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit20)) utilized an ANN to predict sweet gas concentrations in absorption columns that used diethanolamine (DEA) as the solvent. Experimental pilot plant data were used for validation of the model that includes DEA weight per cent in lean amine, concentrations of H[2]S, CO[2] and H[2]O, temperature, pressure and flow rate of input and output gases and lean amine. The statistical parameters and error analysis of the study were satisfactory. Cozma *et al.*^([21](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit21)) used airlift reactors to absorb CO[2] physically from biogas using water as the solvent. The authors used two algorithms, a combination of Clonal Selection (CS) and ANN and the new algorithm nCS-MBK; the second algorithm resulted in better model agreement with experimental data. Ahmad *et al.*^([22](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit22)) used ANN to perform the dynamic modelling of absorption columns. The inputs to the network were the absorption or stripping stages and absorption or stripping factors, and the output was the absorption or stripping stage efficiency. Different error analysis and statistical parameters showed the strength of their model.

#### 14.2.1.3 Adsorption

Adsorption is another separation process that has attracted a lot of attention recently, and many studies have conducted research to speed up the commercialisation of this process. The main advantage of adsorption in comparison to absorption is the lower energy consumption. It is recognised that a considerable amount of energy is consumed during the desorption of solute from solvent.^([23](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit23))

AI has considerable applications in this field. Salehi *et al.*^([24](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit24)) applied Least Squares Support Vector Machines to predict the equilibrium adsorption of copper ions from the water on modified CS/PVA membrane-sorbents. The authors used 72 experimental data points and reported good statistical parameters. Fawzy *et al.*^([25](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit25)) presented an ANFIS model to describe the adsorption of divalent nickel and divalent cadmium ions from aqueous solutions using a biosorbent, which is known as Typha domingensis. By using the ANFIS model the authors recognised the sequence of experimental parameters affecting metal ion removal efficiency. Ghaedi and Vafaei^([26](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit26)) reviewed the application of different AI methods for adsorption of dyes from aqueous solutions. Mazaheri *et al.*^([27](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit27)) used different methods, including AI, to model the adsorption of methylene blue (MB) and divalent cadmium ion from binary aqueous solution by natural walnut carbon. Sensitivity analysis revealed that the adsorbent mass and pH were the critical factors for the removal. Alalm and Nasr^([28](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit28)) adsorbed chlorothalonil, which is a hazardous material, from aqueous solutions using activated carbon and then predicted the adsorption capacity using the ANN model. Using a sensitivity analysis with the developed ANN model, they found that pH was the most significant factor on adsorption capacity. Mahmoud *et al.*^([29](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit29)) focused on the removal of phosphate ions from aqueous solutions using encapsulated nanoscale zero-valent iron. The authors used an ANN with a structure of 5.7.1 (5 input nodes, 7 hidden layer nodes, and 1 output node) to model this adsorption process and reported a coefficient of determination of 97.6%. Sensitivity analysis of the model demonstrated that pH was the most influential input.

### 14.2.2 Application of AI for Modelling and Simulation of Reactors

Reactors and their design can be considered as the most specialised unit operation that chemical engineers deal with. Reactors have wide applications, ranging from polymerisation to energy conversion processes. Modelling of reactors is a complex and time-consuming procedure, so researchers often apply black-box modelling using AI methods to model the reactor.

Azarpour *et al.*^([30](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit30)) developed a hybrid model incorporating a first principle model and an ANN to model the industrial fixed-bed catalytic reactors experiencing catalyst deactivation. The elements of the hybrid model are presented in [Figure 14.3](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#fig3).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00340-f3.jpg)

Figure 14.3 The hybrid model developed for industrial fixed-bed catalytic reactors (FBCRs) experiencing catalyst deactivation.^([30](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit30)) Reproduced from ref. [30](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit30) with permission from Elsevier, Copyright 2017.

Joshi and Singhal^([31](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit31)) coupled GA and ANN to optimise the operational condition of zeaxnathin production. The authors evaluated the effects of varying air flow rate and inoculum size for different incubation times. Volumetric power input and energy input to the bubble column were then correlated using the GA-ANN optimised conditions. Zhu *et al.*^([32](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit32)) introduced a deep learning approach to automatically identify tube regions in a pyrolysis reactor from the raw images. Using this approach, the exact temperature and shape on the pyrolysis tubes can be monitored.

### 14.2.3 Application of AI for Modelling and Simulation of Whole Plants

Mechanistic modelling of a whole chemical plant is a far more complex and challenging task than modelling of a single unit operation. Nevertheless, some studies report using AI to model and analyse whole chemical plants.

A full-scale industrial wastewater treatment process has been modelled using a hybrid ANN model^([33](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit33)) which combines mechanistic and ANN modelling. The authors reported satisfactory results obtained from this hybrid model. Tunckaya and Koklukaya^([34](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit34)) investigated the impact of gas emissions of a real 180 MW coal-fired thermal power plant by means of ANN, autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) and multiple linear regression (MLR) approaches within eight proposed process parameters that affect the stack gas emissions. The ANN model demonstrated better performance than ARIMA and MLR according to statistical parameters and error analysis. Nourani *et al.*^([35](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit35)) utilized different AI methods such as FFNN, ANFIS, SVM, as well as MLR to predict the performance of the Nicosia wastewater treatment plant by means of effluent biological oxygen demand, chemical oxygen demand and total nitrogen. The authors reported that the ANN model was the most successful model.

### 14.2.4 Application of AI for Modelling and Simulation of Energy Management

Another important area in which AI has been applied recently is energy management and energy systems. Many research and review papers have been published in this field, and therefore, only a limited number of them are reviewed here.

Zahraee *et al.*^([36](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit36)) summarised prior research concerning the use of optimisation in artificially intelligent algorithms for designing and planning and also for controlling problems in the field of hybrid energy systems. The authors reviewed more than one hundred relevant papers. Jha *et al.*^([37](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit37)) illustrated the importance of AI in achieving goals related to renewable energy (RE), such as the development of novel technology for optimum production from available natural resources, environmental awareness, and better management and distribution systems. They reviewed the application of AI in different types of RE such as solar, wind, geothermal, hydro, ocean, bioenergy and hydrogen. Sharifzadeh *et al.*^([38](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit38)) quantified uncertainties in the electricity grid and examined the predictability of their behaviour. The predictive methods considered in their study were ANN, support vector regression (SVR) and Gaussian process regression. All models were able to predict wind and solar power, but only the ANN model was effective for the electricity demand. Considering the dynamics of the electricity grid, it was realized that the prediction process for renewable wind and solar power generation, and electricity demand was fast and accurate enough to effectively replace the alternative electricity storage and standby capacity.

## 14.3 Control and Operation

If chemical engineering is the science of converting one thing into another, at scale, then control and operation are integral to the economic success of any process. A common overall aim of process control in all chemical engineering sectors is to achieve stable, steady-state operation, where the facility is operating at or close to its designed point of highest efficiency. Often plants will spread across multiple reactors and have seemingly endless piping, with instrumentation dotted at strategic locations in order to gain insight as to how the reactors are performing and to characterise the input and output streams. The greater the complexity and integration of the plant, the more difficult the process control and operation becomes, which is where new forms of process control are becoming available, notably through machine learning.

### 14.3.1 The Baseline of Process Control

Proportional, integral, and derivative (PID) controllers are taught to most undergraduate engineering students and are widely recognised as being the standard for process control. PID controllers utilise the difference between a set point variable and the actual process variable value to generate an error, which is utilised to calculate the control signal. Variations of these PID loops can be used in series, where the output from one controller provides the set point for another variable controller, thus taking away some of the lag time between actions and simplifying the complexity of overall process control to individual variable control; this is called cascade control.

If we consider complex processes, with multiple variables (temperature, pressure, flow rate, fluid level, and quality) that each need controlling, but are inherently interlinked through the laws of thermodynamics, then PID controllers no longer become the best solution to use. In these simulations, multivariable control techniques can be utilised, which can decouple the competing influences of interlinked variable controls and thus minimise the effort/cost/energy required to achieve an optimised steady state operation. These multivariable control systems can work well if the interaction between variables is well understood (or non-existent), but will fail if there are slight deviations in process operation. For example, if a steam methane reforming reactor was designed to operate at a steam to carbon ratio of 3, but later someone decides it should be 3.5 then the multivariable controller decoupling would not account for this deviation and would be unable to control the reactor accurately.

A potentially better alternative that can overcome process complexity, variable interconnectivity and interdependence, process-measurement lag time, random disturbances, and minimise the effort/cost/energy of reaching a stable set point, is machine learning control or at least it could have been if Model Predictive Control did not come along.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit1))

Model predictive control (MPC) is a very commonly implemented technique of controlling dynamic systems that can be simulated by a linear model while satisfying a set of constraints. MPC uses a model of the process to control dependant variables in the current time step, while calculating and optimising the future values in a moving prediction horizon that takes into account the past values. This control technique is so widely used because processes are often too complex for PID loops alone and because back in the 1980s it was easier and cheaper to implement an MPC algorithm than a control algorithm using machine learning. However, MPC falls down when processes are dependent upon hundreds of variables or the processes are non-linear, which they regularly are, although some processes can be considered linear over a small range of operating conditions. There is the option of combining multiple MPC's together, which can provide a stable control system if the non-linear system can be broken down into multiple independently linear systems;^([39](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit39),[40](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit40)) this approach has been demonstrated for application in refineries,^([41](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit41)) and copolymerisation reactors.^([42](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit42))

### 14.3.2 Machine Learning Used to Control Chemical Processes

Neural networks were demonstrated a few decades ago to be suitable for controlling complex chemical processes.^([43](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit43)) For example, Savkovic-Stavanovic showed that ANN's could be used to control an azeotrope distillation process and demonstrated the ability to improve process control by time-shifting the model's data inputs, which acts to smooth out the controller.^([44](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit44)) Ramchandram and Rhinehart also utilised an ANN to control a distillation process and found the ANN provided superior control compared with a feedforward PI controller, as it was able to account for the “phenomenological process characteristics”, which a standard PI controller simply has no understanding of.^([45](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit45)) These ANN are commonly applied in parallel with the process where they build up experience and knowledge as they watch and predict the process, see [Figure 14.4](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#fig4).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00340-f4.jpg)

Figure 14.4 *ANN training in parallel with a process using the error of its predictions to increase its confidence in process control*.^([46](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit46)) Reproduced from ref. [46](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit46) with permission from Elsevier, Copyright 1992.

ANNs have also been utilised to estimate the liquid levels and compositions of distillation columns, thereby acting as a soft sensor.^([47](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit47)) Soft sensors are often based on ANNs and have been utilised by several researchers to predict unmeasured variables without specific/expensive hardware in order to achieve improved process control,^([48](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit48)) for example in coal-fired power plants,^([49](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit49)) polymerisation processes,^([50](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit50)) ethanol concentration determination in wine production,^([51](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit51)) chemical plants,^([52](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit52)) and some bioprocesses.^([53](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit53),[54](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit54)) Updating soft sensors online, while a process/reactor is fully operational, is key to the long-term impact of these devices. Work by Lu and Chiang^([55](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit55)) has highlighted a way in which this can be achieved; they utilised two key performance indicators and applied Hotelling's T² multivariate statistic to determine if the T² value exceeds some alarm limit where action needed to be taken. The key novelty of this work is that the soft sensors can work at the very edge of where training data exists and system properties are known, and that the soft sensors ‘calibration’ is updated while online and in operation.^([55](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit55)) A key limitation of soft sensors is that they may only be applicable to an individual particular system or reactor set up and, therefore, are not considered to be compatible with another similar process. Processes are often dependent upon unknown/unmeasured variables or information that cannot be easily programmed into a computer (for example, the shape of a reactor, or the precise locations of sensors and their accuracy) thus making soft sensor coding less portable; however, they are relatively quick and easy to train up if a new system was to implement one.

ANN models can work well; however, it should be noted that they are based on training data and are,therefore, only as good as the training data they are fed with; often termed “garbage in, garbage out”. If an ANN has not seen a process state before or if a process variable goes beyond a normal range, then the ANN will apply its mathematics and spit out an answer; whether that answer makes any sense is a different matter. As you can imagine, in a chemical manufacturing facility, it is possible that a thermocouple could randomly dropout, causing an ANN control model to make a corrective action, which could unwittingly cause damage to equipment, the environment, or people. It is analogous to training a model to understand the difference between a cat and a dog by showing it thousands of cat and dog images, but then adding in a photo of a giraffe. The model would have no idea what this patchy long-necked creature is, but will diligently assess the image and give you a prediction of cat or dog, without understanding the image, the context, or knowing that this image lies outside its remit of knowledge. And for any chemical facility this could be very dangerous; understanding the context of a process is vital and it is this kind of knowledge that plant operators build up over many years of experience.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit1)) A solution could be to give the model decades of data, decades of experience of different scenarios where random alarm trips, sensor failures, blockages *etc.* have occurred, but what if this data doesn't exist, or if it's a new process, a first-of-a-kind reactor, what should be done then? Aside from using data from another similar reactor/process, two options are available: the first is unsupervised learning, where the model itself looks for patterns in the data without any feedback on how it is doing; the second is reinforcement learning where the model is punished or rewarded such that the model aims to maximise its reward.

Training ANNs in an unsupervised manner means that a training database is not provided; instead, the model can vary parameters itself and build its own training database, this training database can be updated as the system is in operation. A key benefit of this type of training is that we do not introduce our own human biases into the model. As humans, we are fantastic at making algorithms to solve problems. For example, let us consider a simple reactor with air flow through the centre and an external on/off heating control system, where we want to control the reactor's interior temperature at a specific set point value. The objective function of the control programme minimises the amount of ‘heating on’ time in order to save money. A simple control algorithm for this reactor might read:

1.  If the reactor is too cold, then turn the heating on and wait for it to heat up
2.  If the reactor is too hot, then turn the heating off and wait for it to cool down

We could, of course, train an ANN model to control this reactor, but by defining our reactor's objective function too imprecisely or by not considering all possible scenarios, then the ANN could decide that the best way to minimise the amount of ‘heating on’ time is to not turn the heating on at all.^([56](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit56)) Yes, this would mean that the reactor never heated up and the ANN failed to adhere to one of the objectives but as far as the model is concerned it was successful in saving ‘heating on’ time and the reactor temperature was less important.

Evidently, applying ill-defined objective functions to whole chemical plants could be dangerous, which is why researchers are now exploring ways of not defining the objective function for machine learning chemical reactor control systems and instead allowing the models to build up their own context of the overall process.^([57](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit57)–[59](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit59)) This has been demonstrated to achieve better and safer control than can be achieved by giving the models ‘human knowledge’, as it is difficult to distil every piece of human knowledge into a set of objectives.^([60](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit60)) Deep reinforcement learning has also been applied to a multitude of other simple control situations with high degrees of success but is limited by the amount of time it takes to train the programme.^([61](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit61)) However, by allowing the programme to self-learn and by reinforcing correct control behaviour, the control algorithm generated is transportable to other control problems. Genetic programming has also been successfully applied in a flow control scenario, whereby the objective function was to minimise the recirculation area of a backwards-facing step by varying the incoming jet of water (80% reduction achieved).^([62](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit62)) A multi-agent control system with self-learning has been applied to a continuous cement production line by breaking down the key points of process control (quality control, decision maker, data analyst, knowledge holder).^([57](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit57)) This way, the overall control system is more resilient to random deviations in a process, but also able to adapt to new control rules that are formed by the machine learning control system.

### 14.3.3 Traditional Controllers with Integrated Machine Learning

Machine learning controllers are often implemented to provide an input signal to a traditional PID or MPC controller. This input signal could be the predicted value or a predicted error estimate; the additional information is utilised to provide control that is closer to a desired setpoint, see [Figure 14.5](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#fig5) for an example of the improvement that can be achieved with machine learning enhanced reactor control.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00340-f5.jpg)

Figure 14.5 Temperature response of a continuously stirred tank reactor utilising different forms of reactor control. The black line indicates the machine learning enhanced controller.^([63](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit63)) Reproduced from ref. [63](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit63) with permission from Elsevier, Copyright 2018.

Deepa and Baranilingesan have utilised an MPC with an ANN in the background to benefit from the ANN's ability to learn and store valuable information about a simulated continuously stirred tank reactor. Their research utilised a particle swarm optimisation and gravitation search algorithm to define the initial weights and then tune the ANN to control the process more effectively.^([63](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit63))

With PID controllers still being commonplace, some researchers have utilised machine learning to optimise the tuning process to achieve improved control, notably Chen and Huang,^([64](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit64)) whose research took a pragmatic approach for using linearised ANNs to control non-linear processes; however, they noted that their model needed to be more flexible to different operating ranges, and noise in the data significantly influenced control. A similar attempt at using ML-enhanced controllers was described by Chowdhury *et al.* who utilised a fuzzy PID controller (a set of rules with relative importance) and found the fuzzy controller to be able to track a set point value more accurately and reduce the magnitude of deviations from the set point.^([65](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit65))

The control of a chemical reactor or chemical process is highly dependent on understanding the process in its entirety, which is not always possible due to the size of the reactor and the complexity of the chemistry involved. This is where ML can be utilised to estimate or predict operating parameters.

## 14.4 Estimation and Prediction

The application of AI, particularly ML, in chemical engineering is not limited to modelling and control, but it can also be implemented as an estimator for difficult-to-measure parameters in chemical process, systems for system optimisation, or predictors to predict the properties of materials or products. In this section, we give a detailed overview of AI and ML algorithms implemented as estimators in chemical process systems, along with their practical applications, advantages, and limitations. It aims to provide a guide to researchers in selecting and developing AI-based estimators or predictors in chemical engineering.

### 14.4.1 Available AI Algorithms for Estimators in Chemical Engineering

It is well recognised that some important process parameters or properties of products in chemical process systems are difficult or impossible to measure in real-time due to the limitations of physical sensors or process technology. The application of AI or ML algorithms as estimators and predictors in chemical process systems, with the benefits of robustness, easy formulation, simple design, and flexible adaptation capabilities, can solve these issues. Several algorithms such as ANNs, support vector regression, fuzzy logic (FL), GAs, and ESs are used to design the estimators to estimate the difficult-to-measure parameters in chemical process systems.

Recently, a vast amount of research has been conducted by applying AI as estimators in chemical process systems (*e.g.* product compositions, combustion kinetics, temperature, pressure, and heat transfer of chemical reactor). However, it can be difficult to choose a suitable algorithm for estimators due to the variety and unique features of these algorithms and process complexity. Therefore, an exhaustive survey of each algorithm for estimation and prediction and its applications in chemical process systems is provided in this section, which can guide researchers designing and developing their own estimator in particular chemical process systems (see [Table 14.1](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#tab1)).

ANNs are the most common algorithm applied as an estimator in chemical engineering. Inspired by biological neurons, these can learn complex non-linear and multivariate relationships. The ANN can act as a “black box” that can predict the desired output from a set of input data. In general, an ANN consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer, with neurons in each layer. It can determine relationships between the input and output from historical data by calculating the network weights and bias, creating a trained ANN that can predict the output from given input data. For estimation and prediction in chemical process systems, several types of ANN have been reported, such as feed forward neural networks, recurrent neural networks and radial basis function neural networks. A detailed comparison and description of different types of ANNs can be accessed in.^([66](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit66),[67](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit67)) The size and quality of training data and the ANN architecture determine the performance and accuracy of the models. There is no unique method to obtain the optimum number of hidden layers and neurons in each hidden layer; it is common to use trial and error for this. The degree of generalisation that the model can achieve may also be an issue. For instance, if a trained ANN can perfectly fit the data in the training dataset, but its performance on unseen data is poor, then this typically indicates overfitting. Many methods have been reported to improve generalisation and avoid overfitting such as bootstrap aggregated neural networks,^([68](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit68)–[70](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit70)) regularisation^([71](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit71),[72](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit72)) and cross validation based early stopping.^([73](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit73)–[75](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit75))

SVR, which is an ML adaptation based on Support Vector Machines, SVM,^([76](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit76)) is also widely used as an estimator in chemical process systems. The SVR “maps the input data into higher dimensional feature space *via* a nonlinear mapping and after a linear regression problem is obtained and solved in this feature space”.^([76](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit76)–[78](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit78)) The SVR is generated by the retained kernels, and the data points related to the retained kernels are referred to as the support vectors (SV). The smaller fraction of support vectors leads to a more general solution, which requires less computation to solve for a new and unknown object.^([77](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit77)) In comparison with ANNs, SVR has the following advantages: good generalisation ability of the regression function, robustness of the solution, sparseness of the regression and automatic control of the solution complexity, and extracting the knowledge of the data points.^([76](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit76),[79](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit79)) However, the SVR algorithm is limited by both speed and memory constraints of the available hardware when working with massive datasets.^([79](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit79))

Apart from ANN and SVR, fuzzy logic, GAs, and ESs have been developed as predictors or estimators for different chemical process systems. Fuzzy logic is a type of multi-valued logic that distinguishes more than just TRUE and FALSE values; it can map from a given set of input data to an output based on a set of fuzzy rules.^([67](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit67),[80](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit80),[81](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit81)) It includes four components: fuzzification, the fuzzy rule base, a fuzzy output engine, and defuzzification. Fuzzification converts the input and output into linguistic subsets. The fuzzy rule base includes the construction of fuzzy IF-THEN rules based on expert knowledge and/or available data. The fuzzy output engine considers rules in the fuzzy rule base and learns relationships between a set of inputs and outputs. Finally, defuzzification transfers the fuzzy outputs from the output engine to a numeric value.^([80](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit80),[81](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit81)) Fuzzy logic can relate input to output in a fashion, which is more in-line with human thought than ANNs.^([81](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit81))

Expert systems are an applied AI approach that use computers to emulate the decision-making ability of human experts. Knowledge-based ESs consist of two subsystems, the knowledge base, which is a collection of facts and rules, and the inference engine, which can predict results based on the contents of the knowledge base.^([7](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit7),[82](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit82)) Various applications of ES-based estimators to predict different parameters in chemical process systems can be found in ref. [7](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit7) and [82](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit82)–[85](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit85). Although there are many reports of the use of ES-based estimators in chemical engineering, a reliable ES is time-consuming and expensive to build, and this has limited its adoption.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit1))

The Genetic Algorithm was first introduced by Holland in the 1970s.^([86](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit86)) This numerical optimisation algorithm, which is inspired by genetic and evolutionary mechanisms in nature^([87](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit87),[88](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit88)) involves initial population generation, fitness evaluation and the genetic operations of selection, crossover and mutation.^([87](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit87)) Detailed discussion of GAs can be found in ref. [86](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit86)–[88](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit88). Reports^([87](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit87),[89](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit89)–[97](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit97)) suggest that the GA is an effective tool to estimate parameters in chemical engineering and assist in system optimisation.

As AI-based algorithms are efficient for estimation and prediction in chemical process systems, researchers have combined algorithms together to enhance their model capabilities and solve more complex problems. For instance, ANN and SVM are commonly integrated with intelligent optimisation algorithms such as the GA, simulated annealing and particle swarm optimisation to improve macroscopic performance prediction.^([98](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit98)) In addition, other combinations of algorithms such as ANN/SVR with FL, ANN/SVR with ES, or FL with ES can also overcome the drawbacks of using a single algorithm for estimation and prediction in chemical process systems.

### 14.4.2 Selection and Applications of AI-based Estimators

The selection of a suitable algorithm is a key step in developing an AI-based estimation and prediction system in chemical engineering, because it has a significant impact on the prediction accuracy and generalisation ability. As discussed earlier, each algorithm has its own advantages, and therefore, no one algorithm can be suitable for all problems. [Table 14.2](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#tab2) briefly compares the advantages and limitations of the different AI algorithms for estimation and prediction in chemical engineering.

 

Table 14.2 Comparisons of AI algorithms for estimation and prediction in chemical engineering.

 
| Algorithm || Advantages || Limitations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ANN || 

*   Suitable for non-linear systems
*   Ability to learn from historical data
*   Do not require a domain expert for learning the relationships between input and output
*   Trained ANN models are fast

 || 

*   The performance of ANN models is largely determined by the size and quality of the training dataset.
*   Trial and error may be required to decide the optimal structure of the ANN.

 |
| SVR || 

*   Excellent generalisation capacity with high prediction accuracy
*   Less sensitive to the noise of inputs

 || 

*   High computational demand with large training sets.

 |
| FL || 

*   Easy to design and implement
*   Can deal with imprecise and incomplete data
*   Provide knowledge of the relationship between input and output

 || 

*   Affected by the rules and membership functions
*   Lower prediction accuracy

 |
| GA || 

*   Provide several feasible solutions from which the best can be chosen
*   Do not require knowledge of the problem
*   Can deal with both discrete and continuous variables

 || 

*   Time-consuming
*   Sensitive to the input parameters
*   Complex and difficult to build the GA model

 |
| ES || 

*   Able to predict results from detailed knowledge of the process
*   Fast and easy to exchange knowledge between expert systems

 || 

*   Costly and complex to establish the knowledge base
*   Expansion of the knowledge base depends on the availability of experts

 |
| Combined algorithms || 

*   May overcome the drawbacks of single algorithms for estimation and prediction
*   Improve prediction accuracy
*   Suitable for complex and unique process

 || 

*   Implementation requires knowledge about different algorithms
*   Complex and time-consuming to build hybrid models

 |

A simple workflow for developing AI-based estimators in chemical engineering is shown in [Figure 14.6](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#fig6); this can provide a basic guideline for researchers in applying AI algorithms in estimation and prediction in chemical engineering.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00340-f6.jpg)

Figure 14.6 Workflow for applying AI algorithms for estimation and prediction in chemical engineering.

[Table 14.1](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#tab1) details some of the applications of different AI algorithms that have been applied for estimation and prediction in chemical engineering.

Different properties related to chemical engineering and chemistry can be predicted using AI. Ghiasi and Mohammadi^([123](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit123)) used the least squares support vector machine to model and predict the equilibrium CO[2] absorption in monoethanolamine (MEA), diethanolamine (DEA), and triethanolamine (TEA) aqueous solutions at various alkanolamine concentrations and different temperatures over a wide range of CO[2] partial pressure. They reported a coefficient of determination of 0.98 and the absolute average relative deviation per cent (%AARD) to be less than 6.5% for all studied systems. Norouzbahari *et al.*^([124](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit124)) predicted CO[2] loading using an ANN for a ternary solution of CO[2], Piperazine and H[2]O. They collected the required experimental data from available literature, reporting high values of coefficient of determination for training, test and all the datasets. Afkhamipour *et al.*^([125](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit125)) predicted the heat capacity of different amine solutions that are utilized frequently for CO[2] absorption processes, using an ANN. They considered the heat capacity of amines as a function of system temperature, concentration of the solvents, CO[2] loading, and the molecular weight of solvent. The authors reported that AARD between ANN model results and experimental data of CP for 47 systems of amine solutions studied was 4.3%. For conventional amines, the AARDs for an ANN model and a thermodynamic model in comparison with experimental data were 0.59% and 0.57%, respectively. Borhani *et al.*^([23](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit23)) used experimental data of partial pressure of CO[2] in MEA solution and also k-value data extracted from Aspen Plus and predicted these properties using the GA in combination with MLR and then utilized this equation in process modelling of a rotating packed bed desorber column.

An important recent application of AI is chemometric studies. Quantitative structure–property/activity relationships, proposed and developed by Hansch, Fujita and co-workers,^([126](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit126),[127](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit127)) express links between molecular structure features (descriptors) of materials and their properties/activities. The modelling (regression) approaches in QSPR/QSAR studies differ from linear techniques like MLR, partial least-regression, and principal component regression^([128](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit128)) and such nonlinear ML techniques ANNs, genetic programming, SVM, and adaptive neuro fuzzy inference systems.^([129](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit129),[130](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit130)) In QSPR studies, especially when using MLR, different types of classical algorithms such as stepwise forward selection, or evolutionary or metaheuristic algorithms such as GA, PSO, SA, and ant colony have been used in descriptor selection to reduce the number of descriptors and keep the most influential ones in the prediction of the property under study.^([131](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit131)) Different type of properties can be estimated using this method.^([132](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit132)) The developed models can be used in other types of modelling; a general flowchart of QSAR/QSPR methods is illustrated in [Figure 14.7](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#fig7).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00340-f7.jpg)

Figure 14.7 A flowchart of the QSPR/QSAR model development.

## 14.5 Future Trends and Outlook

Materials development, process estimation, and fault prediction are three areas that are set to be the easiest win areas for AI in the coming years.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit1)) Deep and Convoluted Neural Networks are the favoured forms of ANN's at present; however, hybrid models where multiple types of AI are utilised together or where AI is combined with first-principles knowledge are being explored in greater detail. It is not impossible to imagine that, despite the current interest in neural networks and AI in general, AI might slip out of investors’ focus again (note the previous two ‘AI winters’^([133](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit133))) or that the currently favoured ANN's are replaced by a new type of AI that promises greater things. For chemical engineering at least, there is a lot of untapped potential to be explored with AI and, no doubt, some interesting developments lie ahead.

One final aspect of AI that is beginning to change is the explicability of the AI model itself. It is no longer acceptable by the general public, stakeholders, or process plant managers that AI is a black-box that spits out an answer with no explanation; this degrades trust in the model and its results. Therefore, AI models in the future will need to be able to explain their decisions and thought-processing steps. AI interpretation methods are available including LBP,^([134](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit134)) SHAP,^([135](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit135)) DeepLIFT,^([136](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit136)) and LIME.^([137](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit137)) This explicability should not be underestimated as an easy accomplishment to achieve, AI models are not set up (or rather the underlying mathematics is not set up) to output thought-processing steps; even the AlphaGo programme which defeated the world champion in the game Go, played moves which were unseen before and seemingly wrong but ended up aiding it to beat its human counterpart.^([138](#BK9781788017893-00340.xhtml#cit138)) For the application of ML in chemical engineering, it is essential that we must produce explainable and interpretable models, such that a controller, modeller, or operator can understand how it has reached its decisions so that they can be validated, checked, and confirmed. All this needs to happen before investors, and companies are willing to fund the widespread implementation of AI in Chemical Engineering applications, but when they do, they can expect to reduce operating and maintenance costs and improve process safety and reliability.
