CHAPTER 16

Demystifying Artificial Neural Networks as Generators of New Chemical Knowledge: Antimalarial Drug Discovery as a Case Study

ALEJANDRO SPECK-PLANCHE(![image](images/p076-1.jpg)0000-0002-9544-9016)[\*](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#affc)^([a](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#affa)) AND VALERIA V. KLEANDROVA(![image](images/p076-1.jpg)0000-0002-1928-853X)^([b](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#affb))

^a Programa Institucional de Fomento a la I+D+i, Universidad Tecnológica Metropolitana, Ignacio Valdivieso 2409, San Joaquín, Santiago, Chile

^b Laboratory of Fundamental and Applied Research of Quality and Technology of Food Production, Moscow State University of Food Production, Volokolamskoe shosse 11, 125080, Moscow, Russian Federation

\*Email: [alejspivanovich@yahoo.es](mailto:alejspivanovich@yahoo.es)

## 16.1 Introduction

With the advent of machine learning (ML) methods and computational models, which are crucial in most modern scientific projects, drug discovery has undergone a process of constant change and evolution.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit1)) Nowadays, the important role of ML methods in areas such as data mining and virtual screening is well-established.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit1)–[3](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit3)) Among them, artificial neural networks (ANNs) have become a focus of attention, particularly due to the emergence of revolutionary subfields such as deep learning.^([4](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit4)) In fact, within early drug discovery, ANNs have found impressive applications in the *de novo* design of molecules with desired properties.^([5](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit5)–[8](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit8))

Nevertheless, the efficiency and success of current ANNs are strongly associated with a very high computational cost, and the advanced degree of programming/codification skills that researchers must have; the latter can take too much time to master. In addition to these limitations, two other handicaps prevent the full exploitation of ANNs in drug discovery. From one side, the computational models based on ANNs continue to be treated as black boxes because they lack interpretability; they are not capable of providing a clear interpretation of the physicochemical properties and/or structural features of the chemicals in the databases, which they intend to design and/or predict. On the other hand, the *in silico* models focused on ANNs consider a specific stage (usually the pharmacological activity domain) of the drug discovery process. Considering the multi-scale nature of drug discovery and the vast chemical space that needs to be filtered (10^(60) small to medium-sized organic compounds),^([9](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit9)) one of the greatest challenges is the development of models based on ANNs that can integrate multiple biological data and design seemingly new molecular entities with potent activity, low toxicity, and adequate pharmacokinetic properties.

In the last seven years, several research groups have focused their efforts on the creation of a series of computational tools known as multi-scale models for quantitative structure-biological effect relationships (ms-QSBER).^([10](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit10)) These models can integrate different sources of data, permitting the simultaneous prediction of multiple biological endpoints against many targets of varying degrees of complexity. In this sense, ms-QSBER models (some of them based on ANNs) have been successfully applied to different fields of research such as cancer research,^([11](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit11)) infectious diseases,^([12](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit12)–[22](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit22)) nanomedicine and nanotoxicology,^([23](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit23)–[27](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit27)) immunology and immunotoxicity,^([28](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit28)–[31](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit31)) and neuroscience.^([32](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit32)–[35](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit35)) Also, multi-scale *de novo* drug design^([36](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit36)) has emerged as an encouraging paradigm, combining the predictive capabilities of the ms-QSBER models, chemical reasoning, and concepts from fragment-based drug discovery to accelerate the rational design of molecules that virtually exhibit high activity, low toxicity, and very good pharmacokinetics.^([37](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit37)) Yet, the applications of ANNs in the context of ms-QSBER models have been restricted to performing virtual screening tasks.

Bearing in mind all the previous ideas, this chapter intends to demonstrate that computational models based on ANNs can be used in a chemistry-friendly manner to accelerate the design of virtually new, potent, and safe therapeutics at the preclinical level. Thus, we report the first ms-QSBER model based on an ensemble of ANNs (ms-QSBER-EL) devoted to performing virtual design and prediction of potentially active and safe antimicrobial agents. Here, antimalarial drug discovery is used as a case study for a number of reasons. First, malaria is one of the oldest diseases known by mankind, which has an elevated mortality and morbidity; 445 000 deaths and 216 million cases of malaria occurred worldwide in 2016.^([38](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit38)) Second, the efficacy of antimalarial treatments has diminished because *Plasmodium falciparum*, widely recognized as the main causal agent of malaria, has become resistant to antimalarial drugs.^([39](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit39)) Last, there are serious concerns regarding the adverse reactions associated with the use of antimalarial therapeutics.^([40](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit40))

## 16.2 Materials and Methods

### 16.2.1 Dataset and Molecular Descriptors

The development of the ms-QSBER models has been widely reported,^([13](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit13)–[17](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit17),[37](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit37),[41](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit41)) and therefore, only the procedures specific of this work will be explained. All the chemical and biological data employed to build the ms-QSBER-EL model were extracted from the ChEBML database^([42](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit42)–[44](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit44)) in the form of a Microsoft Excel-compatible file. The dataset used in this study contained 18 798 different drugs/chemicals belonging to many diverse chemical families. Each molecule was experimentally assayed by considering 1 out of 7 measures of biological effects (activity, cytotoxicity, and pharmacokinetic properties) and against at least 1 out of 20 targets (including proteins, *Plasmodium falciparum* strains, mammalian cells, and liver microsomes). If a molecule was found to be assayed more than one time against the same target and by considering the same measure of biological effect, its values were averaged. In any case, notice that most of the drugs/chemicals reported in the present dataset were experimentally tested by considering only one measure of biological effect and against only one target. Thus, the dataset used here ended up containing 21 369 statistical cases and so is characterized by a great dispersion of the data. Nevertheless, the great success of the ms-QSBER models mentioned in the previous section is based on their ability to handle greatly dispersed and heterogeneous data.^([13](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit13)–[17](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit17),[37](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit37),[41](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit41),[45](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit45))

Each statistical case in the dataset was annotated as positive \[*BE*[*i*](*c*[*j*])=1\] or negative \[*BE*[*i*](*c*[*j*])=−1\], *BE*[*i*](*c*[*j*]) being a binary categorical variable that described the biological effect of the *ith* case/chemical under the experimental condition *c*[*j*]. It should be pointed out that a defined experimental condition *c*[*j*] depended on both the *qth* measure of biological effect (*me*) reported in a given assay and the *rth* target (*tg*) against which the assay was performed. Therefore, each experimental condition can be expressed as *c*[*j*](*me*, *tg*). The dataset employed in this work contained 23 unique experimental conditions (combinations of the elements *me* and *tg*).

Assignments of positive and negative cases have been realized by considering different cutoff values that are depicted in [Table 16.1](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#tab1); several reasons justify the selection of these rigorous cutoffs. First, an inspection of the dataset extracted from ChEMBL showed that there are FDA-approved drugs reported with biological effects whose values fell either above or below the cutoffs. This aspect highlights the importance of the selected cutoff values because, if a query molecule is predicted as positive (or negative) by a model derived from the present dataset, it will be possible to compare its potential biological effect with those already reported for the clinically relevant drugs. Second, the assignments of the compounds as positive or negative implies that a classification approach was employed instead of a regression one. In contrast to their regression counterparts, classification approaches do not need to predict the exact values of the different properties in a dataset, and, therefore, they do not need to deal with the potentially great uncertainty of the data. Third, the cutoff values selected in this study prevented the imbalance between the number of molecules assigned as positive and the number of molecules annotated as negative. Last, from a phenomenological point of view, even though several clinically relevant antimalarial drugs are present in the dataset, the purpose of the ms-QSBER-EL model is to perform simultaneous predictions and design of new chemicals exhibiting high antimalarial activity, low cytotoxicity, and adequate pharmacokinetic properties. The design of new molecules with chemical structures differing from those present in antimalarial drugs indicates the idea of searching for novel mechanisms of action of antimalarial activity as well as reducing the toxicity and improving the pharmacokinetic profiles not found in most of the current antimalarial drugs.

 

Table 16.1 Different cutoff values of biological effects used in this study.

| Measure of biological effect (*me*) || Cutoff^([a](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#tab1fna)) || Concept || Targets (*tg*) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IC[50] (nM) || ≤370.00 || Concentration required to inhibit at 50% of the growth of the parasite. || *Plasmodium falciparum* strains. |
| Permeability (µcm s^(−1)) || ≥10 || Permeability across the cell membrane. || Caco-2, MDCK, and MDR1-MDCK cells. |
| PPB (%) || ≤85 || Percentage of a chemical bound to plasma proteins. || Plasma from mouse, rat, and human. |
| *t*[1/2] (h)\_Lvm || ≥0.6 || Time required to reduce the concentration of a chemical to half of its initial value in liver microsomes. || Liver microsomes from rat and human. |
| *t*[1/2] (h)\_Plm || ≥1.5 || Time required to reduce the concentration of a chemical to half of its initial value in plasma. || Plasma from mouse, rat, and human. |
| CC[50] (nM) || ≥25 000 || Cytotoxic concentration causing death to 50% of viable cells. || Different mammalian cells from hamster, mouse, rat, and human. |
| IC[50] (nM)\_HERG || ≥10 000 || Concentration causing 50% inhibition of the ion channel HERG. || The ion channel known as HERG. |

^(*a*) Values from which a chemical was assigned as positive.

To characterize the chemical structures of the molecules present in the dataset, we calculated the molecular descriptors known as the total \[*TnsAq*[k](*x*)\] and local \[*LnsAq*[k](*x*)*Z*\] atom-based quadratic indices of the non-stochastic matrix.^([46](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit46)) Quadratic indices have been demonstrated to exhibit a greater discriminant power^([47](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit47)) than that shown by combining several families of molecular descriptors calculated by popular programs such as DRAGON.^([48](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit48)) The quadratic indices can be calculated according to the following mathematical formalism:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00398-t1.jpg)(16.1)

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00398-t2.jpg)(16.2)

In [eqn (16.1)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn1) and [(16.2)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn2), the element *x* accounts for any atomic physicochemical property such as hydrophobicity (HYD), electronegativity (E), atomic weight (AW), polarizability (POL), and polar surface area (PSA). At the same time, in [eqn (16.1)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn1), the element ![inline](images/bk9781788017893-00398-t3.jpg)characterizes the adjacency between any two atoms of the molecule, while in [eqn (16.2)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn2), ![inline](images/bk9781788017893-00398-t4.jpg)has a similar meaning, except for the fact that it focuses on specific types of atoms (*Z*) such as hydrogen bond acceptors or donors, carbon atoms (both aliphatic and aromatic), and others. Both classes of atom-based quadratic indices consider an atom *i* and its chemical environment (composed of the *jth* neighbors) at the topological distance *d*\=*k*.

To calculate the aforementioned topological indices, the file containing the SMILES codes of all the molecules was manually changed from \*.txt to \*.smi. After, the software Standardizer v19.18.0 was used to transform the SMILES codes to sdf format.^([49](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit49)) The only purpose of converting to sdf format was to obtain the connectivity table for each molecule; no additional standardization actions were used. The sdf file was used as input to calculate quadratic indices by means of the software QuBiLS-MAS v1.0^([47](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit47),[50](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit50)) For such a calculation, the software QuBiLS-MAS v1.0 employed a predefined configuration \[algebraic form: quadratic; constrains: atom-based; matrix forms: non-stochastic; maximum order: 6; cutoff: keep all; groups: total and local (hydrogen bond acceptors, aliphatic carbon atoms, aromatic carbons, terminal methyl groups, halogens, and heteroatoms); properties: already mentioned in the previous paragraph; aggregation: Manhattan distance\].

In [eqn (16.1)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn1) and [(16.2)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn2), the quadratic indices cannot differentiate the chemical structure of a molecule when this is tested by considering multiple measures of the biological effects and against different targets. Fortunately, the ms-QSBER models resolve this issue by applying the Box-Jenkins operators^([17](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit17),[37](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit37),[51](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit51)) to generate new molecular descriptors able to consider both the chemical structure and the set of experimental conditions (*e.g.*, target, the measure of activity, or toxicity, *etc.*) against which a molecule has been assayed:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00398-t5.jpg)(16.3)

In [eqn (16.3)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn3), *n*(*c*[*j*]) is the number of molecules annotated as positive, which were assayed under the same experimental condition *c*[*j*]*, i.e.*, by considering both the same measure of biological effect and the same target.^([52](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit52)) In addition, *QI*[*a*] refers to any quadratic index (total or local), while *avgQI*(*c*[*j*]) is the arithmetic mean of the *QI*[*a*] values for all the molecules assigned as positive and tested under the same assay condition *c*[*j*]. In a second step related to the application of the Box-Jenkins operators, the following expression is used:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00398-t6.jpg)(16.4)

In [eqn (16.4)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn4), *DQI*[*a*](*c*[*j*]) measures how much a molecule structurally deviates from a set of chemicals assigned as positive, all of them being tested under the same assay condition *c*[*j*]. On the other hand, *QI*[*MX*] and *QI*[*MN*] represent the maximum and minimum values for a defined molecular descriptor, respectively; they don't depend on the experimental conditions. Last, *p*(*c*[*j*]) is the *a priori* probability of finding a chemical tested under a specific experimental condition *c*[*j*]:

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00398-t7.jpg)(16.5)

In [eqn (16.5)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn5), the element *n*(*c*[*j*]) has been defined in [eqn (16.3)](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#eqn3), and *N*[*T*] refers to the total number of cases/chemicals present in the training set.

### 16.2.2 Building the Ms-QSBER\_EL model

The steps leading to the generation of the present ms-QSBER-EL model are depicted in [Figure 16.1](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fig1). The dataset formed by the 21 369 cases/chemicals was randomly split into two series: training and test sets. The training set was used to search for the best model and was formed by 6591 cases assigned as positive and 9571 annotated as negative, making a total of 16 162 cases (75.63% of the dataset). The purpose of the test set was to validate the model by assessing its predictive power; this set was formed by 5207 cases (24.37%), 2064 annotated as positive and 3143 assigned as negative.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00398-f1.jpg)

Figure 16.1 Workflow focused on the development and application of the ms-QSBER-EL model. The abbreviation “INTPN” stands for interpretation, which is given for each molecular descriptor from a physicochemical and structural point of view.

To find the best the ms-QSBER-EL model, the two most popular ANN architectures were tested: radial basis function (RBF) and multi-layer perceptron (MLP). The ANN package available in the software STATISTICA v13.5.0.17 was employed to generate the ms-QSBER-EL model.^([53](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit53)) When using the ANN package, the first run was performed to assess the appropriateness of three elements: 1) the most significant ANN architectures, 2) the most influential molecular descriptors, and 3) the correlation between the descriptors.

From one side, the most significant ANN architectures were determined by analyzing the training and test errors (as low as possible) and the values of different statistical indices (set to be as high as possible) such as sensitivity \[*Sn*(%)\], specificity \[*Sp*(%)\], accuracy \[*Ac*(%)\], and the Matthews’ correlation coefficient (*MCC*).^([54](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit54)) These statistical indices were used to estimate the internal quality (training set) and the predictive power (test set) of the ms-QSBER-EL model.

On the other hand, the most influential molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model were assessed by means of a sensitivity analysis, which was performed by the software STATISTICA v13.5.0.17. This analysis was applied as a variable selection strategy, quantifying the effect of each molecular descriptor by calculating its sensitivity/importance value (*SV*). In this context, *SV* was calculated as the error generated in a defined ANN when estimating the value of a molecular descriptor using a missing value procedure, divided by the error generated in that ANN by using the real value of the same molecular descriptor. Only those molecular descriptors with *SV*\>1 were considered to enter in the ms-QSBER-EL model. Also, when selecting the most significant descriptors, the correlation between them was assessed by calculating the Pearson's correlation coefficient (*PCC*),^([55](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit55)) and the cutoff interval used to indicate the lack of redundancy/correlation was −0.7<*PCC* < 0.7.

As defined in the introductory section, the abbreviation “ms-QSBER-EL” stands for multi-scale model for quantitative structure-biological effect relationships combined with ensemble learning. Therefore, as the final step in the development of the ms-QSBER-EL model, instead of selecting a single ANN, the best ensemble of ANNs was chosen. This comes from the fact that when solving a particular problem, and by providing a consensus response, models based on ensembles of different ANNs can often perform better than the single ANNs from which they were created.^([56](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit56))

## 16.3 Results and Discussion

### 16.3.1 Ms-QSBER-EL model

The best ms-QSBER-EL model developed in this work was an ensemble comprised of three ANNs with the profiles MLP 8-61-2, MLP 8-67-2, and MLP 8-80-2. The first ANN was constructed by using the logistic function in the hidden layer and softmax function for the output layer. The second and third ANNs had the same activation function in the hidden layer (hyperbolic tangent). For the output layer, the second ANN employed a logistic function while for the third ANN, the softmax function was employed. Notice that all the ANNs contain 8 nodes (molecular descriptors) in the input layer. The number two is the same for all of them in the output layer because they are all predicting the two possible labels (the values −1 and 1) of the categorical variable of biological effect \[*BE*[*i*](*c*[*j*])\]. In any case, the three ANNs have a different number of neurons in their hidden layers. The symbols and definitions of each molecular descriptor present in the ms-QSBER-EL model are reported in [Table 16.2](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#tab2), while all the chemical and biological data are available in the **Supplementary Information 16.1**.^([†](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fn1)) The files corresponding to the three ANNs can be obtained upon request to the author.

 

Table 16.2 Molecular descriptors present in the ms-QSBER-EL model.

| Molecular Descriptor^([a](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#tab2fna)) || Definition |
| --- | --- |
| ***D*\[*TnsAq*6(*AW*)\]*c*[*j*]** || Deviation of the total non-stochastic (atom-based) quadratic index of order 6 weighted by the atomic weight. |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*1(*POL*)*A*\]*c*[*j*]** || Deviation of the local non-stochastic (atom-based) quadratic index of order 1 weighted by the polarizability. This descriptor focuses on the atoms acting as hydrogen bond acceptors and their chemical environments. |

| ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*E*)*G*\]*c*[*j*]** || Deviation of the local non-stochastic (atom-based) quadratic index of order 2 weighted by the electronegativity. This descriptor focuses on the halogens and their chemical environments. |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*1(*POL*)*G*\]*c*[*j*]** || Deviation of the local non-stochastic (atom-based) quadratic index of order 1 weighted by the polarizability. This descriptor focuses on the halogens and their chemical environments. |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*AW*)*M*\]*c*[*j*]** || Deviation of the local non-stochastic (atom-based) quadratic index of order 6 weighted by the atomic weight. This descriptor focuses on the methyl groups and their chemical environments. |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*AW*)*P*\]*c*[*j*]** || Deviation of the local non-stochastic (atom-based) quadratic index of order 2 weighted by the atomic weight. This descriptor focuses on the aromatic carbons and their chemical environments. |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*HYD*)*Y*\]*c*[*j*]** || Deviation of the local non-stochastic (atom-based) quadratic index of order 6 weighted by the hydrophobicity. This descriptor focuses on the heteroatoms and their chemical environments. |

^(*a*) All these descriptors depend on the chemical structure and the experimental condition *c*[*j*]; the latter gives information regarding the *q*th measure of biological effect employed in the assay (*me*) and the *rt*h target (*tg*) against which the molecules were tested. Thus, *c*[*j*] can be expressed as *c*[*j*](*me*,*tg*).

The ms-QSBER-EL model had *Ac*(%)=91.13% in the training set, meaning that 14 728 out of 16 162 cases were correctly classified, while the same statistical index in the test set was equal to 89.86% (4679 correctly classified cases/chemicals out of 5207). The other statistical indices mentioned in the previous section support the good performance displayed by the ms-QSBER-EL model. Thus, in [Table 16.3](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#tab3), for both training and test sets, *Sn*(%)>85% while *Sp*(%)>90%. Also, the statistic *MCC* is higher than 0.75. Notice that *MCC* can take values from −1 (poor prediction) to +1 (ideal prediction), with the value 0 characterizing a random predictor. Therefore, it can be inferred that in the ms-QSBER-EL model developed here, there is a strong convergence between the observed and predicted values of the variable of biological effect *BE*[*i*](*c*[*j*]). The classification results are available in **Supplementary Information 16.2**.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fn1))

^(*a*) ***N***[**Positive**] – Total number of molecules annotated as positive; ***N***[**Negative**] – Total number of molecules annotated as negative; ***CC***[**Positive**] – Molecules correctly classified as positive; ***CC***[**Negative**] – Molecules correctly classified as negative; ***Sn*(%)** – Sensitivity (percentage of molecules correctly classified as positive); ***Sp*(%)** – Specificity (percentage of molecules correctly classified as negative); ***MCC*** – Matthews’ correlation coefficient.

One should note that the statistical indices *Sn*(%) and *Sp*(%) reflect only the global performance of the model. The magnitudes \[*Sn*(%)\]*c*[*j*] and \[*Sp*(%)\]*c*[*j*] are the local measures of performance of the ms-QSBER-EL model which depends on each specific experimental condition *c*[*j*](*me*, *tg*). The results obtained from the **Supplementary Information 16.3**^([1](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fn1)) indicate that \[*Sp*(%)\]*c*[*j*]\>84% in both training and test sets, while \[*Sn*(%)\]*c*[*j*] exhibited values higher than 75% for most experimental conditions. For only 3 out of the 23 experimental conditions reported in the dataset, the local measure of sensitivity \[*Sn*(%)\]*c*[*j*] indicated a poor performance. The first two experimental conditions involved cytotoxicity assays (measuring CC[50]) MRC5 and L929 cells, while the third one focused on determining the half-life in human plasma. In any case, the fact that 20 out of 23 experimental conditions (86.96%) were assessed with high \[*Sn*(%)\]*c*[*j*] and \[*Sp*(%)\]*c*[*j*] demonstrates the ability of the ms-QSBER-EL model to integrate and accurately predict antimalarial activity, cytotoxicity, and pharmacokinetic profiles of drugs/chemicals.

### 16.3.2 Applicability Domain

The reliability of the classifications/predictions performed by the ms-QSBER-EL model was estimated by defining its applicability domain according to the descriptor space approach.^([57](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit57)) Classically, when using the applicability domain defined by the descriptor space, all the compounds in the training set are used, and the maximum and minimum values of each descriptor present in the model demarcate the boundaries that should not be surpassed; any compound beyond such boundaries will be considered to be outside the applicability domain. Here, the applicability domain derived from the descriptor space approach was applied only to those chemicals correctly classified by the ms-QSBER-EL model in the training set (**Supplementary Information 16.3**^([1](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fn1))). Using information regarding the maximum and minimum values of the different molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model, local scores were assigned to each molecular descriptor. When the descriptor value of a query molecule was between the aforementioned boundaries, the local score was equal to 1; otherwise, the local score was equal to 0. Subsequently, a total score (TSAD) was defined as the sum of the local scores. As the ms-QSBER-EL model was built from eight molecular descriptors, only those compounds with TSAD=8 were considered to be inside the applicability domain.

### 16.3.3 Gathering Physicochemical and Structural Information from the Molecular Descriptors

Nowadays, it is a common practice to use computational models to perform predictions of large and heterogeneous chemical libraries. As a result, the physicochemical and structural information contained in the molecular descriptors employed to construct the models is often neglected, and no mechanistic interpretation is provided. The ms-QSBER-EL model developed in this work predicts very complex data involving several types of biological effects and different targets. Therefore, it is not possible to gain a mechanistic insight regarding the diverse biological and/or biochemical processes that take place when a molecule interacts with a target, either molecular (*e.g.,* proteins) or non-molecular (cells, subcellular components, and *Plasmodium falciparum* strains). However, even though stereochemistry is not considered by the molecular descriptors of the ms-QSBER-EL model, interpreting these descriptors can help find 2D-molecular patterns that are common to the different biological effects regardless of the targets on which they were measured. The purpose here is to interpret the different molecular descriptors present in the ms-QSBER-EL model from a physicochemical and structural point of view so that it will be possible to get a better understanding regarding the features that a chemical should possess to increase its antimalarial activity while decreasing its cytotoxicity and improving its pharmacokinetic profile. In this sense, the interpretations given in this subsection will be based on the combination of four aspects: a) the analysis of the influence of each molecular descriptor in the ms-QSBER-EL model, b) the elucidation of the tendency of variation of the different molecular descriptors, c) the information content of the molecular descriptors, and d) the application of a fragment-based analysis. The first aspect is illustrated in [Figure 16.2](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fig2), where the molecular descriptors are represented according to their sensitivity values (*SV*). The higher the *SV* of a molecular descriptor, the greater will be its influence in the ms-QSBER-EL model.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00398-f2.jpg)

Figure 16.2 Relative importance of the molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model.

The second aspect is reported in [Table 16.4](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#tab4). It is assumed that, by comparing the class-based mean values of each molecular descriptor, one can estimate how a molecular descriptor should vary to cause an increase of the antimalarial activity, a decrease of the cytotoxicity, and/or enhancement of the pharmacokinetic properties. This approach involving the class-based mean values was first applied by Speck-Planche and coworkers as a way to gather information from the molecular descriptors in non-linear models.^([58](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit58)) It should be emphasized that the aforementioned approach was applied only to the chemicals that were correctly classified in the training set. Basically, for each molecular descriptor, two means are calculated: one for the set of compounds assigned and correctly classified as positive, and the other for the set of chemicals annotated and properly classified as negative. Comparison of the two means for each molecular descriptor permits us to determine if the descriptor value should be increased or diminished. One must always keep in mind that we are dealing here with a non-linear model, and therefore, these tendencies of variations elucidated from the molecular descriptors will be relative. Consequently, the approach used here will probably not contain the entire chemical space that the ms-QSBER-EL model may cover. Nevertheless, the approach is intended to focus on a defined region of the chemical space where the compounds with the desired properties may be found, in this case, potentially active and safe antimalarial agents.

 

Table 16.4 Tendency of variation of the molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model according to the classes-based means approach.

| Symbol  || Mean Values || Tendency^([a](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#tab4fna)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive || Negative |
| ***D*\[*TnsAq*6(*AW*)\]*c*[*j*]** || −0.005 || 0.116 || Decrease |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*1(*POL*)*A*\]*c*[*j*]** || −0.011 || 0.162 || Decrease |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*4(*AW*)*C*\]*c*[*j*]** || 0.004 || 0.009 || Decrease |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*E*)*G*\]*c*[*j*]** || 0.010 || −0.043 || Increase |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*1(*POL*)*G*\]*c*[*j*]** || −0.002 || −0.022 || Increase |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*AW*)*M*\]*c*[*j*]** || −0.006 || 0.061 || Decrease |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*AW*)*P*\]*c*[*j*]** || −0.038 || 0.343 || Decrease |
| ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*HYD*)*Y*\]*c*[*j*]** || −0.003 || 0.062 || Decrease |

^(*a*) Tendency–It indicates the variation (increase or decrease) in the value of a descriptor that can simultaneously lead to the increase of the antimalarial activity, the decrease of the cytotoxicity, and the improvement of the pharmacokinetic properties.

Regarding the third aspect, as commented before, the ms-QSBER-EL model was built from the deviations of the total and local non-stochastic (atom-based) quadratic indices, which are symbolized as *D*\[*TnsAq*[*k*](*x*)\]*c*[*j*] and *D*\[*LnsAq*[*k*](*x*)*Z*\]*c*[*j*], respectively. With *x* being any of the physicochemical atomic properties mentioned above and *c*[*j*] indicating the different experimental conditions, the topological distance (*d=k*, where *k* is the *kth* order of the quadratic index). The topological distance is the number of bonds (without counting the bond multiplicity) that exists between any two atoms. The use of this simple but useful concept helps us to rapidly get an accurate idea of how the different types of atoms (*e.g.*, aliphatic and aromatic carbons, halogens, *etc.*) should be distributed throughout the entire structure of a molecule.

The last aspect is focused on the fact that any topological (graph-based) descriptor calculated for a molecule can be represented as a linear combination of the frequency with which diverse fragments (connected and disconnected) appear in that molecule.^([59](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit59)) Consequently, this property of the topological descriptors allows us to directly define different molecular fragments whose presence contributes positively to variation in the value of any topological index; such fragments can then be used to design new molecules.^([60](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit60)–[62](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit62)) The quadratic indices used in the present study are a class of topological descriptors, and therefore, they comply with the aforementioned property. Thus, while interpreting, we will provide a non-exhaustive but useful list of fragments that are suggested to positively contribute to the corresponding variations of each molecular descriptor in the ms-QSBER-EL model (see [Figure 16.3](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fig3)). In this illustration, we have focused on small molecular fragments, and therefore, only the descriptors based on topological distance *d*≤4 are represented. No fragment-based information will be provided for the descriptors focused on *d*≥4, although the physicochemical and structural interpretations for all of them will be explained.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00398-f3.jpg)

Figure 16.3 Molecular fragments with favorable contributions with respect to the different molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model. Here the symbols refer to: A=F, –OH, or –NH[2]; X=O or –NH–; Z=–OH or –NH[2]; Y=O or –NH–; G=F, Cl, or Br; G[2]\=Cl, Br, or I.

Four out of eight descriptors present in the ms-QSBER-EL model are based on the atomic weight, and this already indicates that the most important factors to simultaneously increase the antimalarial activity, decrease the cytotoxicity, and improve the pharmacokinetic profiles are those associated with steric bulk. Notice that, as a property, molecular weight is associated with the size of the molecules. These descriptors based on the atomic weight will depend on the number of atoms in a molecule; they will have a direct impact on the molecular weight, and consequently, on the size of a molecule. We have ***D*\[*TnsAq*6(*AW*)\]*c***[***j***], which characterizes the decrease of the atomic weight of any two atoms placed at the topological distance equal to six. This is the fifth most significant descriptor in the model, and it indicates a decrease in the number of atoms in the molecule, while the number of heavy atoms (halogens except fluorine) should be reduced as much as possible. In convergence with ***D*\[*TnsAq*6(*AW*)\]*c***[***j***], the descriptor ***D*\[*LnsAq*4(*AW*)*C*\]*c***[***j***] (the fourth most important) also indicates the diminution of the atomic weight of any two atoms but at a topological distance equal to four, with at least one of them being an aliphatic carbon. This means that the number of aliphatic carbons should be decreased, and if they are present in a molecule, they should be placed at the topological distance of 4 with respect to other atoms with low atomic weight (carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen). Therefore, as illustrated in [Figure 16.3](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fig3), aromatic and heteroaromatic rings are highly desirable to decrease the presence of aliphatic carbons, decreasing the value of ***D*\[*LnsAq*4(*AW*)*C*\]*c***[***j***]. A third steric descriptor is ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*AW*)*M*\]*c***[***j***], which provides information regarding the diminution of the atomic weight of any two atoms separated by six bonds (topological distance equal to six), with at least one of these atoms being a carbon from a methyl group. This descriptor has the lowest influence in the ms-QSBER-EL model, and its value can be decreased by reducing the number of methyl groups in the molecules. Last, by analyzing ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*AW*)*P*\]*c***[***j***], we have suggested that the atomic weight of any two atoms (at least one of them being an aromatic carbon) placed at the topological distance equal to two should be diminished. Notice that ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*AW*)*P*\]*c***[***j***] is the second most important molecular descriptor, and the presence of aliphatic portions (or rings) and heteroaromatic rings is beneficial for the diminution of the value of ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*AW*)*P*\]*c***[***j***] (see [Figure 16.3](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fig3)).

Besides the four quadratic indices based on the atomic weights, two other descriptors also provide steric information. One of them is ***D*\[*LnsAq*1(*POL*)*A*\]*c***[***j***], characterizing the diminution of the polarizability of the molecules, which depends on the presence of atoms acting as hydrogen bond acceptors (and their adjacent atoms). This descriptor (the seventh most influential) can be diminished by placing fluorine, nitrogen, and oxygen atoms in the periphery of the molecules. In the specific case of the nitrogen atoms, those belonging to primary and secondary aliphatic amine are preferred. The other descriptor that confirms the importance of the steric effect is ***D***\[***LnsAq*1(*POL*)*G*\]*c***[***j***], focused on the increase of the polarizability of the molecules by considering only halogens and their adjacent atoms. Notice that this is the most important descriptor in the ms-QSBER-EL model (see [Figure 16.2](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fig2)), and that its value can be increased by attaching halogens (specifically Cl, Br, and I) to aromatic carbons (see [Figure 16.3](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fig3)).

As described by ***D***\[***LnsAq*1(*POL*)*G*\]*c***[***j***], the presence of halogens in certain regions of the molecules is crucial for the increase of antimalarial activity, the diminution of cytotoxicity, and the enhancement of the pharmacokinetic properties. This information is supported by ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*E*)*G*\]*c***[***j***], which has the third greatest influence in the ms-QSBER-EL model. This descriptor indicates the increment of the electronegativity in those regions where the topological distance between any two atoms (at least one of them being a halogen) is equal to two.

Finally, we have ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*HYD*)*Y*\]*c***[***j***], which characterizes the decrease of the joint hydrophobic contribution of any two atoms placed at a topological distance equal to six, with one of these atoms being nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, or phosphorus. This descriptor is the sixth most significant in the ms-QSBER-EL model. It should be pointed out that the term “joint hydrophobic contribution” refers to the product of the hydrophobicity values of any two atoms. In this sense, according to the approach reported by Ghose and Crippen,^([63](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit63)) each atom in the molecule is described by its neighboring atoms; hydrogen and halogen atoms are classified by the hybridization and oxidation states of the carbon atom to which they are attached, and for hydrogen atoms, heteroatoms attached to a carbon atom in the α position are further considered. Carbon atoms are classified by their hybridization state and depending on whether their neighbors are carbon or heteroatoms.^([63](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit63))

It can be deduced that there are atoms that, depending on their chemical environments, will have a negative hydrophobic contribution, whereas others will have a positive value in that hydrophobicity scale. Examples of atoms with negative contributions are most aliphatic (saturated) carbons, except for those of the form CHX3, CR2X2, CRX3, and CX4, with X being any electronegative atom (O, N, S, P, Se, halogens). Other atoms with negative hydrophobic contributions are almost all nitrogen atoms except for those belonging to pyrrole, amines with at least two aromatic substituents, and tertiary amines. A similar rule can be applied to the oxygen-containing counterparts of the amines mentioned here. The other atoms not mentioned here will have a positive contribution to the hydrophobicity. For the specific case of aromatic carbons, while Ghose and coworkers report different values of hydrophobicities,^([63](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit63)) here, the programmers of the software QuBiLS-MAS v1.0 set the hydrophobic contribution to zero for these types of atoms. That being said, a few examples of pairs of atoms (at the topological distance equal to six) whose joint hydrophobic contributions diminish the value of ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*HYD*)*Y*\]*c***[***j***] are G with any nitrogen or oxygen (excluding the previous exceptions), where G represents halogen, sulfur, selenium, or phosphorus.

Altogether, the information provided by the molecular descriptors suggests that the presence of halogens is mandatory in the structure of the molecules, but they must be confined to the peripheral regions. In addition, judging by the decrease of the atomic weight characterized by four of the eight descriptors, halogens may be present in the following amount: 1) one iodine, 2) two chlorine, 3) two bromine, 4) one chlorine and one bromine, 5) one fluorine and one bromine, or 6) one fluorine, one chlorine, and one bromine. The presence of heteroaromatic rings substituted with halogen is crucial because they decrease the number of aromatic carbons (decreasing the value of ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*AW*)*P*\]*c***[***j***]), and at the same time, they increase the values of the descriptors ***D***\[***LnsAq*1(*POL*)*G*\]*c***[***j***] and/or ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*E*)*G*\]*c***[***j***]. Examples of such fragments are 2-halopyridines, 2-halopyrimidines, and 2-haloazoles. On the other hand, the molecules should not have methyl groups, and aliphatic carbons may be used linkers between the heteroaromatic portions.

### 16.3.4 Computational Design of Virtually Potent and Safe Antimalarial Chemicals

When predicting external chemical libraries, computational models can perform reliable predictions to some extent. This is because the experimental data often contain uncertainties regarding the conditions under which the assays were carried out. Other factors preventing the full exploitation of the computational models as virtual screening tools are the lack of consensus regarding the definition of the applicability domain, and the non-universality of the molecular descriptors; the latter means that the molecular descriptors can characterize only a reduced fraction of the highly diverse and complex chemical space.

It is also important to keep in mind that most of the models will provide predictions according to predetermined values, which correspond to the descriptors of the molecules that are being predicted. In this context, most of these molecules may not follow the rules of the model. This has nothing to do with the applicability domain or any other method to estimate the reliability of the predictions; it is associated with the fact that in any model, the molecular descriptors in the training set have different degrees of hierarchy, and these embody a phenomenological meaning in the sense of describing the physicochemical and structural features that need to be primarily modified for improving the biological effect under study. Therefore, compounds whose molecular descriptors follow such a degree of the hierarchy/importance in the model are expected to be predicted with a higher accuracy, where the theoretical predictions should better match the experimental results. Although considering the degree of the hierarchy of the molecular descriptors is an aspect neglected by most of the current models devoted to screening vast datasets, recent approaches focused on fragment-based topological design have emphasized its essential role for the optimization of the chemical space.^([61](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit61),[64](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit64)–[67](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit67)) As the molecular descriptors of a predictive computational model are not able to “control” the chemical space to be predicted, it has been proposed that in order to achieve a higher certainty in the predictions, the chemicals must be designed according to the physicochemical and structural interpretations of the molecular descriptors in the models.^([61](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit61),[64](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit64)–[67](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit67))

To prove the veracity of such suggestions and estimate the sensitivity of the ms-QSBER-EL model with respect to small changes in the chemical structures of the molecules, we carried out the following experiment. We designed ten different molecules belonging to different chemical families (see [Figure 16.4](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fig4)) according to the following steps. First, for each designed molecule, some of the fragments mentioned above were used as building blocks or seeds. Second, the designed molecules were assembled by fusing or connecting the fragments. Third, when needed, a series of bioisosteric replacements were made, or some atoms or functional groups were added. Last, a series of molecules were designed by rigorously considering the joint interpretation of the molecular descriptors in the ms-QSBER-EL model (from AMA-001 to AMA-004, AMA-008, and AMA-010), while others were designed from the interpretations retrieved from some of the descriptors (AMA-005 to AMA-007, and AMA-009).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00398-f4.jpg)

Figure 16.4 Chemical structures of the designed molecules.

The results of the predictions (applicability domain included) for all the designed molecules are reported in **Supplementary Information 16.4**.^([1](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#fn1)) In addition, [Table 16.5](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#tab5) illustrates a summary of such predictions, which permits a fast comparison of the different biological profiles of the different molecules. As expected, in general, the molecules from AMA-001 to AMA-004 were predicted as very potent and safe antimalarial agents. Nevertheless, we would like to highlight that although excellent predicted biological profiles of these four molecules were very similar between each other, the molecules AMA-002 and AMA-004 were predicted as negative against the cytotoxicity assay performed on RAW264.7 cells. This happened because, in the case of AMA-002, the presence of the carboxamide group is detrimental to ***D*\[*TnsAq*6(*AW*)\]*c***[***j***], increasing the value of this descriptor (which must decrease). A similar situation can be found in the molecule AMA-004, which in addition, has pyrimidine instead of 1,2,4-triazine; this slightly increases the values of ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*AW*)*P*\]*c***[***j***] and ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*HYD*)*Y*\]*c***[***j***] (they both must decrease).

The unfavorable predictions for AMA-005 and AMA-006 are not surprising at all. First, the two halogen atoms appear in a central region instead of being restricted to the periphery of the molecules. These halogens detrimentally increase the value ***D*\[*TnsAq*6(*AW*)\]*c***[***j***]. At the same time, these two halogen atoms are attached to aliphatic carbons, in contrast to the recommendation of attaching them to aromatic carbons, which would favorably increase the value of ***D***\[***LnsAq*1(*POL*)*G*\]*c***[***j***]. Another important fact is that electronegative atoms such as nitrogen and oxygen appear placed at the topological distance different from two, which decreases the value of the descriptor ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*E*)*G*\]*c***[***j***].

The difference between the predicted biological profiles of AMA-007 and AMA-008 is due to the presence of a fluorine atom in AMA-008, which favorably increases the value of ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*E*)*G*\]*c***[***j***] while also desirably decreasing ***D*\[*TnsAq*6(*AW*)\]*c***[***j***]. In the case of AMA-009, as recommended, the three halogen atoms are in the periphery of the molecules. However, the presence of these three chlorine atoms leads to a noticeable increase in the value of ***D*\[*TnsAq*6(*AW*)\]*c***[***j***]. Notice that according to the joint physicochemical and structural interpretation of the molecular descriptors, only two chlorine atoms are recommended instead of three. Finally, AMA-010 is very different from the other nine molecules, and yet, it was predicted to exhibit high activity, low cytotoxicity, and good pharmacokinetic properties except for its half-life against human plasma. Perhaps a simple modification such as switching the positions of the halogens may lead to an analog of AMA-010 with improvements in the predicted biological profiles.

The differences between the predicted biological effects of the designed molecules demonstrate the sensitivity and discriminatory power of the molecular descriptors used to develop the ms-QSBER-EL model. On the other hand, it is clear that each prediction of the biological effect of a molecule does not depend on a single descriptor but in the combination of all the descriptors present in the model. In any case, some physicochemical properties and structural features have more influence than others, and we have explained them by providing the specific descriptors responsible for the observed differences in the chemical structures of the molecules, which translated in different predicted biological profiles.

The most promising molecules are from AMA-001 to AMA-004, AMA-008, and AMA-010. Because of the potentially high antimalarial activity, low cytotoxicity, and adequate pharmacokinetic properties, we searched these molecules in well-known databases such as ChEMBL, ZINC,^([68](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit68)) and ChemSpider^([69](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit69)) for finding similar molecules. For a similarity cutoff value ≥0.8, only one match was found. In this sense, the molecule ChemSpiderID 51375502 was identified to be similar to AMA-001. However, different structural aspects support the chemical dissimilarity of these two molecules. For instance, ChemSpiderID 51375502 contains a 4-bromopyrimidine ring (instead of the crucial fragment 2-bromopyrimidine reported for AMA-001). Also, ChemSpiderID 51375502 is lacking a second bromine atom in the pyridine ring, instead having an ethyl group. In the end, from the point of view of the physicochemical and structural information extracted from the ms-QSBER-EL model, the 4-bromopyrimidine ring in ChemSpiderID 51375502 is slightly detrimental for the increase of the descriptor ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*E*)*G*\]*c***[***j***]. At the same time, the lack of the second bromine atom also unfavorably affects the values of ***D*\[*LnsAq*2(*E*)*G*\]*c***[***j***] and ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*HYD*)*Y*\]*c***[***j***]. Finally, the presence of the methyl moiety in the ethyl group increases the value of ***D*\[*LnsAq*6(*AW*)*M*\]*c***[***j***], whose undesirable effect has been explained before. Thus, in principle, ChemSpiderID 51375502, although promising, should be slightly less desirable than AMA-001 in terms of antimalarial activity and/or safety.

### 16.3.5 Druglikeness

The druglikeness of each molecule was assessed by verifying the compliance with Lipinski's rule of five,^([70](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit70)) which establishes that, in order to exhibit a good oral bioavailability, a molecule should have no more than 5 hydrogen bond donors (HBD), 10 or fewer hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), a molecular weight (MW) lower than 500 Da, and an octanol-water partition coefficient (logP) not greater than 5. A variant of the Lipinski's rule of five suggests logP in the range −0.4 to +5.6, molar refractivity in the interval 40–130 cm³ mol^(−1), MW in the range 180–480 Da, and the number of atoms (nAT) from 20 to70. In addition, Veber and coworkers suggested that only two aspects should be considered when analyzing the potentially good oral bioavailability of a chemical: the polar surface area (PSA) to be lower than ≤140 Å², and the number of rotatable bonds (RBN) to be ≤10.^([71](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit71)) All the properties mentioned above were calculated for the six most promising molecules mentioned above (see [Table 16.6](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#tab6)) by using the software AlvaDesc v1.0.14.^([72](#BK9781788017893-00398.xhtml#cit72)) From the physicochemical point of view, all the designed molecules were in agreement with the Lipinski's rule of five and its variants.

## 16.4 Conclusion

Malaria is an emerging and unresolved public health problem that can be halted by using the most advanced *in silico* approaches in drug discovery. In this context, computational tools are essential for prioritizing the search for novel, potent, and safe antimalarial agents. The predictive models reported to date should go beyond the conventional purpose of screening large chemical libraries. Special attention must be paid to the physicochemical and structural information that can be gathered from the *in silico* models. The ms-QSBER-EL model developed here is capable of integrating antimalarial activity, cytotoxicity, and pharmacokinetic properties, exhibiting a very good accuracy. The combined use of the physicochemical and structural interpretations of the molecular descriptors and the fragment-based analysis permitted the guided design of virtually new molecules as potent and safe antimalarial chemicals, which are now available to the scientific community as potential leads for future biological testing. This work unveils new horizons for the creation of focused libraries for drug discovery against malaria, with a wide range of applications to other tropical diseases.

CHAPTER 17

Machine Learning for Core-loss Spectrum

T. MIZOGUCHI[\*](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#affc)^([a](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#affa)) AND S. KIYOHARA^([a](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#affa),[b](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#affb))

^a The University of Tokyo, Institute of Industrial Science, Komaba, Tokyo 153-8505, Japan

^b Laboratory for Materials and Structures, Institute of Innovative Research, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Yokohama 226-8503, Japan

\*Email: [teru@iis.u-tokyo.ac.jp](mailto:teru@iis.u-tokyo.ac.jp)

## 17.1 Introduction

Unveiling the atomistic configurations, chemical bonding, and vibrational behaviors of molecules and atoms, which are commonly correlated to the functions of a material, is the most important task of materials research. Spectroscopic techniques, such as diffraction, reflection, emission, and absorption, have been used to identify such information because the spectral features are correlated to the material information.

Among existing spectroscopic techniques, core-loss spectroscopy using electrons or X-rays, namely, electron energy-loss near-edge structure (ELNES) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), offer atomic-scale spatial resolution,^([1](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit1)) nanosecond-level time resolution,^([2](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit2)) and high sensitivity^([3](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit3)) and can be considered the “ultimate analysis” in materials science.^([4](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit4)) ELNES and XANES commonly originate from an electron transition from a core orbital to unoccupied states.^([5](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit5),[6](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit6)) As their electron transitions commonly follow an electron dipole transition rule, their spectral features reflect the partial density of states (PDOS) in unoccupied bands. Thus, ELNES and XANES features provide information on the local coordination and chemical bonding of selected elements in the illuminated area.

ELNES and XANES are used as complementary tools. XANES has the advantage of sensitivity, *i.e.,* it can be observed from an element present at ppm-levels,^([3](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit3),[7](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit7),[8](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit8)) while the main advantage of ELNES is its spatial resolution, *i.e.,* it can be observed from a single atomic column (or even a single atom or buried dopant).^([1](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit1),[9](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit9)–[11](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit11)) The recent emergence of monochromator systems has improved the energy resolution of EELS, which facilitates the identification of vibrational spectra using TEM/STEM systems.^([12](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit12)–[15](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit15)) Thus, ELNES/XANES have been used for the characterization of a wide variety of materials systems, such as semiconductors,^([16](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit16)–[19](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit19)) ceramics,^([20](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit20)–[22](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit22)) batteries,^([23](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit23),[24](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit24)) electrical devices,^([25](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit25)–[27](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit27)) and capacitor materials.^([28](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit28)–[31](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit31))

Instrument development has accompanied advancements in the theoretical simulation of ELNES/XANES. The most important aspect of ELNES/XANES simulation is the introduction of a core hole, which is generated in the core orbital during the electron transition process.^([32](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit32),[33](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit33)) Depending on the position of the core state and excited electron, ELNES/XANES simulation can be categorized into three methods: one-particle method,^([34](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit34)–[37](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit37)) two-particle method,^([38](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit38)–[41](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit41)) and multi-particle method.^([42](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit42)–[45](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit45)) The fundamentals of ELNES/XANES simulation using the one-, two-, and multi-particle methods have been reviewed elsewhere.^([46](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit46)–[49](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit49)) In addition to spectrum simulation, theoretical tools for unveiling the relationships between spectral features and material properties have also been proposed.^([50](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit50),[51](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit51)) By combining experimental and theoretical simulations, one can investigate the valence state,^([52](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit52)) local coordination,^([37](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit37)) liquid/gas molecular vibration,^([53](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit53)–[55](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit55)) lattice vibration,^([56](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit56),[57](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit57)) and van der Waals interaction.^([58](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit58))

Recent years have witnessed a rapid increase in spectral data. ELNES/XANES experiments often involve time-resolved and/or spatially resolved observations. For instance, spatially resolved ELNES allows spectral imaging with a resolution of several thousand points in an objective area. In XANES, pico- or nano-second time-resolved observations are possible, and time-resolved experiments for tracing chemical reactions have been performed. Through such spatially/temporally resolved ELNES/XANES observations, up to tens of thousands of spectra can be observed in an experimental session. Individual interpretation through theoretical calculations is infeasible because each ELNES/XANES calculation not only requires extensive experimental and theoretical knowledge but also involves many computations.

Recently, approaches for gaining new insights from big data, namely data-driven approaches, have attracted considerable attention in materials science.^([59](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit59)–[63](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit63)) Analysis based on machine learning (ML) can overcome the limitations of manual multi-dimensional big data analysis. ML is extensively used for materials simulations, characterizations, and discoveries. Such data-driven approaches have facilitated the discovery of desired structures with minimum computation,^([64](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit64),[65](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit65)) new materials with high efficiency,^([66](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit66)–[69](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit69)) and information that could not be previously determined through experiments^([70](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit70),[71](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit71)) or simulations.^([72](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit72),[73](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit73)) ML has also been applied to experimental observations.^([74](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit74)–[76](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit76)) It allows the interpretation of many more spectra compared with manual analysis, as well as the prediction of a scalar value or discrete values in a simple spectrum, such as a chemical shift or peaks in NMR spectra.^([74](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit74)–[76](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit76)) In addition, it has been applied to X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) and extended XAFS (EXAFS) spectra.^([71](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit71),[77](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit77))

We have reported the applications of ML for materials characterizations. In particular, we have used ML to investigate crystalline interfaces^([64](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit64),[65](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit65),[78](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit78)–[82](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit82)) and ELNES/XANES spectra.^([83](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit83),[84](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit84))

This chapter reviews our data-driven approaches for the ELNES/XANES spectrum. First, we review spectrum interpretation and prediction by combining unsupervised hierarchical clustering with supervised decision tree classification.^([83](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit83)) In this method, a “two-tree” comprising a dendrogram obtained by hierarchical clustering and another tree for decision tree classification is used to interpret and predict ELNES/XANES spectra. In addition, we use ML to directly quantify the structures and properties of materials from the spectra.^([84](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit84)) A feedforward neural network is used to predict the local structures, chemical bonding, and transition energy from only the spectral features. Furthermore, the effect of noise on the prediction accuracy is discussed. Finally, data augmentation is used to construct a prediction model that is robust against noise.

## 17.2 Methodology

### 17.2.1 Spectrum Database Construction

This section mainly reviews two tasks: spectral interpretation/prediction and property prediction. To avoid accidental errors and noise, we first constructed the spectrum database *via* simulation (the experimental spectrum and the effect of noise are discussed later). CASTEP^([85](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit85),[86](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit86)) code was used for the ELNES/XANES calculation, which is based on a first-principles plane-wave-basis pseudopotential method. The oxygen K-edge of oxide materials was simulated. Generalized gradient approximation (GGA) of the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional^([87](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit87)) was selected to approximate the exchange–correlation functional, and the cutoff energy was set to 500 eV. To introduce core-hole effects, an excited pseudopotential was generated and applied to the excited oxygen atom in the supercell. To minimize interactions among excited atoms under periodic boundary conditions, sufficiently large supercells (>10 Å) were used in all the cases. The calculated spectrum was obtained by calculating the transition probability based on the Fermi's golden rule. The theoretical transition energy was also simulated similarly to a previous study.^([86](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit86)) The details of the calculated spectra are described below.

### 17.2.2 Spectral Data Clustering

Hierarchical clustering^([88](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit88)) was used to categorize the spectral data. Initially, each spectrum was assigned to its own cluster. Then, the two most similar clusters were combined into a single cluster. The clustering process was repeated until a single cluster was obtained. The similarity was estimated based on the cosine distance between a pair of spectra, which is often used for measuring spectral similarity.^([89](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit89),[90](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit90))

The clustering linkage scheme for measuring the cluster similarity was the “completed” method for the “two-tree” method. In this study, as we directly compared the spectral features, the onsets of all the spectra were aligned to each other. The double differential of the spectrum was used to estimate the position of the onset.

### 17.2.3 Decision Tree for Material Information

A decision tree visualizes classification or regression results using a tree structure. By repeatedly dividing the data into two or more subsets, the decision tree is composed of certain subsets with labels, which are the same as the labels in the training data. As this approach is a type of supervised learning, training labels are necessary. The labels obtained by spectral clustering were used as the training data. The classification and regression tree (CART) algorithm^([91](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit91),[92](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit92)) was used for training.

### 17.2.4 Feedforward Neural Network

Property prediction from the spectral features was performed using a feedforward neural network. A feedforward neural network is the simplest type of neural network. It was selected for this study because it can accommodate high-dimensional input data, such as spectra, and incorporate interactions between them in a non-linear manner. We used backpropagation, based on the Adam scheme,^([93](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit93)) to optimize all the learning parameters in the network, thereby minimizing the mean absolute errors between the model outputs and the training targets. A rectified linear unit (ReLU) was used as the activation function, and the dropout rate was fixed at 0.5 in the hidden layers not linked with the output layer. The hyperparameters, *i.e.*, the number of hidden layers and the regularization parameters, were tuned *via* five-fold cross-validation using the validation datasets.

## 17.3 Results and Discussion

### 17.3.1 Overview of the Data-driven Prediction and Interpretation Method

The proposed data-driven spectral analysis is schematically illustrated in [Figure 17.1(a)–(c)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig1). First, a spectral database, in which each spectrum has a one-to-one correspondence with its material information, was constructed as shown in [Figure 17.1(a)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig1).

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00424-f1.jpg)

Figure 17.1 Strategy for data-driven prediction and interpretation of spectra. Schematics of (a) the spectral database and structures, which have one-to-one correspondence, (b) spectral clustering, and (c) structural classification with the spectral groups as the training data. Adapted from ref. [83](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit83), [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6](http://https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6), under the terms of the CC BY 4.0 licence, [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/](http://https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

As described above, we constructed the spectrum database *via* theoretical simulation. After creating the database, the included spectra are divided into groups according to their “similarity” using hierarchical cluster analysis, which divides spectral data into tree-shaped clusters called “dendrogram”. A dendrogram is schematically shown in [Figure 17.1(b)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig1); the vertical axis corresponds to the “dissimilarity” of the spectra.

In the final step, the materials are classified into some groups by a decision tree based on the material information, such as the bond length, coordination number, the group in the periodic table, and valency. In the example shown in [Figure 17.1(c)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig1), the objective materials are classified using the material information such as “trivalent”: true/false and “long bond length”: true/false. The most important aspect of our method is the classification of the materials into spectral groups, which are used as the training labels for classification. As the decision tree for materials is based on the spectral groups, it establishes a correlation between the material information and the spectral features. In the decision tree for material information (see [Figure 17.1(c)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig1)), the branch points provide the “characteristic” descriptors for classifying the spectra, as discussed later.

Our method uses two trees: the dendrogram (see [Figure 17.1(b)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig1)) and the decision tree (see [Figure 17.1(c)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig1)). The two trees, related to spectrum classification and material information, are correlated with each other because the decision tree is constructed based on spectrum classification. After the two-tree is constructed, the ELNES/XANES spectra can be predicted and interpreted. The strategy for the prediction and interpretation of the spectra is schematically shown in [Figure 17.2](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig2)(a) and (b), respectively.

![image](images/bk9781788017893-00424-f2.jpg)

Figure 17.2 Conceptual schemes of (a) “downstream” spectral prediction and (b) “upstream” spectral interpretation. Adapted from ref. [83](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit83), [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6](http://https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-30994-6), under the terms of the CC BY 4.0 licence, [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/](http://https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

Consider a situation in which the atomic configuration of an objective material is known, but its ELNES/XANES spectral profiles are unknown. Such situations often occur because we generally predict the spectral profile prior to making observations to validate the experiment and sample conditions. For the prediction, we apply geometric and element information, such as the bond length, angles, and valence state, to the material information decision tree (right side of [Figure 17.2(a)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig2)).

Hence, the decision tree becomes a true/false diagram (flowchart), *e.g.*, the true/false diagrams for trivalence and the bond length, as shown in [Figure 17.2(a)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig2). Moving down the true/false diagram using the material (geometric and elemental) information, we arrive at any one of the labels, clusters 1, 2, or 3, as shown in [Figure 17.2(a)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig2). As the decision tree for the material information is correlated to that for the spectrum, the objective spectrum should be similar to that in the cluster. This “downstream” method corresponds to the “prediction” of the unknown spectrum of a known structure.

Next, we describe the interpretation using the two-tree. First, we define the “interpretation” of ELNES/XANES. ELNES/XANES spectra reflect the atomic and electronic structures; thus, the “interpretation of the ELNES/XANES spectrum” corresponds to the determination of the relationship between the spectrum and the atomic and electronic structures.

Consider a situation in which a spectrum of an unknown area/material is observed. In this case, we need to interpret the spectrum, *i.e.*, the relationship between the spectral profile and the material information, such as the bond length and coordination number, needs to be determined. For such interpretation, we again use the two-tree; however, we move up the decision tree as shown in [Figure 17.2(b)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig2).

The strategy for the interpretation is schematically shown in [Figure 17.2(b)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig2). For the ELNES/XANES spectrum of an unknown area/material, the cluster in the spectrum tree that is the most similar to the observed spectrum is first determined. By measuring the dissimilarity between the objective spectrum and all the other spectra in the database, we select the most resembling spectrum to be the most similar to the objective spectrum. In the example shown in [Figure 17.2(b)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig2), assume that the observed spectrum is the most similar to a spectrum in Cluster 3 (red box). Then, by moving up the material information tree starting from Cluster 3, geometric and elemental information, such as the bond length and valency, can be obtained from the branch of the decision tree. Then, the spectrum is interpreted using such atomic and electronic structure information. In the case of [Figure 17.2(b)](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig2), we can determine that the observed spectrum is obtained from a material that has a “short bond length” and is “trivalent”.

The branching points in a decision tree play a critical role in the interpretation, *i.e.*, when the most similar spectral cluster has been determined, the objective material can be expected to have a structure similar to that of the materials in the cluster. However, the “characteristic” information of the corresponding cluster cannot be obtained. The branching points in the decision tree provide the “characteristic” information of the materials in the corresponding cluster.

In the next section, we describe the use of this two-tree method for the prediction and interpretation of oxygen K-edge (O-K edge) ELNES/XANES. The O-K edges are selected because they can be easily calculated using the one-particle method based on density functional theory (DFT) under the GGA framework, and they basically provide all the information for the conduction band.^([46](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit46),[47](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit47),[50](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#cit50))

### 17.3.2 Demonstration Using the O-K Edges of Mono-metal Oxides

We calculated 39 O-K edges of oxide materials, including 14 of mono-metal oxides (listed in [Table 17.1](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#tab1)) and 25 of polymorphous SiO[2] (listed in [Table 17.2](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#tab2)). The 14 mono-metal oxides were selected because they do not have “complex” electronic structures, such as partially occupied 3d-orbitals, or magnetic properties. SiO[2] was selected because it has several polymorphs and wide applications. The 14 O-K edge spectra of the mono-metal oxides were used to demonstrate our method. The actual interpretation and prediction were performed using the 25 O-K edge spectra of polymorphous SiO[2].

By cutting the dendrogram horizontally at a certain level, we can obtain a set of clusters. The selection of the cutting level is arbitrary; we selected the level indicated by the dashed line in the dendrogram, resulting in four clusters, Cluster 1 to Cluster 4 (see [Figure 17.4](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig4)). Eight parameters were selected as descriptors for the decision tree: (1) valence of the cation, (2) group and (3) period in the periodic table, coordination number of the (4) anion and (5) cation, and the number of (6) s, (7) p, and (8) d electrons of the cation in the valence and semi-core states. [Figure 17.5](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig5) shows the constructed decision tree based on supervised learning; the decision tree divided the 14 oxides into two subsets according to whether they initially had d electrons and whether the “1^(st) element or not” divided a subset and the “4th element or not” divided the other. The two constructed trees, shown in [Figures 17.4](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig4) and [17.5](#BK9781788017893-00424.xhtml#fig5), were used for interpretation.
